Christians are called to humble service and sacrificial love, yet Scripture never equates that with becoming a doormat who enables sin, neglects God-given responsibilities, or lives for human approval. Jesus Himself modeled this balance perfectly: He washed feet and laid down His life, yet He also rebuked hypocrisy, withdrew from demanding crowds to pray, and spoke hard truths without apology (Mark 1:35-38; Matthew 23; John 2:13-17). Meekness is strength under control, not weakness or perpetual yielding.

The root issue is often people-pleasing, which Scripture treats as a form of idolatry. Paul asks, “Am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10). Our identity and worth are secured in Christ’s finished work, not in others’ opinions or demands. When we forget justification by grace alone through faith alone, we start performing for people instead of resting in Him. Loving your neighbor includes loving them enough to tell the truth and refuse to participate in what harms them or you (Ephesians 4:15; Proverbs 27:5-6).

Healthy boundaries flow from wisdom and stewardship, not selfishness. Jesus sent His disciples out as “sheep in the midst of wolves,” telling them to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16). Guard your heart diligently (Proverbs 4:23). Say a clear yes or no (Matthew 5:37). Do not enable laziness or exploitation: “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Forgive freely as you have been forgiven, yet forgiveness does not always mean restored access or the removal of consequences. Turn the other cheek regarding personal insults (Matthew 5:39), but protect the vulnerable, including yourself and your household, as a matter of faithful stewardship.

Practically, begin by anchoring daily in who you are in Christ through Scripture and prayer rather than reacting to every request. Ask God for wisdom (James 1:5) and the courage to speak truth in love. Practice gracious, firm refusals: “I cannot take that on right now,” or “That would not be best for either of us.” Involve mature believers in your local church for counsel and accountability; isolation makes doormat patterns worse. If patterns of manipulation or abuse are present, seek help from elders or a certified biblical counselor promptly.

This is not a call to hardness of heart but to Christlike clarity. Serve gladly where the Spirit leads, rest in God’s approval, and refuse to let fear of man rule you (Proverbs 29:25). A concrete next step: open Galatians 1 and Matthew 10 this week, pray through them asking the Lord to show you one relationship where you need clearer boundaries, then discuss it with a trusted brother or sister in your church.

question: What does it mean that the workers are few (Matthew 9:37)?
answer:
**In Matthew 9:37, Jesus means that multitudes of people are ready to hear the gospel and be gathered into God’s kingdom (the plentiful harvest), yet far too few of His followers are actively laboring to proclaim the good news, make disciples, and care for souls.**

Jesus speaks these words right after seeing the crowds and having compassion on them, because they were “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36). The harvest image draws from ordinary agricultural life in first-century Israel: a ripe field will spoil if no one gathers it in time. Spiritually, it points to people whose need for the Savior is urgent and whose hearts God has prepared. The “workers” (or laborers) are those who go out in His name—preaching repentance and faith, teaching the Word, praying, serving, and shepherding.

This is not a complaint about God’s power or the gospel’s effectiveness. It is a sober assessment of the church’s responsibility. Jesus immediately adds the remedy: “Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest” (Matthew 9:38). Prayer is the first work, because only the Lord of the harvest can raise up, equip, and thrust out laborers. The parallel in Luke 10:2 shows the same urgency when Jesus sends the seventy-two. The need continues through the Great Commission: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19), and through Paul’s question, “How can they hear without someone to preach?” (Romans 10:14).

The statement exposes two realities at once. First, God has a vast harvest of elect people still to be reached; His compassion and saving purpose have not failed. Second, ordinary believers are called to join the work rather than leave it to a few specialists. Faithful labor includes personal evangelism, discipleship in the local church, supporting missions, and persevering prayer—not merely professional ministry.

A concrete next step is to pray daily, by name if possible, for the Lord to raise up and send workers into specific fields you know (your neighborhood, workplace, an unreached people group, or your own church’s outreach). Then ask Him how you yourself might step into the harvest this week—perhaps by sharing a clear testimony of Christ’s death and resurrection, inviting someone to read the Gospels with you, or serving in a way that opens doors for the gospel. The same Lord who saw the crowds still sees them, and He delights to use those who answer His call.

question: What was the purpose of the Levitical Law?
answer:
The Levitical Law (the statutes given through Moses, especially in Leviticus) was given to reveal God’s holiness, set Israel apart as His covenant people, expose human sin, regulate their worship and daily life, and point forward to the perfect sacrifice and priesthood of Jesus Christ.

God declared the central aim when He said, “For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44; see also Leviticus 19:2). The detailed commands about sacrifices, purity, priesthood, and festivals trained Israel to approach a holy God only through atonement and mediation, while marking them off from the surrounding nations as “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:5–6).

The New Testament clarifies the Law’s deeper purposes. It was “added because of transgressions” (Galatians 3:19) and functions as a mirror that brings “knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20; Romans 7:7). In this way it served as a guardian or tutor “to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith” (Galatians 3:24). Every sacrifice, priest, and purity rite foreshadowed the once-for-all atonement and perfect high priesthood of Jesus, who fulfilled the Law and inaugurated the new covenant (Hebrews 7–10; Matthew 5:17).

For believers today the ceremonial and civil aspects of the Levitical code have been fulfilled in Christ and are no longer binding as covenant stipulations, yet the moral will of God revealed in the Law continues to instruct us in holiness as we walk by the Spirit. The Law still drives us to the cross, where Jesus bore the curse we deserved, and then teaches us how to live as those already declared righteous by faith alone. 

A simple next step is to read Leviticus 16 (the Day of Atonement) alongside Hebrews 9–10, asking the Lord to deepen your gratitude for the finished work of Christ.

question: What does the Bible say about confession of sin to a priest?
answer:
The Bible teaches that confession of sin is directed first and foremost to God Himself, who alone forgives sin, and it also calls believers to confess sins to one another for mutual prayer and healing. It does not establish a special class of priests to whom sins must be confessed in order to receive forgiveness.

Scripture is clear that God alone forgives sins. First John 1:9 says, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” Psalm 32:5 records David’s pattern: “Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,’ and You forgave the guilt of my sin.” Jesus Christ is the one Mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5), and He is our great High Priest who has offered the once-for-all sacrifice for sin (Hebrews 4:14–16; Hebrews 7:27; Hebrews 10:11–14). Because of His finished work, every believer has direct access to the throne of grace.

The New Testament also encourages horizontal confession among believers. James 5:16 instructs, “Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.” This is mutual, not hierarchical; it takes place within the body of Christ for accountability, restoration, and prayer, not as a sacramental requirement for absolution.

Some historic Christian traditions, particularly Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy, understand certain passages (such as John 20:22–23, where Jesus tells the apostles, “If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven; if you withhold forgiveness from anyone, it is withheld,” and Matthew 16:19; Matthew 18:18) as authorizing ordained priests to hear confessions and pronounce absolution in Christ’s name as part of the sacrament of penance. They see continuity with the Old Testament priesthood and view the priest as acting in persona Christi.

From a Reformed Baptist reading of Scripture, those texts commission the apostles (and by extension the church) to declare the terms of forgiveness already secured by Christ—the gospel itself—rather than instituting a continuing mediatorial priesthood that stands between the believer and God. The New Testament presents the priesthood of all believers (1 Peter 2:5; 1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6) and the unique, unrepeatable high priesthood of Christ. Forgiveness is received by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not through a human priestly act (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:1). Confession to a pastor or mature brother or sister can be wise and biblical for accountability and counsel, yet it is never required as the means of obtaining God’s pardon.

Practically, if you are carrying guilt, go first to the Lord in honest prayer, naming your sin and resting in Christ’s finished work. Then, where appropriate, seek out a trusted fellow believer or elder in your local church for confession, prayer, and encouragement toward repentance and obedience. That pattern honors both the vertical and horizontal dimensions the Bible actually teaches.

question: Should Christians go to nightclubs? Is clubbing a sin?
answer:
**No, clubbing is not named as a sin in Scripture the way drunkenness, sexual immorality, or idolatry are, yet many faithful Christians wisely avoid nightclubs because the typical environment so often pulls against holiness, purity, and a clear witness for Christ.**

This falls in the category of Christian liberty and personal wisdom rather than a direct command that defines orthodoxy. Faithful believers can and do reach different conclusions here without one side being “less Christian.” Scripture gives clear principles but does not list every modern venue, so we apply the Bible’s teaching on the heart, the body, the world, and love for others (Romans 14:1–23; 1 Corinthians 8–10).

Two common historic Christian approaches illustrate the range:
- One view holds that nightclubs, as commonly experienced, are so saturated with drunkenness, sensual dancing, crude music, and sexual provocation that a Christian should simply stay away for the sake of purity and testimony. The call to “come out from among them and be separate” and not to love the world’s lusts (2 Corinthians 6:17; 1 John 2:15–17) is applied directly to such settings.
- Another view stresses liberty of conscience: if a believer can attend without getting drunk, lusting, causing a weaker brother or sister to stumble, or compromising their own walk, and if their motive is truly neutral fellowship or celebration rather than fleshly indulgence, then it is not automatically forbidden. “Everything is permissible, but not everything is beneficial” and “whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:23, 31) become the governing tests.

I lean toward the first approach as the safer and more consistent path for most believers. Nightclubs are rarely neutral spaces; they are usually designed around alcohol-fueled sensuality, darkness that hides rather than exposes sin, and music that normalizes what God calls us to flee. Scripture repeatedly warns us to flee sexual immorality, not to get drunk with wine but be filled with the Spirit, to make no provision for the flesh, and to remember that bad company corrupts good character (1 Corinthians 6:18–20; Ephesians 5:18; Romans 13:14; 1 Corinthians 15:33). The atmosphere itself often makes those commands harder, not easier, to obey. Progressive sanctification means the Holy Spirit is conforming us to Christ’s likeness; environments that constantly stir the opposite desires work against that grace.

Ask yourself concrete questions before deciding:  
- Can I honestly glorify God there with my eyes, ears, body, and conversations?  
- Would I be comfortable if Jesus walked in beside me, or if my pastor or a new believer saw me?  
- Does this help me love God and neighbor more, or does it feed old patterns I am called to put to death?  
- Am I free, or am I rationalizing?

If the honest answers raise red flags, joyfully choose something better—hospitality with brothers and sisters, a clean celebration, outdoor fellowship, or simply resting in the ordinary means of grace. Talk it over with mature believers in your local church who know you; elders and older saints can give counsel tailored to your situation. Pray through passages like Psalm 1, Romans 12:1–2, and Philippians 4:8, asking the Lord to align your desires with His holiness and to give you wisdom that is pure and peaceable.

Christ died and rose to redeem us from empty ways of living and to make us a people zealous for good works. That freedom is far richer than any dance floor.

question: Does the statue outside the United Nations have any connection to the beast of the end times?
answer:
**No, the statue outside the United Nations has no connection to the beast of the end times in Scripture.**

The Bible’s descriptions of end-times beasts (especially in Daniel 7 and Revelation 13) are prophetic symbols of successive kingdoms, empires, and a final blasphemous world power that opposes God and persecutes His people. They are not predictions of a modern sculpture. Revelation 13:1–2 describes a beast rising from the sea that combines features “like a leopard,” with “feet like those of a bear,” and “a mouth like the mouth of a lion,” drawing directly from the four beasts in Daniel 7. These images represent political powers and a culminating figure of rebellion, not a literal statue or artwork.

### Why the speculation exists
In 2021 a large bronze sculpture titled “The Guardian of International Peace and Security” (a gift from Mexico) was installed near UN headquarters. It is a chimeric figure blending animal traits in a style inspired by Mexican indigenous art. Some observers noticed a visual resemblance to the composite beast imagery in Daniel and Revelation and began circulating claims that it fulfills or signals biblical prophecy. That resemblance is coincidental and artistic; the Bible never mentions the United Nations, New York, or any such statue. Prophetic texts point to real historical and future kingdoms under God’s sovereign timeline, not to public art installations.

### How Christians should approach this
Eschatology (views of the end times) is a tertiary matter on which faithful believers have differed for centuries—premillennial, amillennial, and other historic frameworks—without compromising the core gospel. Scripture calls us to watchfulness and holiness, not to decode every cultural artifact as a prophetic sign. Jesus Himself warned against date-setting and speculative frenzy (Matthew 24:36; Acts 1:7). The clear center of biblical prophecy is the person and work of Christ: His first coming to die for sinners and rise again, and His personal, bodily return to judge the living and the dead and renew all things.

God remains fully sovereign over nations and history (Daniel 2:21; Psalm 2). The “beast” systems of this age will ultimately fall before the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 17:14; Revelation 19:11–21). Our calling is not to hunt for hidden fulfillments in sculptures but to trust the finished work of Jesus, proclaim the gospel, and live ready for His appearing.

If this question stirs curiosity about biblical prophecy, a wise next step is to read Daniel 7 and Revelation 13 slowly in context, perhaps with a trusted study Bible or alongside mature believers in your local church. Ask the Lord for wisdom and keep the focus on Christ crucified, risen, and returning rather than on internet theories. He is the true Guardian of His people.

question: What is the sign of Jonah?
answer:
The sign of Jonah is the prophetic parallel Jesus Himself drew between Jonah’s three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish and His own death, burial, and resurrection after three days in the heart of the earth.

In Matthew 12:39–40 Jesus answered the scribes and Pharisees who demanded a miraculous sign: “A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.” He repeated the same point in Matthew 16:4 and Luke 11:29–30. The historical account in Jonah 1:17 records that “the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish.” Jesus treats that event as real history and as a deliberate type pointing forward to His own bodily resurrection.

The sign therefore centers on Christ’s victory over death. Jonah’s deliverance from the fish foreshadowed the greater deliverance when Jesus rose bodily on the third day, proving He is the Son of God and confirming that His sacrificial death on the cross truly atoned for sin. The people of Nineveh repented at Jonah’s preaching (Jonah 3:5–10); Jesus warned that those who reject the greater reality—His death and resurrection—stand under greater judgment (Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:32).

This sign calls every hearer to the same response of repentance and faith. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for the forgiveness of sins and new life. If you would like to explore the passages further or talk about what trusting Christ looks like day to day, I am glad to walk through them with you.

question: What does it mean to walk worthy?
answer:
To walk worthy means to live in a manner that matches the high calling God has given you in Christ, so that your daily conduct reflects the gospel you have received. The apostle Paul uses this language repeatedly to urge believers toward a life of consistent, Spirit-empowered obedience rather than empty profession.

In Ephesians 4:1 he writes, “As a prisoner in the Lord, then, I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received.” The Greek word for “worthy” (*axiōs*) carries the idea of balancing the scales: your life should weigh as heavily as the grace that saved you. Paul immediately fills in the content of that worthy walk: “with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, and with diligence to preserve the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:2–3). Similar charges appear in Philippians 1:27 (“conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ”), Colossians 1:10 (“walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God”), and 1 Thessalonians 2:12 (“walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory”).

This is the language of progressive sanctification. Justification declares us righteous by faith alone in Christ alone; sanctification is the Spirit’s ongoing work of making our character and conduct increasingly resemble the One who justified us. Walking worthy is not earning salvation but living out the salvation already secured by Christ’s penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection.

Practically, it looks like choosing humility over self-promotion, patience over irritation, and peacemaking over division, especially inside the local church. A concrete next step is to open Ephesians 4:1–16 this week, ask the Lord to show you one relationship or habit that currently does not match your calling, and take one obedient action (a hard conversation, a quiet act of service, or a deliberate turning from a known sin) before the day ends.

question: What is a divine appointment?
answer:
A divine appointment is a God-orchestrated encounter or circumstance, arranged by His sovereign providence, that advances His purposes in a person’s life or the lives of others—far more than mere coincidence or human planning.

Christians use this phrase to describe moments when the Lord brings people together, opens doors, or aligns events in ways that display His wisdom and care. Scripture teaches that God “works out everything by the counsel of His will” (Ephesians 1:11) and that “a man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). These appointments flow from God’s meticulous providence: He is neither distant nor reactive, but actively rules over details great and small for the good of His people and the glory of His name (Romans 8:28).

A clear biblical example appears in Acts 8:26–39. The Holy Spirit directs Philip to a desert road at the precise moment an Ethiopian official is reading Isaiah. Their meeting leads to the man’s conversion and baptism. Another is Esther’s rise to queenship “for such a time as this” (Esther 4:14), positioning her to intercede for her people. Jesus Himself speaks of the Father’s timing when He says, “My time has not yet come” (John 7:6), underscoring that even the incarnation and cross unfolded according to divine appointment.

Practically, recognizing a divine appointment calls for humble attentiveness rather than anxious striving. Stay faithful in ordinary obedience—prayer, Scripture, local church fellowship, and love of neighbor—while remaining ready for interruptions. When an unexpected conversation, delay, or connection arises, pause and ask the Lord for wisdom to steward it well. You might pray something like, “Father, if this is from You, help me listen and respond in faith.” Over time, such moments often become clear evidences of God’s fatherly care, strengthening trust in the One who numbers our days and orders our steps.

question: What is the Qur’an?
answer:
The Qur’an is the central religious text of Islam, which Muslims regard as the literal word of Allah (God) as revealed to the prophet Muhammad over roughly 23 years in the early 7th century AD through the angel Gabriel, later compiled into a single book after his death.

Muslims hold it to be the final, perfect, and uncreated revelation that corrects and supersedes earlier scriptures, including the Torah and the Gospel. It is written in Arabic, consists of 114 chapters (surahs), and addresses theology, law, morality, and guidance for life. Recitation and memorization hold a central place in Islamic practice.

Christians respectfully disagree with this claim of divine origin and final authority. The Bible teaches that God’s revelation reaches its fullness and completion in Jesus Christ, the eternal Word made flesh (John 1:1–14; Hebrews 1:1–2). Scripture presents itself as the inspired, inerrant Word of God, sufficient for faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17; 2 Peter 1:20–21), and warns against adding to or altering what God has spoken (Deuteronomy 4:2; Revelation 22:18–19). The New Testament affirms that the apostles and prophets laid the foundation once for all (Ephesians 2:20; Jude 1:3), so no later book can stand as equal or superior revelation.

A key difference appears in how each book presents Jesus: the Qur’an honors Him as a prophet and the Messiah born of a virgin, yet denies His deity, crucifixion, and bodily resurrection—truths the Bible treats as essential to the Gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; John 20:27–28). Christians therefore receive the Qur’an as a significant historical and religious document that has shaped billions of lives, but not as the Word of God.

If you are exploring these questions sincerely, I encourage you to read the Gospel accounts (especially John) for yourself and ask God to show you who Jesus truly is. The Bible invites everyone to turn from sin and trust in Christ alone, who died and rose again for the forgiveness of sins and new life. What prompted your question about the Qur’an today?

question: What would have happened “if the Lord had not been on our side” (Psalm 124:2)?
answer:
**If the LORD had not been on our side, Israel would have been swallowed alive, engulfed by a flood, swept away by raging waters, given as prey to the teeth of their enemies, and trapped like a bird in a snare.**

Psalm 124 answers its own question plainly. David leads the people to declare:

“If the LORD had not been on our side when men attacked us, when their anger flared against us, they would have swallowed us alive, when the torrents raged against us, the flood would have engulfed us, the raging waters would have swept us away” (Psalm 124:2–5).  

The images pile up: a monster gulping its prey whole, a sudden flash flood in a dry wadi, and a fowler’s snare closing on a bird. Without the LORD’s active presence and help, God’s people would have been utterly destroyed—no escape, no remnant, no hope.

The psalm then turns to praise: “Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth. We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped. Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth” (Psalm 124:6–8).  

This is not mere poetry. It testifies to the living God’s covenant faithfulness and sovereign protection. He is not a distant observer; He takes the side of His people, breaks the snare, and proves Himself their only true help. The same truth runs through Scripture: “God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble” (Psalm 46:1); “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

For the believer today, the psalm invites honest remembrance. Look back at dangers, opposition, temptations, or trials that should have crushed you. The reason you stand is not your strength or cleverness, but that the LORD was on your side—supremely through Christ’s death and resurrection, by which He defeated sin, death, and the devil for His people.  

A simple next step: take ten quiet minutes to name two or three specific deliverances in your own life (or in the life of your church), then thank God aloud using the words of Psalm 124:6–8. Let gratitude for past help strengthen present trust.

question: What did Jesus mean when He said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to get into heaven?
answer:
Jesus meant that it is humanly impossible for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God by their own power or merit, because wealth so easily becomes an idol that fosters self-reliance rather than humble dependence on God. He used vivid hyperbole (a deliberate exaggeration common in Jewish teaching) to drive the point home: a camel, the largest animal familiar in that region, cannot pass through the tiny opening of a sewing needle. The saying appears in the account of the rich young ruler (Matthew 19:16–30; Mark 10:17–31; Luke 18:18–30).

After the man went away sorrowful, unwilling to surrender his great possessions to follow Jesus, the Lord said, “Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24). The disciples were astonished and asked who then could be saved. Jesus answered, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26). The impossibility lies not in money itself but in the heart’s attachment to it; riches often blind people to their need for the Savior and tempt them to trust what they own rather than the God who alone justifies the ungodly by grace through faith.

This underscores the Gospel truth that no one, rich or poor, enters heaven by works, status, or resources. Salvation is secured only by Christ’s atoning death and bodily resurrection, received through repentance and faith alone. A practical next step is to examine your own heart before the Lord: ask Him to reveal any place where money or comfort has taken the throne that belongs to Him, and then rest afresh in the finished work of Jesus who makes the impossible possible.

question: How do we decide which books belong in the Bible since the Bible does not say which books belong in the Bible?
answer:
The books of the Bible belong in the canon because God inspired them as His Word, and the Holy Spirit enabled His people to recognize and receive them as such. The church did not create or invent the canon by later vote; it discovered and affirmed what God had already given. This process rests on God's providence, the self-attesting character of Scripture, and historical reception rather than a single verse that lists every title.

Scripture itself teaches that God spoke through chosen human authors: "All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness" (2 Timothy 3:16). "No prophecy of Scripture comes from one's own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever brought about through human initiative, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit" (2 Peter 1:20-21). The authority is inherent because of divine origin, not because a council later stamped approval.

### Old Testament Canon
Jesus and the apostles treated the Hebrew Scriptures as a fixed, authoritative collection. Jesus referred to "the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms" (Luke 24:44), the standard threefold division of the Jewish canon. He and the New Testament writers quote from virtually every section of that collection as the Word of God and never treat the later Apocryphal/Deuterocanonical books (accepted in some traditions) with the same authority. The Jewish community had already recognized these books long before Christ; the early church simply received the same Old Testament that Jesus affirmed.

### New Testament Canon
The New Testament books were written in the first century by apostles or their close associates under the Spirit's inspiration. They were immediately treated as authoritative in the churches. Peter already refers to Paul's letters as "Scripture" alongside the Old Testament (2 Peter 3:15-16). Paul commands that his letters be read in the churches (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27). Recognition unfolded through ordinary means God provided:

- **Apostolic origin or connection**: Direct link to the apostles who were commissioned by Christ.
- **Orthodoxy**: Consistency with the teaching already received from Christ and the Old Testament (no contradictions on core doctrine).
- **Catholicity**: Wide, continuous use and acceptance across the churches, not merely local or temporary popularity.
- **Internal witness**: The books bear the marks of divine quality, power, and harmony; the Spirit testifies to the people of God that these are His words (see John 10:27, where Christ's sheep hear His voice).

By the end of the second century the four Gospels, Acts, Paul's letters, and most other New Testament books were already functioning as Scripture. Later councils (such as Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397) simply listed what the churches had long received; they did not bestow authority. A few books (Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude, Revelation) faced longer discussion because of questions about authorship or limited early circulation, yet they met the same criteria and were universally received.

### Addressing the Concern Directly
It is true that no single verse says, "Here is the exact table of contents." That does not leave us in uncertainty. God has always preserved His Word for His people (Psalm 119:89; Isaiah 40:8; Matthew 24:35). The same Spirit who inspired the books illuminates the church to recognize them. This is not a vicious circle; it is the ordinary way revelation works: God speaks, and His people, by grace, hear and submit. Alternative ancient writings (Gnostic gospels, for example) failed the tests of apostolicity, orthodoxy, and catholicity and were never received as Scripture by the historic church.

Faithful Christians have differed on the status of the Apocrypha (Roman Catholics and Orthodox include additional books; Protestants do not). These differences do not touch the 66 books held in common, which contain the full Gospel of Christ. The Protestant recognition follows the Hebrew canon Jesus used and the early church's clearest consensus on the New Testament.

You can trust that the Bible you hold is the Word God intended His people to have. A concrete next step is to read one of the Gospels (start with John) while asking God to confirm His voice through the text itself, and to discuss any lingering questions with a pastor or mature believer in a local church who can walk through the historical evidence with you. The Shepherd still speaks through His Word, and His sheep still hear Him.

question: What does it mean to walk by the Spirit (Galatians 5:16)?
answer:
To walk by the Spirit means to live your daily life under the continual guidance, power, and control of the Holy Spirit so that you do not carry out the sinful desires of the flesh. Galatians 5:16 states it plainly: “So I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.”

In the immediate context of Galatians 5, Paul is addressing believers who have been set free by Christ yet face two equal dangers: returning to law-keeping for righteousness or using freedom as an excuse for sin. Walking by the Spirit is the God-given alternative. The Greek verb for “walk” (*peripateō*) pictures an ongoing way of life, a steady conduct rather than a single moment. It is the practical outworking of progressive sanctification, in which the Holy Spirit enables believers to put sin to death and bear His fruit (love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control; Galatians 5:22–23).

This walk is not passive or automatic. It involves actively yielding to the Spirit’s leading through the ordinary means of grace: hearing and obeying Scripture, prayerful dependence, and fellowship with other believers. The flesh (our remaining sinful nature) still wages war against the Spirit (Galatians 5:17), yet the promise is sure: as we walk by the Spirit we will not gratify those desires. Romans 8:4–5 confirms the same reality: those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit, and the righteous requirement of the law is fulfilled in them.

A concrete next step is to begin each day by asking the Lord to fill you with His Spirit and then open Galatians 5 or Romans 8, asking Him to show you one specific desire of the flesh to resist and one fruit of the Spirit to pursue that day. As you do, remember that this walk rests on Christ’s finished work; you are already justified by grace alone through faith alone, and the same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead now empowers your obedience (Romans 8:11).

question: What does the Bible mean when it says "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God'"?
answer:
The Bible means that the person who inwardly denies God is not merely uninformed but morally corrupt and spiritually rebellious, rejecting the God whose existence is plain and living as if accountable to no one. 

This statement opens both Psalm 14:1 and Psalm 53:1: “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’ They are corrupt; their acts are vile. There is no one who does good.” In the Hebrew Scriptures the word for “fool” (*nabal*) does not primarily describe low intelligence; it describes a person who is morally senseless, closed to wisdom, and practically wicked. The denial happens “in his heart,” the control center of the will and affections, not merely in public debate. The immediate result, the psalm says, is corruption and the absence of genuine good.

David writes these psalms to portray the universal human condition apart from God’s grace. The same psalm continues, “The LORD looks down from heaven upon the sons of men to see if any understand, if any seek God. All have turned away, they have together become corrupt; there is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm 14:2–3). The New Testament cites this very passage to establish that every person is under sin and needs the righteousness that comes only through faith in Christ (Romans 3:10–12). In other words, practical atheism is the fruit of a heart that suppresses the truth God has already made known through creation and conscience (Romans 1:18–22).

Christians therefore read the verse as both diagnosis and warning. It diagnoses the root of human evil: we prefer autonomy to the holy God who made us. It warns that intellectual arguments alone cannot cure the deeper problem; the heart itself must be made new. The good news is that God has acted. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived the perfect life we could not live, died as a penal substitute for sinners, and rose bodily on the third day. All who turn from self-rule and trust in Him alone receive forgiveness and a new heart that says, “You are my God.”

If this verse has unsettled you, a simple next step is to read Psalm 14 slowly and then Romans 1–3, asking the Lord to show you where you may still be living as if He were absent. Talk with a mature believer in a local church who can walk with you in the Scriptures.

question: What is onanism? Is onanism a sin?
answer:
**Onanism** refers to the act of Onan in Genesis 38:9, in which he practiced *coitus interruptus* (withdrawal) by spilling his semen on the ground. The term has also been used historically (especially in older medical and moral literature) as a synonym for masturbation.

### The Biblical Account
Genesis 38:8–10 states:  
“Then Judah said to Onan, ‘Sleep with your brother’s wife and fulfill your duty to her as a brother-in-law to raise up offspring for your brother.’ But Onan knew that the offspring would not be his; so whenever he slept with his brother’s wife, he spilled his semen on the ground to avoid providing offspring for his brother. What he did was wicked in the Lord’s sight; so the Lord put him to death also.”

Onan’s wickedness was not merely a particular sexual technique. In the context of levirate marriage (the duty to raise up offspring for a deceased brother; see Deuteronomy 25:5–6), he selfishly refused that covenantal obligation while still taking sexual pleasure. God judged the heart and the deliberate frustration of the family line He had commanded.

### Is Onanism a Sin?
- **Onan’s specific act**: Yes. Scripture explicitly calls what he did wicked, and the Lord put him to death for it. The core issue was rebellion against God’s revealed will in that situation, compounded by lustful self-gratification without covenantal responsibility.
- **Masturbation (the common extended meaning)**: Scripture never uses the word “masturbation,” yet it consistently frames sexual desire and activity within clear boundaries. Sexual intimacy is designed by God for the covenant of marriage between one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6; 1 Corinthians 7:2–5). Outside that context, Scripture warns against sexual immorality (*porneia*), lust, impurity, and lack of self-control (Matthew 5:27–28; 1 Corinthians 6:18–20; Galatians 5:19–21; 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5; Ephesians 5:3).

Most historic Christian teaching has therefore regarded masturbation as sinful when it involves lustful fantasy (which it ordinarily does) or treats sexual climax as an end in itself rather than as part of the one-flesh union God ordained. It trains the heart toward self-centered gratification instead of the self-giving love that images Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25–32). Even if someone claims an absence of lustful mental images, the practice still falls outside the biblical pattern of sexuality and easily becomes a dominating habit that hinders holiness and self-control—the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23).

Christian traditions have differed on questions such as non-abortifacient contraception *within marriage*; those are matters of conscience and Christian liberty where Scripture is less explicit (Romans 14). Solo sexual activity, however, has not been treated as a mere liberty issue in mainstream historic Christianity because it detaches sex from the marital covenant.

### Pastoral Hope
If this is a personal struggle, you are not alone, and you are not beyond the reach of grace. Sexual sin (like all sin) is serious because God is holy, yet the gospel is that Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived the pure life we have not, died as a sin-bearing substitute on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. All who repent and trust in Him alone are forgiven, counted righteous, and given the Holy Spirit to put sin to death over time (Romans 8:13; 1 John 1:9; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

A concrete next step: confess it honestly to God and, if needed, to a mature same-sex believer or pastor for accountability (James 5:16). Immerse your mind in Scripture that reorients desire (for example, regularly read and pray through 1 Thessalonians 4:1–8 and Psalm 51). Flee tempting situations and fill the space with prayer, fellowship, and service. God’s design is not repression for its own sake but joyful holiness that leads to human flourishing.

If you are wrestling with guilt, habit, or how to walk in purity, feel free to share more of the context—I am glad to point you further to Christ and to practical help within a local church.

question: Is Israel and the church the same thing? Does God still have a plan for Israel?
answer:
No, Israel and the church are not simply the same thing, though the church is the fulfilled people of God who inherit the Abrahamic promises through faith in Christ.

One major opposing view (classic dispensationalism) holds that Israel and the church are two entirely distinct peoples with separate covenants and destinies, so that God’s program for national Israel is paused during the church age and will resume in a future earthly kingdom.

From a covenant theology perspective (including historic Reformed Baptist “1689 Federalism”), Scripture presents one unified people of God across redemptive history: the church is the eschatological Israel, composed of believing Jews and Gentiles grafted into the same olive tree, while God still has a gracious plan that includes the future salvation of a large number of ethnic Israelites. 

Paul makes this plain in Romans 11. Ethnic Israel has experienced a partial hardening, yet “all Israel will be saved” after the full number of the Gentiles comes in (Romans 11:25–26). The natural branches that were broken off can be grafted in again if they do not continue in unbelief (Romans 11:23–24). The promises to Abraham find their “Yes” in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), and those who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to the promise (Galatians 3:29). At the same time, God’s gifts and calling to Israel are irrevocable (Romans 11:29), so we should expect a future turning of many Jewish people to their Messiah.

This keeps the continuity of the one covenant people while honoring the distinctiveness of the new covenant and the ongoing place of ethnic Israel in God’s mercy. The practical call for us is to pray for the peace of Jerusalem, share the gospel with Jewish neighbors without arrogance, and rest in the kindness and severity of God who saves both Jew and Gentile by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

question: Are Catholic beliefs and practices biblical?
answer:
**Some Catholic beliefs are thoroughly biblical, but several core teachings and common practices are not.** Historic Christianity shares vital ground with Roman Catholicism on the Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Christ (the hypostatic union), the virgin birth, Christ’s bodily resurrection, and the authority of the Old and New Testament Scriptures as God’s Word. Yet on the questions that define the Gospel itself—how a sinner is made right with God, the sole sufficiency of Scripture, and the finished work of Christ—official Catholic doctrine and many popular practices depart from the plain teaching of the Bible.

### Shared Foundations
Catholics rightly confess one God in three persons, the incarnation, and that Jesus died for sins and rose again. These are non-negotiable. The problem arises when additional authorities and requirements are placed alongside or above Scripture and the finished work of Christ.

### Authority: Scripture Alone
The Bible presents itself as the sufficient, final rule for faith and practice. Jesus rebuked traditions that nullified God’s Word (Mark 7:6–13). Paul insists that Scripture equips the man of God “for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:16–17) and warns against any gospel contrary to the one already preached, even if delivered by an angel (Galatians 1:8–9).  
Catholic teaching elevates Sacred Tradition and the Magisterium (including papal infallibility under certain conditions) to a co-equal authority with Scripture. That move is not taught in the New Testament and undermines the unique sufficiency of the apostolic writings.

### Justification by Grace Alone through Faith Alone
This is the heart of the Gospel. Scripture teaches that sinners are declared righteous (justified) by God’s grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, apart from works of the law:  
“For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:28).  
“For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).  
“He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy” (Titus 3:5).  

Christ’s once-for-all sacrificial death fully satisfies God’s justice (penal substitution); no further meritorious works, satisfactions, or purgatorial purging can add to it (Hebrews 10:10–14; Romans 5:1; 8:1).  
The Council of Trent and the current Catechism teach that justification is a process involving faith plus baptismal regeneration, ongoing cooperation with infused grace, and works that merit increase of justification. That formulation contradicts the biblical doctrine of justification as a once-for-all forensic declaration received by faith. Good works are the necessary fruit and evidence of genuine faith (James 2:14–26; Ephesians 2:10), never the root or contributing cause of our right standing before God.

### Other Significant Departures
- **The Mass as a propitiatory sacrifice**: Hebrews repeatedly states that Christ’s single offering perfected forever those who are being sanctified and that there remains no further sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 9:24–28; 10:11–18). Treating the Eucharist as a re-presentation or continuation of Calvary’s sacrifice undermines the finality of the cross.  
- **Veneration of Mary and the saints, and prayers directed to them**: Scripture calls us to pray to God alone through the one Mediator, Jesus Christ (1 Timothy 2:5; John 14:6; Hebrews 4:14–16). Mary is blessed among women and a model of faith (Luke 1:42–48), yet the New Testament never instructs believers to pray to her, attribute co-redemptive roles to her, or seek her intercession. The same applies to departed saints.  
- **Purgatory and indulgences**: No clear biblical text teaches a post-mortem purging of remaining sin or the transfer of merit. Believers who die are immediately with Christ (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23; Luke 23:43).  
- **Baptismal regeneration and sacramentalism as ordinarily necessary for salvation**: While baptism is a commanded ordinance that beautifully pictures union with Christ (Romans 6:3–4), the New Testament consistently ties salvation to repentance and faith (Acts 16:31; John 3:16–18; 5:24).  

These are not minor preferences; they touch the Gospel and the unique glory of Christ.

### A Pastoral Word
Many individual Catholics love Jesus, read Scripture, and rest in His mercy more consistently than official documents might suggest. God alone knows the heart. Still, the official system adds layers that obscure the freeness of grace and the finished work of the cross. The Reformation recovered the biblical clarity that sinners are accepted by God solely on the basis of Christ’s righteousness imputed to them and received by faith.

If you are examining these things, open the Bible itself—especially Romans, Galatians, Hebrews, and the Gospel of John—and ask the Holy Spirit for light. Compare every teaching and practice with the text. Find a local church where the Gospel of grace alone through faith alone is clearly preached, the ordinances are kept simple according to Scripture, and believers are shepherded under the Word.  

Turn from every confidence in your own works, religious performance, or human mediators, and trust wholly in Jesus Christ, who died for your sins and rose again. He alone is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25). If you have further questions about a specific doctrine or passage, I am glad to walk through the Scriptures with you.

question: What should we learn from the tribe of Simeon?
answer:
**The tribe of Simeon teaches us the sober consequences of unchecked violence and anger, the certainty of God's disciplinary word, and the mercy that still preserves a place for the repentant among God's people.**

Simeon was the second son of Jacob and Leah. Leah named him Simeon (“heard”), saying, “Because the LORD has heard that I am unloved, He has given me this son also” (Genesis 29:33). The tribe descended from him became one of the twelve tribes of Israel.

### Key Moments in Simeon’s Story
The defining early episode is the massacre at Shechem. After Shechem violated their sister Dinah, Simeon and Levi deceitfully slaughtered the men of the city (Genesis 34). Jacob later rebuked them prophetically:

“Simeon and Levi are brothers; their swords are weapons of violence. Let me not enter their council, let me not join their assembly, for they have killed men in their anger and hamstrung oxen as they pleased. Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their fury, for it is cruel! I will scatter them in Jacob and disperse them in Israel” (Genesis 49:5–7).

That word was fulfilled. In the land allotment, Simeon received no independent territorial inheritance of its own but cities scattered inside Judah’s portion (Joshua 19:1–9). In the wilderness censuses the tribe’s numbers also dropped sharply (from 59,300 in Numbers 1 to 22,200 in Numbers 26), and a Simeonite leader was publicly judged in the Baal-peor idolatry and immorality (Numbers 25:14). Moses’ blessing of the tribes in Deuteronomy 33 notably omits Simeon.

Yet the story does not end in pure judgment. Later Simeonites appear among those who sought the Lord in Hezekiah’s day and expanded into remaining Amalekite territory (1 Chronicles 4:24–43). In the vision of the sealed servants of God, 12,000 from the tribe of Simeon are still named among the redeemed (Revelation 7:7).

### What We Should Learn
1. **Anger and personal vengeance destroy rather than protect**  
   Simeon and Levi’s rage was fierce and cruel; they took justice into their own hands instead of leaving room for God. Scripture consistently warns that “man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires” (James 1:20) and that vengeance belongs to the Lord (Romans 12:19). Unchecked bitterness still scatters families, churches, and witness today.

2. **God’s disciplinary word is sure, yet He does not cast off His covenant people entirely**  
   The scattering prophesied in Genesis 49 came to pass. At the same time, Simeon was never erased from Israel. A remnant remained, was given cities, and later showed zeal for the Lord. This displays both the holiness and the patience of God: He judges sin, yet preserves a people for Himself by grace.

3. **True identity and security are found inside the larger people of God, not in independent strength**  
   Simeon’s inheritance lay within Judah. Their survival depended on relationship to the royal and messianic tribe rather than on their own numbers or power. In Christ the dividing walls are broken down; every believer’s security is now located in union with the Lion of Judah, not in tribal pride or self-sufficiency.

4. **Past failure does not have to be the final word**  
   The same tribe once known for violence later produced men who “struck down the remnant of the Amalekites” in obedience and sought pasture under God’s blessing (1 Chronicles 4). God can redeem a legacy when people turn back to Him.

### Concrete Application
Examine where anger, score-settling, or harsh words have been given free rein in your own life or relationships. Confess them specifically to the Lord, and where needed seek reconciliation. Ask Him to replace fierce self-protection with the meekness of Christ, who entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Then actively locate your identity inside the local church—the present expression of God’s covenant people—rather than living as a scattered, independent Christian.

Simeon’s name still reminds us that the Lord *hears*. He heard Leah in her pain; He hears the repentant today. Turn from self-willed anger, trust the finished work of Christ who bore the curse we deserved, and walk in the security of belonging to His people.

question: What is the hypostatic union?
answer:
The hypostatic union is the biblical truth that in the one eternal Person of Jesus Christ, two complete natures—one fully divine and one fully human—are united forever without confusion, change, division, or separation.

This term comes from the Greek word *hypostasis*, meaning “person” or “subsistence,” and it summarizes what Scripture teaches about the incarnate Son. The eternal Word who was with God and was God took on true human flesh and nature (John 1:1; John 1:14). He is not partly God and partly man, nor a mixture of the two, but one Person who is truly God and truly man at the same time (Vera Deus, vera homo). Colossians 2:9 declares, “For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form,” while passages such as Hebrews 2:14–17 and Philippians 2:5–8 show that He shared fully in our humanity, yet without sin.

The early church articulated this at the Council of Chalcedon (AD 451) to guard the plain teaching of Scripture against errors that either denied Christ’s full deity, denied His full humanity, or split Him into two persons. Because of the hypostatic union, Jesus could live a perfect human life in our place, offer Himself as a sufficient atoning sacrifice, and rise bodily as the firstfruits of the new creation. This reality means the One who saves us is both able to represent us as man and powerful to redeem us as God.

A concrete way this truth shapes daily faith is to trust that the same Jesus who knows human weakness from the inside (Hebrews 4:15) is also the sovereign Lord who upholds all things and intercedes for you right now. You can bring every need to Him with confidence that He both understands and is able to help.

question: Doubting God — how can I overcome doubt in my relationship with God?
answer:
**Doubting God is a heavy, common struggle**—even mature believers walk through seasons where God’s presence feels distant, His promises seem unclear, or hard circumstances shake confidence. You are not alone, and bringing this honestly is already a step toward Him.

Scripture never pretends faith is the absence of questions. The father in Mark 9:24 cried, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” and Jesus met him with compassion and power. Thomas doubted the resurrection until he saw the risen Christ; Jesus invited him to touch the wounds and then blessed those who believe without seeing (John 20:24–29). The psalmists repeatedly poured out confusion and fear yet ended by anchoring in God’s character (see Psalm 73:21–28). Doubt is not the opposite of faith; unbelief that turns away is. Faith is trusting God’s proven character and Word even while questions remain.

### Why doubt arises and how the Gospel steadies us
Doubt often grows from suffering, unanswered prayer, intellectual pressure, unconfessed sin, neglect of Scripture and prayer, or isolation. The Bible teaches that our relationship with God rests not on the strength of our feelings but on Christ’s finished work. He is truly God and truly man, lived sinlessly, died as our substitute for sin, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. Even weak faith, if it is in the real Jesus, unites us to Him. He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion (Philippians 1:6). Your standing is secured by His faithfulness, not your perfect certainty.

### Concrete ways to overcome doubt
- **Bring the doubt to God directly.** Pray honestly—tell Him exactly where it hurts or what confuses you. Ask Him to strengthen your faith as you open His Word. Do not wait until you “feel” spiritual; He already knows (Hebrews 4:14–16).
- **Feed on Scripture.** Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ (Romans 10:17). Doubt starves in the light of God’s self-revelation. Read passages that display His character, promises, and the historical reality of Jesus’ death and resurrection.
- **Remember and rehearse truth.** Recall specific ways God has been faithful in your life and in redemptive history. The empty tomb is objective fact that anchors subjective feelings.
- **Stay connected to Christ’s body.** Isolation feeds doubt. Share with a mature believer, elder, or pastor in your local church who can pray with you and point you back to Scripture. “The prayer of a righteous person has great power” (James 5:16).
- **Obey in the small things.** Walk in the light you already have—ordinary means of grace (Word, prayer, fellowship, the Lord’s Supper). Clarity often follows obedience rather than preceding it.

**One actionable next step:** Over the next seven days, read the Gospel of John (about three chapters a day). Each day note one truth about who Jesus is and one promise He makes. Then pray simply: thank God for that truth, confess any specific doubt, and ask Him to make it real to your heart. If possible, tell one trusted Christian friend what you are doing so they can check in and pray.

God is not threatened by your questions. He invites you to draw near, and He is kind to the bruised reed. Keep turning to Him; He delights to meet you there and to deepen your assurance in Christ. If the struggle feels overwhelming or tied to deeper despair, reach out today to a pastor or a certified biblical counselor—you do not have to walk this alone.

question: Did God create other people in addition to Adam and Eve?
answer:
**No. The Bible teaches that God specially created Adam and Eve as the first human beings and the sole progenitors of the entire human race.**

Scripture presents this as historical reality, not myth or partial account. In Genesis 1:26–27 God creates mankind in His own image, “male and female He created them.” Genesis 2 then details the formation of Adam from the dust and Eve from Adam’s side as the suitable helper corresponding to him, with no other humans present. Genesis 3:20 explicitly calls Eve “the mother of all the living.”

The New Testament confirms this unity of origin. Acts 17:26 states that God “made from one man every nation of men to inhabit the whole earth.” Romans 5:12–19 and 1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45 treat Adam as the historical head of the human race through whom sin and death entered the world, with Christ as the last Adam who brings life. The doctrines of original sin, federal headship, and the universal need for the gospel rest on this single origin.

A common question arises in Genesis 4 about Cain’s wife and the people he feared. Genesis 5:4 notes that Adam “had other sons and daughters” after Seth. In the earliest generations, marriage between close relatives was necessary and not yet forbidden (the Mosaic law later prohibited it as the human population grew and genetic risks increased). Cain built a city later, after further population growth through ordinary means of begetting children. The text gives no hint of separately created peoples, pre-Adamites, or other contemporaneous human lines.

Some modern theories propose additional creations or evolutionary populations alongside Adam and Eve. These stand outside the plain reading of Scripture and undermine the biblical teaching that all people share one blood, one fallen nature in Adam, and one Savior in Christ. Faithful Christians may differ on the age of the earth or the precise length of the “days” in Genesis 1 (tertiary matters), yet the special, historical creation of Adam and Eve as the first pair remains essential to the Bible’s storyline and the gospel itself.

All humanity therefore shares equal dignity as image-bearers and equal need of redemption. If this raises further questions about Genesis, human origins, or how this connects to the person and work of Jesus, feel free to share them.

question: What does the Bible say about self-discipline?
answer:
The Bible presents self-discipline (often called self-control) as essential to godly living, a fruit of the Holy Spirit rather than mere human willpower, and a mark of those trained by God's grace. Galatians 5:22-23 lists it among the fruit of the Spirit: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law."

Scripture ties self-discipline directly to following Christ and growing in holiness. In 1 Corinthians 9:24-27, Paul compares the Christian life to an athlete's rigorous training: "Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way as to take the prize. Everyone who competes in the games trains with strict discipline. They do it for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable. Therefore I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air. No, I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified." Proverbs 25:28 warns of the danger without it: "Like a city whose walls are broken down is a man who lacks self-control." Titus 2:11-12 shows that God's grace itself produces this: "For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone. It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age."

This self-discipline belongs to progressive sanctification, the Spirit's ongoing work of conforming believers to Christ's image. 2 Timothy 1:7 reminds us of its source: "For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control." Hebrews 12:11 adds that the Lord's loving discipline yields "the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it."

A concrete next step is to choose one area (speech, appetites, time, or thoughts) and submit it daily to the Lord through Scripture meditation and prayer, asking the Spirit for strength while staying accountable in your local church. Self-discipline is not self-reliance; it is Spirit-empowered obedience that frees us to love God and neighbor well.

question: What is original sin?
answer:
**Original sin** is the biblical teaching that every human being inherits both the guilt of Adam’s first disobedience and a corrupted nature inclined toward sin from the moment of conception.

In Genesis 3, Adam, as the federal head (representative) of the human race, sinned against God. Romans 5:12 states, “Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned.” Paul continues in Romans 5:18–19 that “one trespass brought condemnation for all men” and “through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners.” Psalm 51:5 likewise confesses, “Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me.” Ephesians 2:3 describes us as “by nature children of wrath.”

This inherited condition (sometimes called total depravity) does not mean every person is as wicked as possible, but that every part of our being—mind, will, and affections—is affected by sin and unable to please God or seek Him apart from grace (Romans 3:10–12; 8:7–8). Original sin is therefore the root reason we need the new birth and the perfect obedience and penal substitutionary atonement of Jesus Christ, the last Adam (Romans 5:19; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45).

A concrete next step is to examine your own heart in light of this truth: confess specific sins to God, thank Him that Christ’s righteousness is credited to all who trust Him, and ask Him daily for the Spirit’s help to put sin to death (Romans 8:13). If this raises questions about your standing before God, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

question: Are intrusive thoughts sin? Are spontaneous violent, sexual, or blasphemous thoughts sin?
answer:
**No, spontaneous intrusive thoughts are not sin in themselves.** Sin involves the willful consent of the heart, the nurturing of desire, or acting upon evil—not the mere unbidden arrival of a violent, sexual, or blasphemous thought that distresses you.

Scripture is clear that evil can arise from within our fallen nature. Jesus taught, “For from within the hearts of men come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness. All these evils come from within, and these are what defile a man” (Mark 7:21-23). Our minds are affected by the flesh, the world, and the devil’s accusations. Yet the Bible also distinguishes *temptation* from *sin*. Jesus Himself “has been tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). James explains the process: “But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed. Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is fully grown, gives birth to death” (James 1:14-15). A thought that flashes uninvited and is immediately resisted has not “conceived.”

### How to Discern
- **Intrusive / spontaneous thoughts**: These often feel alien, unwanted, and alarming (especially blasphemous ones). They can be the residue of a fallen mind, residual habits, anxiety, or spiritual attack. The fact that they grieve you is evidence of the Holy Spirit’s work, not proof you have committed the thought as sin. The unpardonable sin (persistent, knowing, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s testimony to Christ—see Matthew 12:31-32) is the opposite of a believer’s horrified reaction to a blasphemous intrusion.
- **Sinful response**: Dwelling on the thought with pleasure, rehearsing it, agreeing with it, or planning to act on it crosses into sin. “But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28) addresses cultivated lust, not a fleeting unwanted image. Likewise, “We demolish arguments and every presumption set up against the knowledge of God; and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5) assumes thoughts will come and must be actively refused.

Many faithful Christians experience exactly these intrusive spikes—violent images, sexual flashes, or sudden blasphemies—and then fear they have lost their salvation. That fear itself is usually a sign of a tender conscience, not condemnation. Romans 7 records Paul’s own anguish over unwanted impulses: “For I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do… What a wretched man I am!” yet he immediately clings to deliverance “through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:19, 24-25).

### Gospel Hope and Practical Next Step
Christ’s penal substitutionary death covers every sin of thought, word, and deed for those who are in Him. You are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone—not by the purity of your mental stream. If you have entertained such thoughts, confess them specifically, turn from them, and rest in the finished work of the cross and the empty tomb. “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). The same power that raised Jesus progressively sanctifies the mind.

**One concrete step today**: When an intrusive thought hits, do not argue with it or spiral in shame. Immediately name it (“This is not from the Lord”), refuse it aloud or in prayer (“I reject this in Jesus’ name”), and replace it with a specific truth—quote a verse such as Philippians 4:8 or Romans 8:1. Then thank God that the blood of Christ is sufficient. If these thoughts are frequent, intense, or paired with compulsive rituals or deep anxiety, talk with a trusted pastor or a certified biblical counselor (ACBC) who can help you apply Scripture while also wisely considering whether additional support is needed. You are not alone, and you are not defined by the noise in your head. Christ is greater.

question: Book of 1 Corinthians - Bible Survey
answer:
**1 Corinthians** is a letter from the Apostle Paul to the church in Corinth, written around AD 55 from Ephesus, addressing divisions, immorality, and questions about Christian living in a pagan culture.

Paul founded the church during his second missionary journey (Acts 18:1–17) and wrote this epistle after receiving troubling reports from Chloe’s household and a letter from the Corinthians themselves. Corinth was a wealthy, immoral port city known for idolatry and sexual license; the young congregation struggled to live out the gospel amid that setting. Paul writes as their spiritual father to call them back to unity in Christ, holiness, and sound doctrine.

### Purpose and Occasion
The letter confronts factionalism (some claiming “I follow Paul,” others “I follow Apollos”), lawsuits among believers, sexual sin, misuse of Christian liberty, disorder in worship, and denial of the bodily resurrection. Paul answers specific questions on marriage, food offered to idols, spiritual gifts, and the collection for the saints. His aim is pastoral correction rooted in the cross: “For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1:18).

### Key Themes
- **Unity in Christ** over human leaders or wisdom (1 Corinthians 1–4).
- **Sexual purity and church discipline** as marks of a holy people (1 Corinthians 5–6).
- **Christian liberty** guided by love and the glory of God rather than selfish rights (1 Corinthians 8–10).
- **Orderly worship and the proper use of spiritual gifts**, especially the supremacy of love (1 Corinthians 11–14).
- **The bodily resurrection** of Christ and believers as the foundation of hope (1 Corinthians 15).
- **Stewardship and gospel partnership** (1 Corinthians 16).

The famous “love chapter” (1 Corinthians 13) sits at the heart of the gifts discussion, showing that without agape love even the most spectacular gifts are empty. Chapter 15 gives the clearest New Testament defense of Christ’s resurrection and its implications for our future resurrection, underscoring penal substitution and victory over sin and death.

### Simple Outline
1. Greeting and thanksgiving (1 Corinthians 1:1–9)  
2. Divisions and the wisdom of the cross (1 Corinthians 1:10–4:21)  
3. Moral scandals and lawsuits (1 Corinthians 5:1–6:20)  
4. Answers on marriage, divorce, and singleness (1 Corinthians 7)  
5. Food, idols, and liberty (1 Corinthians 8:1–11:1)  
6. Worship: head coverings, the Lord’s Supper, and gifts (1 Corinthians 11:2–14:40)  
7. The resurrection (1 Corinthians 15)  
8. Final instructions and greetings (1 Corinthians 16)

### Doctrinal and Pastoral Significance
1 Corinthians shows how the gospel of justification by grace through faith in Christ alone produces progressive sanctification in messy church life. It refuses both legalism and license, calling believers to glorify God in their bodies because they were “bought at a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20). The letter remains intensely practical: it teaches local churches to practice loving discipline, pursue unity around the cross rather than personalities, exercise gifts for edification, and anchor every hope in the risen Christ.

A concrete next step is to read the entire letter in one sitting (it takes about an hour), noting every time Paul points back to the cross or the resurrection, then discuss one area of application with a mature believer in your local church.

question: How do I identify my spiritual gift?
answer:
**Spiritual gifts are special enablements given by the Holy Spirit to every believer for the common good and the building up of Christ’s church.** You identify them primarily through prayerful dependence on God, careful study of Scripture, active service in the local church, and wise counsel from mature believers, rather than through self-focused inventories alone.

Scripture teaches that the Spirit distributes gifts sovereignly: “There are different gifts, but the same Spirit. There are different ministries, but the same Lord. There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all people. Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:4–7). Lists of gifts appear in Romans 12:6–8, 1 Corinthians 12:8–10 and 28–30, Ephesians 4:11–12, and 1 Peter 4:10–11. These include both speaking gifts (such as teaching, exhortation, and evangelism) and serving gifts (such as mercy, giving, administration, and helps). The purpose is always edification of the body, not personal status (1 Corinthians 12:7; Ephesians 4:12; 1 Peter 4:10).

### Practical steps to identify your gift
1. **Pray and submit to the Spirit’s leading.** Ask God for wisdom and a heart ready to serve wherever He places you (James 1:5). Spiritual gifts are discovered in the context of walking with Christ, not apart from Him.

2. **Study the biblical lists and their context.** Read 1 Corinthians 12–14, Romans 12, and Ephesians 4 slowly. Note that gifts are diverse, given by grace, and measured by love and usefulness to others, not by dramatic display. Some historic Christian traditions (including the Reformed Baptist view shaped by the 1689 Confession) hold that the miraculous sign gifts (tongues, prophecy of new revelation, healings as authenticating signs) ceased with the apostolic foundation of the church, while the ordinary gifts for ongoing ministry continue. Other faithful Christians hold a cautious continuationist view that some miraculous gifts may still operate under strict scriptural testing. In either case, the emphasis remains on serving the body in love rather than chasing experiences.

3. **Serve faithfully in your local church and watch for fruit.** Gifts become clear as you obey and meet real needs. Volunteer in areas of teaching, hospitality, mercy ministry, administration, or evangelism. Notice where your efforts consistently bless others, where you experience Spirit-given joy and endurance, and where the church affirms effectiveness. Desire alone is not decisive; confirmed usefulness is (1 Peter 4:10–11).

4. **Seek confirmation from elders and mature believers.** Your pastors and trusted brothers and sisters can observe what you may miss. Ask them: “Where have you seen God use me to strengthen the church?” This guards against both pride and false humility.

5. **Evaluate motives and pursue love above all.** Even genuine gifts are worthless without love (1 Corinthians 13:1–3). If a supposed gift consistently produces division, self-promotion, or neglect of clear biblical duties, it needs re-examination.

A concrete next step: This week, read 1 Corinthians 12 prayerfully each day, then speak with one of your church elders or a mature member about one area of service you can begin or continue. Ask them to help you watch for how God may be gifting you as you simply obey. Stay rooted in the ordinary means of grace (Word, prayer, fellowship, and the ordinances), because the Spirit who gives gifts also sanctifies us through these means.

God delights to equip His people. As you seek Him first and serve His body, He will make the path clearer. If you are still uncertain about your standing with Christ Himself, remember that the greatest gift is salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, who died for our sins and rose again. Turn from sin and trust Him, and the Spirit will take up residence to gift and grow you for His glory. How is your local church already helping you serve?

question: What is lacking in Christ’s afflictions (Colossians 1:24)?
answer:
**Nothing is lacking in the atoning, redemptive value of Christ’s sufferings on the cross.** Those were finished, perfect, and fully sufficient once for all. In Colossians 1:24 Paul means that he is filling up, in his own body, the remaining share of afflictions that still fall upon Christ’s body (the church) as the gospel advances in a hostile world.

Colossians 1:24 says: “Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions, for the sake of His body, which is the church.”

Christ’s personal sufferings for sin were completed at the cross. He Himself declared, “It is finished” (John 19:30). Hebrews 10:12–14 confirms that “when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God... For by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.” The doctrine of penal substitutionary atonement stands complete; nothing can be added to the price He paid to reconcile sinners to God.

What remains is the ongoing participation of believers in the afflictions that mark union with Christ. Scripture repeatedly speaks of this reality:
- “that I may know Him and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings” (Philippians 3:10);
- “For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows” (2 Corinthians 1:5);
- “If we suffer with Him, we will also be glorified with Him” (Romans 8:17).

Paul, writing from prison, sees his hardships as part of the appointed measure of suffering that the church must still endure while the gospel is proclaimed to the nations. These are not redemptive sufferings that atone for sin; they are ministerial and missional sufferings that serve the growth and purity of Christ’s body. In that sense he “fills up” what is still lacking—the full quota of affliction allotted to the church in this age until Christ returns.
