A concrete application: when you face hardship for the sake of faithfulness to Christ or the good of His people, you are not adding to the cross; you are sharing in the same pattern of costly love that marked your Savior. Rejoice as Paul did, knowing those sufferings are not wasted. They display the gospel, strengthen the church, and will be met with Christ’s own comfort and future glory.

If this verse has raised questions about whether Christ’s work is truly finished, rest in the clear testimony of Scripture: His atoning death and bodily resurrection secure full justification by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone. Turn from any trust in your own sufferings or works and trust wholly in the finished work of Jesus.

question: How can I get my prayers answered by God?
answer:
God hears and answers prayer, but not as a formula or vending machine. He responds as a holy, loving Father to those who belong to Him through Jesus Christ.

Scripture shows that answered prayer flows from a living relationship with God, not from techniques. Jesus said, “If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you” (John 15:7). The starting point is faith in Christ’s death and resurrection for the forgiveness of your sins. Apart from Him we have no confident access to the Father (John 14:6; Hebrews 4:14–16). If you have not yet turned from sin and trusted Christ alone, that is the first and greatest “answer” you need: call on Him today for salvation.

For those who are in Christ, the Bible gives clear conditions and patterns:

- **Pray according to God’s will.** “This is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us” (1 John 5:14). God’s will is revealed in Scripture, so let the Bible shape what you ask. He may say yes, no, or wait, always for His glory and your good (Romans 8:28).
- **Pray in Jesus’ name.** This means coming on the basis of His finished work and for His purposes, not merely adding a phrase at the end (John 14:13–14).
- **Pray with faith and without double-mindedness.** “Ask in faith, without doubting” (James 1:6). Trust God’s character even when the answer differs from your desire.
- **Confess known sin and seek a clean heart.** “If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened” (Psalm 66:18). Keep short accounts with God through ongoing repentance (1 John 1:9).
- **Check your motives.** “You ask and do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures” (James 4:3). Prayer is not for self-exaltation but for God’s kingdom and name.
- **Persist.** Jesus taught us to keep asking, seeking, and knocking (Luke 11:9–10; Luke 18:1–8). Delay is not always denial.

God’s answers are perfect because He is sovereign, wise, and good. Sometimes the deepest answer is His sustaining presence rather than the removal of the trial (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

**A concrete next step:** Set aside 10–15 quiet minutes today. Read John 15:1–11 slowly. Then pray the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13) as a guide, pausing after each phrase to make it personal: praise God’s name, ask for His will in a specific situation, confess sin, and thank Him for daily bread and forgiveness. Do this in dependence on the Holy Spirit, and consider sharing the request with a mature believer in your local church so they can pray with you (James 5:16).

God delights to give good gifts to His children (Matthew 7:11). Keep drawing near.

question: What is the more excellent way (1 Corinthians 12:31)?
answer:
The more excellent way Paul points to in 1 Corinthians 12:31 is love.

After urging the Corinthian believers to “eagerly desire the greater gifts,” he immediately adds, “And now I will show you a more excellent way” (1 Corinthians 12:31). That way is unfolded in the next chapter: the way of agape love, the self-giving, Christlike love that never fails. Paul shows that even the most impressive spiritual gifts (tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith that moves mountains, lavish generosity, or martyrdom) amount to nothing without love (1 Corinthians 13:1–3). Love is patient and kind; it does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude; it does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice at wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth; it bears, believes, hopes, and endures all things (1 Corinthians 13:4–7). Prophecies, tongues, and knowledge will pass away, but “love never ends” (1 Corinthians 13:8). Faith, hope, and love remain, “but the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13).

In the flow of 1 Corinthians 12–14, Paul is correcting a church that prized spectacular gifts while fracturing into rivalry and pride. The “more excellent way” is not a replacement for spiritual gifts but the indispensable atmosphere in which every gift must operate. Gifts without love become noisy gongs; love rightly orders and sweetens the exercise of every gift for the building up of the body of Christ.

A concrete next step is to examine one relationship or ministry setting this week and ask the Lord to help you put 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 into practice there, letting love govern how you speak, serve, and respond.

question: What is the open heaven concept?
answer:
**The “open heaven” concept** refers to the idea of a spiritual condition or season in which God’s presence, revelation, blessing, angelic activity, or supernatural power seems especially accessible and unhindered.

### Biblical Occurrences
Scripture records several moments when “the heavens were opened”:
- **Ezekiel 1:1** – Ezekiel receives visions of God.
- **Matthew 3:16** – At Jesus’ baptism the heavens open, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks.
- **Acts 7:56** – Stephen sees the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand.
- **Revelation 4:1** – A door stands open in heaven for John’s vision.
- Genesis 28:12 (Jacob’s ladder) and other passages also picture heaven and earth connected.

In these texts the opening of heaven marks decisive divine initiative—revelation, the inauguration of Jesus’ public ministry, or eschatological vision—not a repeatable technique or atmospheric condition believers create.

### Modern Usage
In some charismatic and Pentecostal teaching, “open heavens” has become a broader concept describing:
- A regional or personal spiritual climate of heightened favor, miracles, dreams, or prophetic insight.
- The opposite of a “closed heaven” (often linked to sin, idolatry, or spiritual opposition, drawing loosely from Deuteronomy 28:23 or similar passages).
- Practices aimed at “keeping the heavens open” through worship, repentance, or intercession.

### A Biblical and Pastoral Perspective
Through Christ’s finished work the way to God is permanently opened. The torn veil (Matthew 27:51) and our confidence to “enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19–22) mean believers already have bold access to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16). We do not wait for special seasons of openness; every Christian lives under the New Covenant reality of the Spirit’s indwelling (1 Corinthians 6:19; Ephesians 1:3).

Faithful Christians differ on the degree to which extraordinary manifestations continue today. Cessationists (the historic Reformed and confessional view) hold that the revelatory and sign gifts tied to the apostolic foundation have ceased, while the ordinary means of grace—Word, prayer, sacraments, and fellowship—remain fully sufficient. Continuationists expect ongoing miraculous gifts but should still test everything by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:21) and avoid turning “open heavens” language into a performance-based or geographically limited spirituality.

**Concrete next step:** Read Hebrews 4:14–16 and 10:19–25 slowly this week. Thank God that, because of Jesus, the heavens are already open to you in prayer and communion with Him. Then ask Him to deepen your ordinary, daily dependence on His Word rather than chasing special atmospheres.

The greatest “open heaven” is Christ Himself, in whom every spiritual blessing is already ours.

question: What is the origin of baptism?
answer:
**Christian baptism originates in the ministry of John the Baptist as a baptism of repentance, and it was instituted by Jesus Christ Himself as an ordinance for His disciples and the church.**

John appeared in the wilderness “preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins” (Mark 1:4), drawing on Jewish ritual washings (such as those associated with purity and conversion) yet giving the practice a distinct, eschatological focus that pointed to the coming Messiah. Jesus submitted to John’s baptism to “fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15), identifying with sinners though Himself sinless, and later commanded His followers: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). After His resurrection and exaltation, the apostles practiced baptism immediately upon repentance and faith (Acts 2:38; Acts 8:36–38; Acts 10:47–48), treating it as the God-ordained sign of union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12).

In short, while earlier Jewish purification rites provide historical background, the origin and authority of Christian baptism rest solely on Christ’s example and explicit command. It is not a human invention or mere continuation of earlier customs, but a New Covenant ordinance that publicly portrays the gospel—death to sin and new life in Christ—received by grace through faith alone.

This understanding undergirds believer’s baptism by immersion as the New Testament pattern: the ordinance follows personal repentance and faith and vividly pictures burial and rising with Christ. Other historic Christian traditions (such as those practicing infant baptism) see greater continuity with Old Testament circumcision as a covenant sign applied to households; that view seeks to honor God’s covenantal dealings across the Testaments, though it differs on the subjects and timing of the rite. As a matter of secondary doctrine, the plain New Testament examples and the meaning of baptism as a sign of inward regeneration lead me to affirm credo-baptism for those who profess faith.

If you are considering baptism yourself, speak with the elders of a local Bible-believing church; they can walk with you through the Scriptures, hear your testimony of faith in Christ, and help you obey this joyful command in the context of the gathered body.

question: What is historical criticism?
answer:
**Historical criticism** is a cluster of academic methods for studying the Bible (and other ancient literature) that aim to reconstruct a text’s origins, authorship, sources, original setting, and possible stages of development by using tools drawn from secular historiography, archaeology, linguistics, and comparative literature.

It commonly includes sub-disciplines such as source criticism (identifying hypothetical earlier documents), form criticism (classifying oral or literary units by genre and setting), and redaction criticism (examining how editors supposedly shaped the material). These approaches grew prominent in the Enlightenment and nineteenth-century European universities and often treat the biblical books primarily as human products whose claims must be tested against external historical criteria.

Christians rightly value careful historical study because the Bible presents real events in real time and space; the incarnation, cross, and bodily resurrection of Jesus are not myths but history (Luke 1:1–4; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8). The grammatical-historical method of interpretation, long practiced in the church, seeks the plain sense of the text in its original languages and contexts while submitting to Scripture’s own testimony that it is God-breathed, inerrant, and fully trustworthy (2 Timothy 3:16–17; 2 Peter 1:20–21).

Much modern historical criticism, however, begins with naturalistic presuppositions that rule out miracles, predictive prophecy, and divine inspiration in advance. When those assumptions lead scholars to deny the traditional authorship of books, the unity of Isaiah, the historical reliability of the Gospels, or the resurrection itself, the method has moved outside the bounds of orthodox Christian faith. The authority of Scripture is a core doctrine: the Bible stands as the ultimate standard over any scholarly consensus.

A concrete next step is to read a passage such as the Gospel of Mark while noting both its first-century Jewish and Roman setting and its clear claim to report the words and deeds of the Son of God. Let historical details illuminate the text; do not let skeptical theories sit in judgment over it. If you are wrestling with critical claims you have encountered, bring them to a trusted pastor or mature believer in your local church who holds the full inspiration and reliability of Scripture, and keep reading the Bible itself with prayer for the Spirit’s illumination.

question: What does the Bible say about paying taxes?
answer:
The Bible clearly teaches that believers should pay taxes as an act of submission to the governing authorities God has established. 

Jesus addressed this directly when religious leaders tried to trap Him with a question about paying the imperial tax to Caesar. He replied, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21; see also Mark 12:17; Luke 20:25). In doing so, He affirmed the legitimate right of civil government to collect taxes while reserving ultimate allegiance for God alone.

The apostle Paul expands on this principle: “Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which is from God. The authorities that exist have been appointed by God... This is also why you pay taxes, for the authorities are God’s servants, who devote themselves to their work. Pay everyone what you owe him: taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue is due, respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due” (Romans 13:1, 6–7). Peter likewise urges believers to “submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human institution” (1 Peter 2:13).

This teaching rests on God’s sovereignty over all earthly powers. Paying taxes is not merely a civic duty but an expression of trust that God ordains governments for order and justice, even imperfect ones. At the same time, when human commands directly contradict God’s Word, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). 

In practice, this means Christians should pay their taxes honestly and promptly as a quiet witness to integrity, while praying for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and keeping their deepest loyalty fixed on Christ.

question: Should Christian women wear pants?
answer:
**No, Scripture does not require Christian women to avoid pants.** Whether women wear pants is a tertiary matter of Christian liberty and cultural application where faithful believers may disagree without compromising the gospel or orthodoxy.

The Bible never commands a specific garment such as skirts versus pants. Clothing styles change across history and cultures; in biblical times both men and women typically wore robe-like garments that differed mainly in cut, length, and ornamentation. The enduring principles are modesty, clear gender distinction, and a heart oriented toward godliness rather than external rules.

### Two Common Christian Views
- **Some conservative traditions** (certain Holiness, fundamentalist, or Anabaptist-influenced groups) teach that women should wear only dresses or skirts. They often appeal to Deuteronomy 22:5 (“A woman must not wear men’s clothing, and a man must not wear women’s clothing, for whoever does these things is detestable to the LORD your God”) and interpret pants as inherently masculine, plus concerns for modesty and visible femininity.
- **Most evangelical and Reformed Christians** hold that pants designed for women are permissible when they are modest, feminine in cut and fit, and worn with a clear desire to honor the Lord. They note that Deuteronomy 22:5 addresses deliberate gender confusion or pagan cross-dressing practices, not fabric shape per se, and that New Testament emphasis falls on the heart and overall propriety (1 Timothy 2:9–10; 1 Peter 3:3–4).

Christian liberty applies here. Romans 14:1–6 and Romans 14:13–23 teach that believers must not pass judgment on disputable matters of conscience, nor cause a brother or sister to stumble. What matters is acting in faith, with thanksgiving, and without violating one’s own conscience or the weaker conscience of others in one’s local context.

### Guiding Principles Rather Than a Uniform Rule
Scripture calls women (and men) to:
- **Modesty and self-control** — “likewise, I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, but with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God” (1 Timothy 2:9–10). Clothing should not be sexually provocative or draw undue attention.
- **Inward beauty over outward show** — “Your beauty should not come from outward adornment such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes, but from the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God’s sight” (1 Peter 3:3–4).
- **Clear male-female distinction** — God created humanity male and female (Genesis 1:27). Dress should not intentionally blur or reject that good design.
- **Love for neighbor and witness** — Consider what edifies your church family, family members, and the watching world in your culture.

Pants that are modest, appropriately feminine, and worn with a clean conscience fit comfortably within these principles for many believers. Extremely tight, revealing, or deliberately androgynous clothing would violate them regardless of whether the item is called “pants” or a “skirt.”

If this question arises from personal conviction, family expectation, or church teaching, examine your motives before the Lord, search the passages above, and talk with your husband (if married) and the elders or mature women in your local church. Pray for wisdom and a heart that delights more in Christ than in either rigid rules or careless freedom. The goal is not uniformity of wardrobe but unity in the gospel and lives that adorn the doctrine of God our Savior (Titus 2:10).

question: Why wasn't Jesus named Immanuel?
answer:
Jesus was named Jesus (not Immanuel) because the angel explicitly commanded Joseph to give Him that name, as it points to His mission of salvation: “She will give birth to a Son, and you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Immanuel is not a personal name He was to bear in daily life, but a prophetic title meaning “God with us,” which Matthew immediately applies to Jesus to show that the virgin-born child fulfills Isaiah’s promise through the incarnation.

Isaiah 7:14 had declared, “Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.” Matthew 1:22-23 quotes this and explains, “All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet: ‘Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel’ (which means, ‘God with us’).” The phrase “they will call Him” indicates how people would recognize and describe Him, not the legal name given at birth. In the same way Scripture can speak of the Messiah by many names and titles (Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Prince of Peace in Isaiah 9:6, or Lamb of God, Son of Man, and others), Jesus’ given name highlights His work as Savior while Immanuel highlights His identity as the eternal Son who took on human nature to dwell among us.

This dual reality is at the heart of the Gospel: the One who is truly God and truly man came near in the flesh, lived a sinless life, died as a substitute for sinners, and rose bodily so that all who repent and trust in Him alone receive forgiveness and new life. The name Jesus assures us He saves; the title Immanuel assures us God Himself has drawn near to accomplish it.

question: How is choosing a good name better than choosing riches (Proverbs 22:1)?
answer:
A good name is better than riches because a reputation marked by integrity, trustworthiness, and godly character brings lasting favor with God and people, while wealth is temporary, uncertain, and cannot purchase true honor or peace.

Proverbs 22:1 states, “A good name is more desirable than great riches; favor is better than silver and gold.” In the wisdom literature of Scripture, a “good name” refers to a life of moral integrity and faithful reputation, not mere public image or self-promotion. The Hebrew idea behind “name” often carries the sense of one’s character and standing before others. Riches can vanish through misfortune, folly, or death (Proverbs 23:4–5; Proverbs 27:24), but a good name endures and opens doors of influence, trust, and blessing that money cannot buy. Favor (the goodwill and esteem of others) flows from consistent righteousness and proves more valuable than silver or gold because it reflects the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7).

This priority guards the heart against the love of money, which Scripture warns is a root of all kinds of evil (1 Timothy 6:10). A person known for honesty, kindness, and faithfulness experiences relational stability and a clear conscience, whereas wealth gained or kept without integrity often breeds isolation, anxiety, and judgment. Ultimately, our standing before God matters most. In Christ we receive the greatest “name” of all: we are justified by grace alone through faith alone, credited with His perfect righteousness, and adopted as children of God (Romans 5:1; 2 Corinthians 5:21). That secure identity frees us to pursue a good name not as a way to earn salvation, but as grateful obedience that adorns the gospel.

Practically, ask the Lord to search your heart and reveal any area where reputation is being traded for gain or convenience. Then take one concrete step this week: keep a small commitment you have made, speak truthfully even when it costs you, or restore a strained relationship through humble confession. A good name grows through daily faithfulness, and Christ Himself is both the model and the power for that life.

question: What is the lust of the eyes?
answer:
The lust of the eyes is the sinful craving for things we see that captivate and pull our hearts away from God toward worldly possessions, appearances, or pleasures. Scripture names it plainly in 1 John 2:16: “For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life—is not from the Father but from the world.”

In its immediate context, the apostle John warns believers not to love the world. The “desires of the eyes” (Greek *epithymia tōn ophthalmōn*) refers to covetous longing stirred by sight: wanting what looks attractive, impressive, or enviable, whether material goods, status symbols, physical beauty used for self-gratification, or anything that promises satisfaction apart from God. It is closely tied to the Tenth Commandment’s prohibition against coveting (Exodus 20:17) and to Jesus’ warning that “everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). The eyes become a gateway for disordered desire that treats created things as ultimate.

This is not mere appreciation of beauty or lawful enjoyment of God’s gifts. It is the restless hunger that says, “I must have that,” elevating the visible and temporary above the eternal. Theologically it belongs to the broader category of concupiscence (inordinate desire) that flows from our fallen nature and stands opposed to the love of the Father.

A concrete way to fight it is to practice deliberate redirection of sight and desire: when something visual stirs covetousness or impure longing, turn immediately to prayer and to Scripture that reorients the heart (for example, Psalm 119:37: “Turn my eyes away from worthless things; revive me with Your word”). Regularly fix your gaze on Christ in the Word and in the gathered church, asking the Holy Spirit to cultivate contentment and gratitude instead of craving.

question: What does the Bible say about Voodoo? How should a Christian view Voodoo?
answer:
The Bible does not mention Voodoo by name, yet it clearly and repeatedly forbids the core practices that define it: spirit worship, consulting the dead or lesser spirits, sorcery, charms, curses, and any attempt to manipulate spiritual powers apart from the one true God.

Scripture treats these as idolatry and occult rebellion. In Deuteronomy 18:10–12 the Lord says, “Let no one be found among you who sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire, practices divination or conjury, interprets omens, practices sorcery, casts spells, consults a medium or spiritist, or inquires of the dead. For whoever does these things is detestable to the LORD.” Leviticus 19:31 adds, “You must not turn to mediums or spiritists; do not seek them out, or you will be defiled by them. I am the LORD your God.” Galatians 5:19–21 lists sorcery among the works of the flesh that exclude people from the kingdom of God, and 1 Corinthians 10:20–21 warns that pagan sacrifices are offered to demons, not to God: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too.”

Voodoo (whether Haitian Vodou, Louisiana Voodoo, or related West African traditions) centers on serving loa/lwa (spirits), ancestral veneration, ritual possession, magical workings, and often syncretism with Catholic saints. The Bible identifies such spirits as demonic counterfeits, not benevolent guides or ancestors to be honored in worship. God alone is to be feared, trusted, and approached (Exodus 20:3–5; Isaiah 8:19–20). Any system that seeks power, protection, healing, or guidance through spirits other than the triune God places a person in spiritual danger and under God’s judgment.

A Christian must therefore view Voodoo as incompatible with faith in Jesus Christ. It is not a neutral cultural expression or harmless folk practice; it is a form of idolatry that opens doors to demonic influence and keeps people from the true and living God. Participation, even out of curiosity, tradition, or desperation, is sin. The call of Scripture is clear: turn from every false spiritual power and cling to Christ alone.

Jesus Christ is the only mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5). He alone died on the cross as the perfect atoning sacrifice for sin, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, triumphing over every power and authority (Colossians 2:15). Those who repent of occult involvement and trust in Him receive full forgiveness, freedom from spiritual bondage, and the indwelling Holy Spirit. If you or someone you love has been involved in Voodoo, the path forward is to renounce it completely, destroy any related objects (Acts 19:18–19), confess it to God and to mature believers in a local church, and rest in the finished work of Christ.

A practical next step is to open the Gospel of John and read slowly, asking God to show you the supremacy of Jesus over every spirit. Then speak with a pastor or elder in a Bible-believing church who can walk with you in prayer and discipleship. The Lord is mighty to save and to set captives free.

question: What is the meaning of Lent?
answer:
**Lent is a traditional season of about 40 days (not counting Sundays) leading up to Easter Sunday, observed by many Christians as a time of prayer, fasting, repentance, and spiritual preparation that recalls Jesus’ 40 days of fasting and temptation in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13).**

It is a non-essential practice where faithful Christians may disagree. Scripture does not command a yearly Lenten season, so observance falls under Christian liberty and matters of conscience rather than a required mark of orthodoxy (Romans 14:5–6; Colossians 2:16–17).

Two major historic approaches illustrate the range:
- Many liturgical traditions (such as Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican, and some Lutheran or Methodist churches) treat Lent as a valuable, structured season of self-examination, almsgiving, and intensified devotion that helps believers prepare their hearts for the celebration of Christ’s death and resurrection.
- Many evangelical, Reformed, and Baptist churches do not formally observe Lent on the church calendar. They emphasize that repentance, prayer, fasting, and focus on the cross are callings for the whole Christian life rather than one season, and they caution against any practice that could become merely external or burdensome.

In the Reformed Baptist tradition shaped by the 1689 London Baptist Confession, Lent is not prescribed. Believers are free to use (or not use) seasons of focused fasting and prayer as a personal aid to godliness, provided it remains voluntary, gospel-centered, and free of superstition or merit-seeking. The heart of the matter is always Christ Himself: His perfect obedience, penal substitutionary atonement on the cross, and bodily resurrection, received by grace alone through faith alone.

If you find a season of intentional repentance and Scripture meditation helpful, you might choose a simple plan such as reading through the Gospel accounts of the passion or setting aside regular time for confession and thanksgiving. Whatever rhythm you adopt, let it drive you to deeper reliance on Jesus rather than self-denial for its own sake. How has the approach of your local church or your own walk shaped your thinking about seasons like this?

question: What doth every sin deserve?
answer:
Every sin deserves God’s wrath and curse, both in this life and in the life to come.

Scripture teaches this plainly. “For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23). Death here is not merely physical; it includes spiritual separation from God and the just penalty of His holy judgment. Paul also writes that “the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men” (Romans 1:18), and that those who remain in sin are “by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2:3). Galatians 3:10 adds, “Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law.”

Even one sin is cosmic treason against the infinitely holy God. Because He is perfectly just, every violation of His law—whether in thought, word, or deed—merits His righteous anger and the curse of condemnation. This is not harshness for its own sake; it is the necessary expression of God’s unchanging holiness and justice.

Yet the same Bible that announces this deserved wrath also announces the only escape. Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, took that wrath and curse upon Himself at the cross. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). He died in the place of sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, securing full forgiveness and peace with God for all who turn from sin and trust in Him alone.

If this truth weighs on your conscience, do not try to atone for yourself by effort or religious performance. Repent and believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, who bore the wrath your sins deserve, and you will be saved. Speak honestly with God about your need, and seek out a faithful local church where the gospel is preached and believers can walk with you.

question: What does the Bible say about diligence?
answer:
The Bible consistently commends diligence as a wise and godly virtue that honors the Lord, produces fruit, and contrasts sharply with laziness or sluggishness. Diligence means steady, careful, and wholehearted effort in work, responsibilities, and the pursuit of godliness.

In the Old Testament, Proverbs especially highlights this theme. “Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth” (Proverbs 10:4). “The hand of the diligent will rule, but laziness ends in forced labor” (Proverbs 12:24). “The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, but the soul of the diligent is richly supplied” (Proverbs 13:4). “The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty” (Proverbs 21:5). These sayings present diligence as part of living wisely under God’s design for human labor and stewardship.

The New Testament carries the same call into everyday work and spiritual life. Believers are told, “Do not let your zeal subside; keep your spiritual fervor, serving the Lord” (Romans 12:11). Paul writes, “Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men, because you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving” (Colossians 3:23-24). Peter urges, “For this very reason, make every effort to add to your faith virtue; and to virtue, knowledge” (2 Peter 1:5), showing that diligence belongs to progressive growth in Christlikeness. Hebrews likewise exhorts, “We want each of you to show this same diligence to the very end, in order to make your hope sure. Then you will not be sluggish, but will imitate those who through faith and patience inherit what has been promised” (Hebrews 6:11-12).

Biblically, diligence is never mere self-powered striving. It flows from faith, gratitude for grace, and the desire to please God who has already accepted us in Christ. It is an expression of faithful stewardship of the time, gifts, and callings He has given, and it belongs to the Spirit’s work of sanctification as we use the ordinary means of grace (Scripture, prayer, and fellowship).

A concrete next step is to choose one ordinary area of your life this week (your work, a family duty, or a spiritual habit such as daily Bible reading) and deliberately practice wholehearted effort there as service to Christ, asking Him each morning for strength to be diligent rather than half-hearted.

question: What is agnosticism?
answer:
**Agnosticism** is the view that the existence of God (or ultimate reality) is unknown or unknowable. An agnostic typically claims neither firm belief that God exists nor firm denial that He does; instead, the person holds that sufficient evidence is lacking or that such knowledge lies beyond human reach.

The term comes from the Greek *a-* (“without”) and *gnōsis* (“knowledge”). It differs from atheism (which asserts there is no God) by remaining suspended in uncertainty rather than making a positive denial. Some agnostics are “soft” (open to evidence) while others are “hard” (convinced the question is permanently unanswerable).

Scripture does not treat knowledge of God as unreachable. The Bible teaches that God has made Himself known through creation and conscience so that people are “without excuse”: “For what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse” (Romans 1:19-20). Special revelation in Scripture and supremely in Jesus Christ further removes the claim of total unknowability (John 1:18; Hebrews 1:1-3).

Christians therefore regard agnosticism as an unstable middle position: the created order, moral law written on the heart, and the historical resurrection of Jesus supply real knowledge of God, calling every person to move from uncertainty to trust. If you are wrestling with questions about God’s existence, a helpful next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly and ask God (even if tentatively) to show you whether Jesus is who He claimed to be.

question: What does it mean to “be angry and do not sin” (Psalm 4:4)?
answer:
**“Be angry and do not sin” means that anger itself is not automatically sinful, yet it must be restrained so that it does not give birth to sinful words, actions, or lingering bitterness.**

In Psalm 4:4 the Berean Standard Bible reads: “Be angry, yet do not sin; on your bed, search your heart and be still. Selah.” David is addressing people who are agitated, perhaps over injustice or personal trouble. He does not forbid the emotion of anger; he commands that it stay within holy bounds. The same wording is taken up by the apostle Paul in Ephesians 4:26–27: “Be angry, yet do not sin. Do not let the sun set upon your anger, and do not give the devil a foothold.”

### What the phrase protects and prohibits
- **Righteous indignation is possible.** Scripture shows holy anger: God is “angry with the wicked every day” (Psalm 7:11), Jesus looked around “with anger, grieved by their hardness of heart” (Mark 3:5), and believers are told to hate what is evil (Romans 12:9). Anger aimed at real evil, injustice, or dishonor to God can be a fitting response.
- **Sinful anger is forbidden.** The moment anger becomes self-centered rage, nurses grudges, seeks personal revenge, explodes in harsh speech, or settles into resentment, it crosses into sin (James 1:19–20; Proverbs 29:11; Matthew 5:22). That kind of anger “does not produce the righteousness that God desires.”

### Practical shape of obedience
The psalm itself supplies the next step: “on your bed, search your heart and be still.” When anger rises,
1. Pause before you speak or act.
2. Examine the motive: Is this zeal for God’s glory and true justice, or wounded pride and the desire to win?
3. Bring it quickly to the Lord in prayer rather than letting it simmer overnight (Ephesians 4:26).
4. Seek reconciliation or righteous action as soon as possible, refusing to give the devil a foothold through prolonged bitterness.

In short, the command is not “never feel anger,” but “rule the anger that you feel so that it serves love and holiness rather than destroying them.” When we fail, the same gospel that justifies us by grace through faith in Christ’s finished work also restores us; we confess the sin, receive cleansing (1 John 1:9), and keep walking in the Spirit who produces self-control.

question: How will the covenant with death be annulled (Isaiah 28:18)?
answer:
**The covenant with death in Isaiah 28:18 will be annulled by the overwhelming scourge of God’s judgment, which will pass through and trample those who trusted in their false refuge.**

Isaiah 28 addresses the proud leaders of Judah (and earlier Ephraim) who boasted of a “covenant with death” and an “agreement with Sheol.” They imagined that lies and political alliances would shield them when judgment came (Isaiah 28:15). God replies that this covenant “will be annulled” (or dissolved) and “will not stand.” The very disaster they thought they had escaped—the “overwhelming scourge”—will sweep over them and crush them (Isaiah 28:18–19). Their man-made security is exposed as worthless because the Lord Himself brings the judgment and measures everything by the plumb line of justice and righteousness (Isaiah 28:17).

In the same breath God sets forth the true alternative: “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken” (Isaiah 28:16). That cornerstone is fulfilled in Jesus Christ (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:6–8). All human schemes that promise safety apart from Him—whether political power, self-righteousness, or denial of coming judgment—are covenants with death that God will cancel. Only faith resting on Christ, the sure foundation, endures.

This passage therefore calls us to abandon every false refuge and cling to the One who alone cancels the real covenant of death incurred by our sin through His cross and resurrection. If you are resting on anything else today, turn to Him in repentance and trust; He is the only foundation that cannot be swept away.

question: What is the Hindu caste system?
answer:
The Hindu caste system is a traditional hereditary social hierarchy in Hinduism that ranks people into fixed groups based primarily on birth, with roots in ancient texts such as the Rig Veda and later law codes like the Manusmriti. It organizes society around the four main varnas (classes): Brahmins (priests and teachers), Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), Vaishyas (merchants and farmers), and Shudras (laborers and servants), while those outside the system, often called Dalits or "untouchables," have historically faced severe exclusion and discrimination.

This structure is tied to Hindu concepts of dharma (duty according to one's caste), karma (actions determining rebirth), and samsara (the cycle of reincarnation), teaching that one's position results from previous lives and must be accepted to progress spiritually. In practice it has shaped marriage, occupation, diet, and social interaction for centuries in India and among some diaspora communities, though modern Indian law formally abolished caste discrimination and many reformers have challenged its rigidity.

The Bible presents a sharply different vision of human dignity and society. Scripture teaches that every person is created in the image of God with equal worth, regardless of birth, ethnicity, or status (Genesis 1:27). In Christ, earthly divisions of class or heritage are overcome: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). The gospel calls people from every background to repent and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God without partiality.

question: What does the Bible say about rest and relaxation?
answer:
The Bible presents rest as a good gift from God, woven into creation itself, commanded for human flourishing, and ultimately fulfilled in the spiritual rest found through faith in Jesus Christ.

In the beginning, God Himself modeled rest. After six days of creating, “by the seventh day God had finished the work He had been doing, so on that day He rested from all His work. Then God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on that day He rested from all the work of creation that He had accomplished” (Genesis 2:2-3). This was not because God was weary, but to set a pattern of ceasing from labor and delighting in what He had made. He later codified this for Israel in the fourth commandment: “Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God” (Exodus 20:8-10). The Sabbath protected workers, families, and even animals from endless toil, reminding God’s people that their worth and provision come from Him, not from ceaseless productivity (Exodus 20:11; Deuteronomy 5:14-15).

Jesus affirmed the goodness of rest while revealing its deeper purpose. He invited the weary: “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light” (Matthew 11:28-30). He also told His disciples, “Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while” (Mark 6:31), showing that physical withdrawal and renewal matter. At the same time, Jesus is “Lord of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:28), and the New Testament points to a greater rest: entering God’s rest by faith, ceasing from dead works, and trusting Christ’s finished work (Hebrews 4:9-11). Physical rest is real and needed; the deepest rest is justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

Scripture also guards against two opposite errors. On one side, it rebukes laziness and idle neglect of duty: “How long will you lie there, O sluggard? When will you get up from your sleep?” (Proverbs 6:9). Work is honorable, and “if anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). On the other side, it warns against anxious, restless striving that forgets God’s care: “In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat—for He gives sleep to His beloved” (Psalm 127:2). Rest is not optional self-indulgence; it is trust expressed in stopping.

A concrete next step is to set apart one half-day this week—perhaps the Lord’s Day or another quiet block—to cease ordinary work, read a Gospel passage slowly (start with Matthew 11), thank God for Christ’s finished work, and simply enjoy His good gifts without productivity pressure. Talk with a mature believer in your local church about how they practice rhythms of rest so you can encourage one another. True rest begins when you turn from self-reliance and trust the One who died and rose for you.

question: What is deism? What do deists believe?
answer:
**Deism** is the belief that a supreme God created the universe and established its natural laws, but does not intervene in it afterward through miracles, revelation, providence, or personal relationship.

### What Deists Typically Believe
Deists generally hold that:
- God exists as a rational, distant Creator (often compared to a watchmaker who designs and winds a watch, then lets it run on its own).
- The universe operates by fixed natural laws discoverable through human reason and observation of nature.
- Special revelation (such as the Bible as inspired Scripture), miracles, prophecy, the incarnation, the Trinity, and answered prayer are rejected as unnecessary or contrary to reason.
- Morality and knowledge of God come primarily from reason and the created order, not from Scripture or divine intervention.
- Many classical deists (especially in the 17th–18th centuries, like some Enlightenment thinkers) affirmed a form of divine judgment or afterlife based on moral living, while others were more skeptical.

Deism arose largely as a reaction against perceived excesses of institutional religion and supernatural claims, emphasizing natural theology over revealed religion.

### Biblical Contrast
Scripture presents a very different God: not a remote architect, but the living, personal, triune God who actively sustains creation, speaks through His Word, works miracles, entered history in the person of Jesus Christ, and relates to His people. 

- God is intimately involved: “The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature, upholding all things by His powerful word” (Hebrews 1:3). 
- He reveals Himself specially: “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). 
- He acts redemptively in history, most clearly in the incarnation, atoning death, and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ.

Christians affirm that general revelation in nature points to God’s existence and power (Romans 1:19–20; Psalm 19:1), yet it is insufficient for salvation; we need the gospel of Christ crucified and risen. Deism’s distant deity cannot account for the God who “so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son” (John 3:16) or who draws near to the brokenhearted.

If you are exploring this because of questions about God’s involvement in the world, suffering, or how we can know Him, I am glad to discuss further from Scripture.

question: Is the distinction between clergy and laity biblical?
answer:
No, the rigid distinction between a special clerical caste and ordinary laity is not biblical; Scripture teaches the priesthood of all believers while establishing functional offices of elder and deacon for leadership and service in the church.

Some historic traditions (such as Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and certain Anglican views) argue that ordained clergy form a distinct priestly order with unique sacramental authority and mediating functions, continuing aspects of Old Testament priesthood through apostolic succession.

From a Reformed Baptist perspective, every true Christian is a priest with direct access to God through Christ the sole Mediator, yet the New Testament clearly appoints qualified elders (also called overseers or pastors) to teach, govern, and shepherd, and deacons to serve, without creating a hierarchical spiritual class. 

The New Testament never uses the word “priest” for Christian ministers; that title belongs to Christ alone as our great High Priest and to the entire people of God. First Peter 2:5 and 1 Peter 2:9 declare that believers are “a holy priesthood” and “a royal priesthood,” offering spiritual sacrifices and proclaiming God’s excellencies. Revelation 1:6 and Revelation 5:10 echo the same truth: Christ has made us “a kingdom, priests to His God and Father.” First Timothy 2:5 anchors this reality: “For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”

At the same time, God gifts and appoints leaders. Ephesians 4:11–12 shows that Christ gave “the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for works of ministry.” First Timothy 3:1–13 and Titus 1:5–9 give clear qualifications for overseers and deacons. Hebrews 13:17 calls the church to “obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls.” These are real offices with real authority, yet they exist to equip the whole body, not to monopolize ministry or stand as a mediating priesthood.

The practical difference is profound: no minister stands between you and God, and every believer is called to serve according to the gifts the Spirit has given. A healthy next step is to examine your own local church’s practice of eldership and member service in light of these texts, then talk with your elders about how you can grow in both receiving shepherding care and exercising your priestly calling in the body.

question: What does it mean to have a wilderness experience?
answer:
A wilderness experience is a season of spiritual testing, dryness, isolation, or hardship in which God strips away self-reliance, deepens dependence on Him, and prepares His people for greater fruitfulness or clarity in their walk with Christ.

Scripture repeatedly portrays the wilderness this way. After the exodus, the Lord led Israel through the wilderness for forty years “to humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments” (Deuteronomy 8:2). He allowed hunger so they would learn that “man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the Lord” (Deuteronomy 8:3). Jesus Himself was “led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil” (Matthew 4:1), emerging ready for public ministry. Moses spent years in Midian, Elijah fled to the desert, and David hid in wilderness strongholds—each time God used the barren place to shape character, reveal Himself, and ready His servants.

These seasons are not always punishment. They often serve progressive sanctification: God exposes idols, silences competing voices, and trains us to trust His provision and presence when comforts are removed. The same God who met Hagar by a spring, fed Elijah by ravens, and sent angels to minister to Jesus still meets His people in lonely places. The wilderness can feel like abandonment, yet it is frequently the classroom of grace where faith is refined “more precious than gold” (1 Peter 1:7).

If you are in such a season, take one concrete step today: open the Psalms (especially Psalm 63 or Psalm 42) and pray the words honestly back to God, telling Him the dryness or fear you feel and asking Him to satisfy you with His steadfast love. Stay connected to a local church body; isolation is part of the trial, but God normally uses the fellowship of believers as one of His means of grace.

question: What does Malachi 2:16 mean when God says, ‘I hate divorce’?
answer:
**Malachi 2:16** means that God detests divorce as an act of covenant treachery that harms the spouse and violates the sacred bond He established in marriage.

In the Berean Standard Bible the verse reads: “For I hate divorce,” says the LORD, the God of Israel. “And he who covers his garment with violence,” says the LORD of Hosts. “So guard yourselves in your spirit, and do not break faith.” The immediate context (Malachi 2:10–16) addresses men in post-exilic Judah who were dealing treacherously with the wives of their youth, divorcing them (often to marry foreign women who led them into idolatry). Marriage is called a “covenant” before God (Malachi 2:14), so breaking it is faithlessness that “covers one’s garment with violence,” a vivid picture of injustice and harm done to the abandoned wife. God hates this because it assaults the one-flesh union He created (Genesis 2:24) and mirrors the unfaithfulness Israel had shown toward Him.

This does not mean every divorce is unforgivable or that God never permits it. Jesus later explains that Moses allowed divorce because of the hardness of human hearts, yet from the beginning it was not so; He permits it in cases of sexual immorality (Matthew 19:3–9). Paul adds the case of an unbelieving spouse who abandons a believer (1 Corinthians 7:12–15). Still, the plain force of Malachi 2:16 stands: divorce is grievous to God, never His ideal, and often the fruit of sin that needs repentance.

Faithful Christians have differed on the precise grounds and whether remarriage is always permitted after a biblical divorce. Some hold a very strict permanence view (divorce and remarriage only after death); others accept the Matthean and Pauline exceptions as legitimate releases from the bond. Both seek to honor Scripture’s high view of the marriage covenant.

The call of the text is clear and pastoral: “Guard yourselves in your spirit, and do not break faith.” If you are married, pursue covenant faithfulness through prayer, repentance where needed, and the ordinary means of grace in a local church. If you have experienced divorce, the same God who hates the destruction it brings still offers full forgiveness and cleansing through the atoning death and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ. Turn from sin and trust in Him alone; He restores the broken. Speak with a trusted pastor or mature believer in your church for counsel tailored to your situation, and ask the Lord for a heart that treasures the permanence and purity He designed.

question: How transparent should church finances be?
answer:
**Church finances should be meaningfully transparent to the congregation**, with clear reporting, accountable oversight, and enough detail for members to exercise wise stewardship and trust, while protecting legitimate privacy and security.

This is a matter of wise church practice and Christian liberty rather than a core doctrine that defines the faith. Faithful churches can differ on the exact degree and format of disclosure (for example, how much salary detail or vendor information is shared, or whether reports go beyond members) because Scripture emphasizes integrity and accountability more than a single mandated spreadsheet format. Romans 14 reminds us to extend charity in disputable matters of application.

### Biblical Foundations
Scripture treats church resources as the Lord’s money entrusted to stewards, not private funds. Leaders must handle them above reproach:
- Paul deliberately arranged the collection for Jerusalem with multiple trustworthy men so “no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man” (2 Corinthians 8:20-21). Transparency guards against suspicion.
- Elders/overseers must be “above reproach” and “not greedy for gain” (Titus 1:7; 1 Peter 5:2-3), which is far easier to demonstrate when finances are open to godly scrutiny.
- The early church practiced open sharing and accountability under the apostles (Acts 4:32-37), and deception about money brought severe judgment (Acts 5:1-11).
- Broader wisdom literature calls for honest scales and faithful handling of another’s resources (Proverbs 11:1; Luke 16:10-12). Congregations that give are right to expect clear reporting on how the money advances the gospel, cares for needs, and supports qualified workers (1 Corinthians 9:14; Galatians 6:6; 1 Timothy 5:17-18).

### Two Common Approaches Among Faithful Churches
- **High congregational transparency**: Annual (or more frequent) detailed budgets, actual income/expense reports, and major decisions are presented to members for review or vote. Many elder-led congregational churches (including those shaped by confessions like the 1689) practice this because the congregation bears responsibility for the church’s doctrine and order; members can ask questions, and salaries or large expenditures are not hidden. This builds trust and guards against abuse.
- **More limited or filtered reporting**: Some churches share summary budgets and key categories with members while keeping individual staff compensation ranges, donor names, or sensitive security-related items restricted to elders or a finance team. The aim is still accountability, but with added protection for privacy, staff families, or risk management. Hierarchical or larger institutional settings sometimes lean this way.

Both can be practiced with integrity when the motive is faithfulness rather than concealment. What is *not* compatible with biblical stewardship is chronic secrecy, unaccountable control by one person, resistance to reasonable questions, or lavish spending that contradicts the gospel’s call to generosity and simplicity of life.

### Practical Guidance
In a healthy church the elders (and any finance team) should be able to explain the budget in light of the church’s mission—Word ministry, care for members, mercy, and missions—without defensiveness. Members should be able to see that funds are used lawfully, prudently, and for kingdom purposes. Many churches find it wise to:
- Provide written financial reports at least annually (and ideally more often).
- Have multiple signatories, outside or internal review, and clear policies.
- Distinguish between general-fund transparency and the confidentiality of individual gifts (Matthew 6:2-4).

If you are a member, a concrete next step is to read your church’s governing documents, review the most recent financial summary, and humbly ask an elder or treasurer how decisions are made and reported. If something seems unclear, raise it graciously with the aim of strengthening trust, not suspicion. If you lead, model the openness of 2 Corinthians 8 so that the church’s handling of money adorns the gospel rather than distracts from it.

Transparency serves love and unity when it helps the body give cheerfully, pray specifically, and hold leaders accountable as fellow stewards under Christ, the Head of the church.

question: Is intinction the correct way to do communion?
answer:
**No, intinction is not required or the single “correct” way to observe the Lord’s Supper.**

Intinction (dipping the bread into the cup so both elements are received together) is a practice some historic Christian traditions have used for convenience, reverence, or pastoral care, yet Scripture records Jesus taking the bread, giving thanks, breaking it, and distributing it, then separately taking the cup, giving thanks, and giving it (Matthew 26:26–27; Mark 14:22–23; Luke 22:19–20; 1 Corinthians 11:23–25). The apostolic pattern therefore presents two distinct actions with the two elements.

Many faithful Christians who practice intinction argue it still conveys the one sacrifice of Christ and can guard against spilling or accommodate those unable to drink easily, viewing the mode as a matter of edifying order rather than essence.  

As a matter of secondary practice shaped by the plain pattern of institution, I hold that the elements are best received separately (bread then cup) so that the church visibly follows Christ’s own words and actions, “Take, eat” and “Drink of it, all of you,” while still affirming His spiritual presence nourishing believers by faith. This remains an area where churches may differ in charity without breaking fellowship, provided the Supper is kept as a memorial of Christ’s body and blood, received by baptized believers in a worthy manner (1 Corinthians 11:27–29).

If your church is wrestling with the question, the most helpful next step is to open 1 Corinthians 11 together with your elders, pray for unity in the truth, and ask how the congregation can most clearly proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.

question: What is the church suffering?
answer:
The church suffers trials, persecution, and afflictions in this present age, just as Jesus promised His followers would. He said, “If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first” (John 15:18), and “In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Scripture treats this as a normal mark of faithful discipleship, not a strange exception: “Indeed, all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (2 Timothy 3:12).

Biblically, the church’s suffering takes several forms. Externally it faces hostility from a world opposed to Christ—ridicule, legal pressure, violence, or social exclusion—because the gospel confronts sin and idolatry. Internally it endures false teaching, division, moral failure, and spiritual attack, as Paul warned the Ephesian elders that “savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock” (Acts 20:29). Believers also share in the sufferings of Christ Himself, so that His life is displayed in us (Philippians 3:10; Colossians 1:24; 2 Corinthians 4:10–11). None of this is pointless. God uses it to refine faith, produce endurance, deepen dependence on Him, and display the surpassing worth of Christ (1 Peter 1:6–7; Romans 5:3–5; James 1:2–4).

At the same time, the church is never abandoned. Christ is present with His people (Matthew 28:20), the Spirit helps us in our weakness (Romans 8:26), and the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed (Romans 8:18). Final justice and restoration are certain when Jesus returns to judge and renew all things.

If you are walking through a season of hardship in your local congregation—whether persecution, conflict, or weariness—stay planted in the ordinary means of grace: the Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, and the fellowship of believers. One concrete next step is to pray regularly for the persecuted church worldwide and for your own elders and members, asking God for steadfastness and gospel boldness. You might also open 1 Peter with a trusted brother or sister and talk through how its teaching lands in your situation.

What particular suffering or situation prompted your question? I am glad to listen and point further to Scripture.

question: What does it mean that a person will not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:9-11)?
answer:
**It means that those who practice unrighteousness as an ongoing, unrepentant way of life will not enter or possess God’s eternal kingdom.**

In 1 Corinthians 6:9-11 the apostle Paul writes: “Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God. And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”

“Inherit the kingdom of God” refers to receiving eternal life and sharing in the full blessings of God’s reign, both now in union with Christ and forever in the new creation (see also Galatians 5:19-21; Ephesians 5:5; Revelation 21:7-8). Paul is not teaching that a single stumble or past sin automatically bars someone forever. He is warning that a settled pattern of unrepentant sin—living as “the unrighteous”—is incompatible with belonging to Christ. Those whose lives are characterized by these practices show they have not been truly converted.

The list is representative, not exhaustive. It names sins that violate God’s holy design for sexuality, worship, property, speech, and self-control. Scripture treats them as real moral evils that separate people from a holy God (Romans 1:18-32; 1 John 3:4-10). God is both loving and just; His wrath against sin is real, and He will not overlook unrepentant rebellion.

Yet the gospel hope blazes in verse 11: “And that is what some of you were.” Some in the Corinthian church had lived in exactly these patterns. Then came the decisive change: they were **washed** (cleansed from guilt), **sanctified** (set apart as holy), and **justified** (declared righteous) through faith in Jesus Christ and by the Holy Spirit. This is penal substitutionary atonement applied—Christ died for sinners, rose bodily, and now transforms those who trust Him. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by cleaning ourselves up first (Ephesians 2:8-9; Titus 3:3-7).

If you see yourself in any part of that list, or feel the weight of guilt, the same grace is offered today. Turn (repent) from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. He receives all who come to Him.

A concrete next step: Open 1 Corinthians 6 slowly this week, pray through each verse asking the Lord to search your heart (Psalm 139:23-24), and speak with a trusted pastor or mature believer in a local church about walking in repentance and faith. God delights to save and keep those who belong to His Son.

question: Is it wise for Christian teens to be dating?
answer:
**No, recreational dating is generally unwise for most Christian teens.** Scripture calls young people to pursue purity, self-control, and wisdom rather than premature romantic pairing that often stirs desires before the proper time and context of marriage.

The Bible never endorses modern “dating” as a recreational activity. Instead it warns, “Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right” (Song of Solomon 2:7; 3:5; 8:4). It commands believers to “flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18) and to treat one another “with absolute purity” (1 Timothy 5:2). Proverbs repeatedly urges the young to guard the heart, pursue wisdom, and honor father and mother (Proverbs 4:23; Proverbs 1:8–9). Because teenage years are typically a season of incomplete maturity, limited life experience, and heightened temptation, pairing off one-on-one frequently leads to emotional entanglement, physical compromise, or heartbreak that distracts from growing in Christ.

Faithful Christians have differed on the exact form relationships should take before marriage (some prefer group fellowship and delayed one-on-one time; others allow carefully supervised courtship when marriage is a realistic near-term possibility). What is not optional is sexual purity, parental involvement, and the understanding that romantic affection is ordered toward covenant marriage, not casual experimentation (Hebrews 13:4; Genesis 2:24).

A wiser path for most teens is to:
- Invest heavily in friendships, family, church community, and personal godliness.
- Treat peers of the opposite sex as brothers and sisters in Christ.
- Wait until you are mature enough, spiritually and practically, for a relationship that is intentionally moving toward marriage under the counsel of parents and church elders.

If you are already in a dating relationship or feeling pressure to date, talk openly with your parents or a trusted pastor this week. Ask them to help you evaluate motives, set clear boundaries, and refocus on Christ. Read 1 Thessalonians 4:1–8 together and pray for a heart that treasures purity and trusts God’s timing more than cultural expectations. The Lord is kind to those who seek Him first; He will not withhold any good thing from those who walk uprightly (Psalm 84:11).

question: Why does God allow us to go through trials and tribulations?
answer:
**God allows trials and tribulations for our ultimate good and His glory, refining our faith, producing Christlike character, and drawing us closer to Himself.**

Trials hurt. They can leave us weary, confused, or wondering if God has forgotten us. Scripture never pretends otherwise. Yet the Bible consistently teaches that our sovereign, wise, and loving Father does not waste suffering. He uses it purposefully in the lives of His children.

### Key Biblical Purposes
God uses hardship to **test and purify our faith**, much like fire refines gold so that what is genuine remains and shines. The apostle Peter writes: “In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in various trials, so that the proven character of your faith—more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire—may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:6-7). James adds that we can “consider it pure joy… whenever you face trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith develops perseverance. Allow perseverance to finish its work, so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything” (James 1:2-4).

Trials also produce **endurance, character, and hope**. Paul explains: “Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope. And hope does not disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5:3-5). This is part of progressive **sanctification**—the Holy Spirit’s work of making us more like Jesus.

Our Father lovingly **disciplines** those He receives as sons and daughters, not to crush us but to train us in holiness: “God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His holiness. No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:10-11). He is conforming us to the image of His Son (Romans 8:28-29), and that process often involves the removal of self-reliance, worldly attachments, and remaining sin.

Suffering can also display God’s strength in our weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9-10), equip us to comfort others with the comfort we ourselves have received (2 Corinthians 1:3-4), and keep us humble and dependent on grace. Even Jesus, though sinless, “learned obedience from what He suffered” (Hebrews 5:8) and is able to sympathize with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15-16).

### The Bigger Story
None of this means God authors evil or delights in our pain. He is holy, good, and just. Because of human sin, the world is broken (Genesis 3; Romans 8:20-22). Yet God remains sovereign over every trial and works all things together for the good of those who love Him and are called according to His purpose (Romans 8:28). The cross itself is the supreme example: the greatest evil became the means of our redemption through Christ’s penal substitutionary atonement—His death in our place and His bodily resurrection.

If you belong to Christ by grace through faith, your trials are not random or meaningless. They are under the hand of a Father who will not let you finally fall away (perseverance of the saints) and who promises that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed (Romans 8:18).

### A Next Step
Bring your specific trial honestly to the Lord in prayer today. Tell Him the pain, the questions, and the fear. Then open Scripture—perhaps slowly reading Romans 8, James 1, or Psalm 23—and ask the Holy Spirit to steady your heart with His truth. Share the burden with a mature believer or elder in your local church so you do not walk alone.

God has not abandoned you in the fire. He is with you in it, and He is faithful to finish the good work He began (Philippians 1:6).

question: What does Deuteronomy 10:12 tell us God requires of us?
answer:
Deuteronomy 10:12 tells us that the LORD requires His people to fear Him, walk in all His ways, love Him, and serve Him with all their heart and soul.

The verse reads: “And now, O Israel, what does the LORD your God ask of you but to fear the LORD your God by walking in all His ways, to love Him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 10:12). The next verse adds the call to keep His commandments and statutes for our good (Deuteronomy 10:13).

In its original setting, Moses is summarizing covenant faithfulness for Israel after recalling God’s mercy and the giving of the law. “Fear” here means reverent awe that leads to obedience, not cringing terror. Walking in His ways, loving Him, and serving Him wholeheartedly describe undivided loyalty, the same whole-person devotion Jesus later identifies as the greatest commandment (Matthew 22:37–38; Deuteronomy 6:5).

This is not a ladder we climb to earn standing with God; it is the grateful response of those already redeemed by His grace. For the Christian, these same requirements find their fulfillment and power in Christ, who perfectly feared, loved, and served the Father, and who now enables us by the Holy Spirit to walk in newness of life (Romans 8:3–4).

A simple next step is to pray through this verse slowly today, asking the Lord to show you one concrete area (speech, habits, relationships, or priorities) where your heart can more fully fear, love, and serve Him.

question: Is it okay to get tattoos if they are of a Christian nature?
answer:
**No, Scripture does not forbid tattoos in an absolute sense for Christians, including those of a Christian nature; this is a tertiary matter of Christian liberty where faithful believers may disagree.**

The Bible never directly addresses modern decorative or confessional tattoos in the New Testament. The main Old Testament text people cite is Leviticus 19:28: “You must not make any cuts in your bodies for the dead or put tattoo marks on yourselves. I am the LORD.” In its original context this prohibited pagan mourning and idolatrous practices common among Israel’s neighbors, not every form of body marking. Under the new covenant, ceremonial and civil aspects of the Mosaic law are fulfilled in Christ and are not binding in the same way (see Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 8:13), while the moral law continues. Passages about the body as a temple (1 Corinthians 6:19–20) primarily address sexual immorality, and the call not to conform to the world (Romans 12:2) concerns heart allegiance more than external marks.

Two common historic Christian perspectives are held with integrity:
- Some believers abstain entirely, viewing any tattoo as a potential violation of the Leviticus principle, a risk of worldly conformity, or an unwise permanent alteration of the body God gave. They emphasize stewardship and avoiding even the appearance of pagan association.
- Others see Christian-themed tattoos (crosses, Scripture verses, symbols of faith) as permissible expressions of devotion, testimony, or remembrance, provided the motive is to honor Christ rather than self-exaltation. They treat the issue under liberty of conscience since the New Testament is silent on a direct ban.

Romans 14:1–6 and Romans 14:22–23 give the framework: “Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions… Each of them should be fully convinced in his own mind… Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves. But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because his eating is not from faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin.” What is not clearly commanded or forbidden falls to personal conviction before God, love for weaker brothers and sisters, and concern for witness.

In practice, weigh permanence, your motives (is this truly for God’s glory or personal identity/image?), how it may affect your ability to serve or be received in different cultural settings, and whether it could cause a fellow believer to stumble. If you are still uncertain, pause; “everything that is not from faith is sin.” Talk it through with mature elders in your local church who know you, and search the Scriptures prayerfully (Psalm 119:105). Seek to glorify God with your body in whatever you decide (1 Corinthians 10:31).

question: What day is the Sabbath, Saturday or Sunday?
answer:
The Sabbath question is a non-essential matter where faithful Christians may disagree in good conscience, largely because the New Testament does not explicitly restate the seventh-day command in the same form as the Old Testament while clearly showing early believers gathering on the first day.

One major view holds that the Sabbath remains Saturday (the seventh day). This rests on the creation pattern in Genesis 2:2-3, the Fourth Commandment in Exodus 20:8-11, and the conviction that the moral law has not been altered. Groups such as Seventh-day Adventists and some Messianic believers follow this, seeing Sunday observance as a later tradition rather than a biblical mandate.

Another major view holds that Christians observe Sunday, the first day of the week, as the Lord’s Day. This rests on Christ’s resurrection on the first day (Matthew 28:1; Mark 16:2; Luke 24:1; John 20:1), the apostolic pattern of gathering on that day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), and John’s reference to “the Lord’s day” (Revelation 1:10). Most historic Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox churches have followed this, often treating Sunday as the Christian fulfillment or transfer of the Sabbath principle of rest and worship.

Scripture itself urges charity here: “One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. He who observes a special day does so to the Lord” (Romans 14:5-6). The greater concern is that we do not neglect assembling together (Hebrews 10:25) and that we honor Christ as Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:27-28).

In the Reformed Baptist tradition I represent, the second view is held: the Lord’s Day (Sunday) is the Christian day of worship and rest, in keeping with the resurrection and the practice of the early church. Yet this is offered as one faithful option within historic Christianity, not as a test of orthodoxy. What matters most is that you belong to a local church, hear the Word, and set aside regular time to rest in Christ’s finished work.

If you are wrestling with how to practice this personally, a simple next step is to read Romans 14 and Colossians 2:16-17 slowly this week, asking the Lord for wisdom, and then talk it over with your pastor or elders so your observance grows out of conviction rather than pressure.

question: Why did God punish Pharaoh for Abram’s lie (Genesis 12:17)?
answer:
**God afflicted Pharaoh and his household with plagues because Pharaoh had taken Sarai, who was Abram’s wife, into his house (Genesis 12:17).** The text explicitly ties the judgment to her status as Abram’s wife, not merely to the deception itself. God intervened to protect Sarai, preserve the marriage He had established, and safeguard the covenant promises He had just made to Abram.

In Genesis 12:10–20, a famine drives Abram to Egypt. Fearing for his life because of Sarai’s beauty, Abram instructs her to say she is his sister (a partial truth, since she was his half-sister, but a deliberate concealment of the marriage). Pharaoh takes her, and Abram benefits materially. Then “the LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Abram’s wife Sarai” (Genesis 12:17).
