**“Truly, truly” (or “Verily, verily”) is Jesus’ solemn way of prefacing a statement to declare that what follows is absolutely certain, authoritative, and worthy of full trust.**

In the original Greek of the New Testament, this phrase is *amēn amēn legō humin* (“Amen, amen, I say to you”). *Amen* comes from a Hebrew root meaning “firm,” “faithful,” or “true.” In Jewish practice, people normally said “Amen” at the *end* of a prayer or statement to affirm agreement. Jesus uniquely places it at the *beginning*, and in John’s Gospel He doubles it, to put His own divine stamp of certainty on the words that follow. It functions like a prophetic “Thus says the Lord,” but spoken in the first person by the Son of God Himself.

This usage appears especially in John (about 25 times), though a single “Truly I say to you” is common in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Examples include:
- John 3:3: “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.”
- John 5:24: “Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment.”
- John 8:58: “Truly, truly, I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!”

By speaking this way, Jesus claims the authority that belongs to God alone. He is not offering opinions or possibilities; He is revealing truth as the One who *is* “the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6). The doubled “Amen” underscores both the reliability of His teaching and the urgency of responding to it in faith. It is a mark of His unique identity as the incarnate Word whose every statement carries the weight of heaven.

When you encounter these words in Scripture, slow down and receive them as the very voice of Christ calling for trust and obedience. A simple next step is to read one of the “Truly, truly” passages (such as John 3 or John 5) slowly, then pray, asking the Lord to help you believe and live what He has declared with such certainty.

question: What should we learn from the tribe of Asher?
answer:
**Asher teaches us that true blessedness comes from God, that His people are called to enjoy His good gifts while walking in full obedience, and that steadfast faith can mark even a quiet tribe across generations.**

Asher was Jacob’s eighth son, born to Zilpah (Genesis 30:12-13). His name means “happy” or “blessed,” and Leah exclaimed, “How happy I am! For the women will call me happy.” That theme of happiness rooted in God’s favor runs through the tribe’s story.

### God’s Blessings of Abundance and Strength
Jacob prophesied: “Asher’s food will be rich; he shall provide royal delicacies” (Genesis 49:20). Moses later blessed the tribe: “Most blessed of sons is Asher; let him be favored by his brothers, and let him dip his foot in oil. The bolts of your gates will be iron and bronze, and your strength will equal your days” (Deuteronomy 33:24-25).

Asher’s allotted territory in the fertile northern coastal region (Joshua 19:24-31) was well suited to olive oil, grain, and trade. The lessons are plain: God delights to give good gifts, material provision can be a genuine blessing, and He supplies strength that matches the length of our days. Believers today can receive God’s common and special grace with gratitude rather than guilt, while remembering that every good gift is meant to lead us to worship the Giver (James 1:17) and to serve others.

### The Danger of Incomplete Obedience
Judges 1:31-32 records that Asher did not drive out the Canaanite inhabitants of its cities but lived among them. Like several other tribes, Asher settled for coexistence instead of full conquest. The result was lingering idolatry and weakness that affected the whole nation. Prosperity without wholehearted obedience easily becomes compromise. The call remains: enjoy God’s gifts, yet refuse to make peace with sin or half-hearted discipleship (Romans 6:12-13; 2 Corinthians 6:14-18).

### Faithfulness That Outlasts Obscurity
In the New Testament, Anna the prophetess, “of the tribe of Asher,” appears as a widow who “never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying.” She recognized the infant Jesus and “spoke about the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem” (Luke 2:36-38). Centuries after the tribe’s mixed record, God preserved a remnant of devoted faith. Asher is also named among the sealed servants of God in Revelation 7:6, showing the Lord’s keeping power.

From Anna we learn patient, habitual devotion, readiness to recognize Christ, and the joy of testifying about Him. Ordinary faithfulness in prayer, Scripture, and worship still matters, even when a family or church history is uneven.

### Practical Takeaway
Thank God specifically for the “oil” and strength He has already given you—provision, relationships, daily mercies—and ask Him to expose any area where you have grown comfortable with incomplete obedience. Then imitate Anna: set aside regular time in the Word and prayer this week, watching expectantly for Christ’s work in and around you, and speak of Him to someone who is hungry for hope. God’s desire is that His people be both richly supplied and wholly His, happy in the blessing that is found in Christ alone.

question: Why does the Bible speak against braided hair?
answer:
The Bible does not issue a blanket ban on braided hair itself. Instead, 1 Timothy 2:9–10 and 1 Peter 3:3–4 warn against elaborate, showy hairstyles (along with gold, pearls, and costly clothing) when they become a focus of outward display rather than a reflection of inner godliness and modesty.

In 1 Timothy 2:9–10 the apostle Paul writes, “Likewise, I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, but with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God.” Peter echoes the same concern: “Your beauty should not come from outward adornment such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes, but from the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God’s sight” (1 Peter 3:3–4). Both passages sit in contexts that call believers to lives marked by holiness, good works, and a quiet confidence in God rather than social status or sensual appeal.

In the first-century Greco-Roman world, “braided hair” often referred to intricate, time-consuming styles woven with gold threads, jewels, or ornaments. These were status symbols among the wealthy and could signal vanity, worldliness, or even association with temple prostitution and pagan fashion. The apostles are therefore applying a broader biblical principle of modesty and contentment: external appearance must not overshadow the heart’s devotion or become a means of drawing attention to self (see also Proverbs 31:30; Isaiah 3:16–24 for Old Testament parallels that rebuke ostentatious display).

The issue is not the simple act of braiding hair for neatness or practicality. It is the heart motive—whether dress and grooming serve humility and love of neighbor or feed pride and distraction from Christ. This falls under Christian liberty and the call to progressive sanctification: believers are free in matters of personal appearance so long as they pursue what edifies, avoids stumbling others, and keeps the focus on the gospel (Romans 14:1–23; 1 Corinthians 10:31–33).

A practical next step is to examine your own motives before the Lord in prayer, asking whether your appearance choices (or any other habit) help you and others fix their eyes on Jesus, then talk it through with a mature believer or elder in your local church for wise accountability.

question: What is the difference between a covenant and a contract?
answer:
A contract is a negotiated, conditional agreement between roughly equal parties that rests on mutual performance and can be voided or litigated when terms are broken. A covenant, by contrast, is a solemn, binding commitment—often initiated by a greater party—sealed by oath or blood, emphasizing enduring relationship and loyalty rather than mere exchange of goods or services.

In Scripture this distinction matters deeply. God’s covenants (the Hebrew term *berith* and the Greek *diatheke*) are not business deals we haggle over; they are gracious bonds He establishes and keeps by His own faithfulness. When the Lord cut a covenant with Abram in Genesis 15, Abram was asleep while God alone passed between the pieces, pledging Himself to fulfill the promises even at the cost of His own life. The new covenant in Christ’s blood (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:6–13) likewise rests on Jesus’ perfect obedience and penal substitutionary atonement, not on our ability to keep up our end of a bargain. Justification is therefore by grace alone through faith alone, secured by God’s covenant loyalty rather than contractual merit.

This shapes everyday discipleship: you approach God as a beloved child in covenant, not as a nervous employee fearing termination. When you fail, you run to the throne of grace rather than trying to renegotiate terms. A simple next step is to read Genesis 15 and Hebrews 8 slowly this week, thanking God that His commitment to you in Christ does not rise or fall with your performance.

question: If Jesus was God, why did He say "No one is good but God alone"?
answer:
**Jesus was not denying His deity or His own goodness when He said that; He was challenging the rich young ruler to think carefully about what “good” really means and who Jesus Himself is.**

In Mark 10:17–18 we read: “As Jesus started on His way, a man ran up and knelt before Him. ‘Good Teacher,’ he asked, ‘what must I do to inherit eternal life?’ ‘Why do you call Me good?’ Jesus replied. ‘No one is good except God alone.’” (See also Luke 18:18–19.) The man approached Jesus as a respected rabbi or moral teacher. Jesus’ reply does not say “I am not good” or “I am not God.” Instead, it presses the logic of the man’s own words: absolute goodness belongs to God alone. If the man is prepared to call Jesus truly good in that ultimate sense, he must reckon with Jesus’ divine identity. If he is merely using polite flattery, he needs to stop and recognize the holy standard of the one true God.

This fits the wider witness of Scripture. Jesus is truly God and truly man (the hypostatic union). As the sinless Son, He could ask, “Which of you can prove Me guilty of sin?” (John 8:46) and receive worship without rebuke (Matthew 14:33; John 20:28). He claimed unity with the Father (“I and the Father are one,” John 10:30) and the divine name (“before Abraham was born, I am,” John 8:58). The same Gospels that record His words to the rich young ruler present Him as the unique Son who forgives sins, commands nature, and will judge the world—prerogatives that belong to God alone. His statement therefore upholds God’s exclusive moral perfection while inviting the hearer to see that perfection embodied in Christ.

The encounter also exposes the man’s self-reliance. He claimed to have kept the commandments, yet Jesus lovingly revealed the idol of wealth that still ruled his heart (Mark 10:21–22). Only God is good; therefore no one inherits eternal life by personal achievement. Salvation comes through the One who is Himself the good God incarnate—Jesus Christ, who lived the perfect life we could not live, died as a substitutionary sacrifice for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works.

You may have heard this verse used to suggest Jesus was merely a good teacher who rejected any claim to deity. That reading overlooks both the immediate challenge Jesus issues and the consistent testimony of the rest of Scripture. The Bible presents Him as the Lord who alone is good and who alone can save.

If this question stirs uncertainty about who Jesus is or where you stand with God, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. A simple next step is to read the Gospel of Mark slowly this week, asking God to show you the real Jesus, and to talk with a trusted pastor or mature believer in a local church about what you find. I am glad to keep exploring any part of this with you.

question: What does it mean that God will reveal the hidden things (Daniel 2:22 and 28)?
answer:
In Daniel 2:22 and 28, the statement that God reveals the hidden things means that the one true God alone possesses perfect knowledge of all mysteries, secrets, and future events, and He sovereignly discloses them according to His wise purposes.

Daniel is speaking to King Nebuchadnezzar after the king demanded that his wise men both recount and interpret a troubling dream he refused to describe. Human wisdom failed completely. Daniel then declares that “He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him” (Daniel 2:22), and later affirms, “there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and He has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days” (Daniel 2:28). The immediate fulfillment is that God gave Daniel both the forgotten dream and its interpretation: a statue representing successive earthly kingdoms that would be shattered by God’s everlasting kingdom.

This reveals God’s omniscience and His gracious act of divine revelation. What is concealed from human sight or reason is fully open to Him, and He chooses to make known what serves His redemptive plan. The same God who exposed the king’s private thoughts later unveiled far greater mysteries in the coming of Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). Scripture itself is the sufficient record of what God has chosen to reveal for our salvation and obedience.

A concrete next step is to bring any present uncertainty or “hidden” burden to the Lord in prayer while reading a portion of Daniel 2 slowly, asking Him to deepen your trust that nothing in your life lies outside His knowledge or care.

question: What items should be included in a church constitution?
answer:
A church constitution (sometimes paired with bylaws) is a governing document that describes how a local congregation will order its life under the lordship of Christ and the authority of Scripture. It is not itself inspired, yet it wisely applies biblical principles of church order so that the body can walk in unity, clarity, and accountability.

### Core Items to Include
Most faithful congregations include the following elements:

1. **Name, Purpose, and Affiliation**  
   State the church’s legal name, its biblical mission (worship, discipleship, evangelism, and mutual care), and any voluntary associations with like-minded churches while affirming local-church autonomy.

2. **Statement of Faith**  
   Affirm the essential doctrines of the Christian faith (Trinity, deity and humanity of Christ, authority of Scripture, justification by faith alone, etc.). Many Reformed Baptist churches adopt or summarize the 1689 London Baptist Confession as their confessional standard, making clear what the church believes and teaches.

3. **Church Covenant**  
   A brief, mutual pledge among members to walk together in love, holiness, prayer, and accountability, rooted in passages such as Romans 12:9–21 and Ephesians 4:1–6.

4. **Membership**  
   Define biblical qualifications (credible profession of faith, believer’s baptism by immersion, and commitment to the church’s doctrine and life), the process of reception, duties of members, and how membership may be transferred or ended.

5. **Church Officers**  
   Describe the offices of elder (pastor/overseer) and deacon, their biblical qualifications (1 Timothy 3:1–13; Titus 1:5–9), how they are recognized or elected, their respective duties, terms of service, and procedures for removal if necessary. An elder-led congregational model is common: elders lead and teach while the gathered congregation retains final authority in key decisions (Acts 6:1–6; Acts 15:22).

6. **Congregational Meetings and Decision-Making**  
   Specify regular and special meetings, quorum, voting eligibility, and which matters require congregational vote (for example, calling elders, budget approval, discipline, or major property decisions).

7. **Ordinances**  
   Affirm believer’s baptism by immersion as a sign of union with Christ and the Lord’s Supper as a means of spiritual nourishment and proclamation of His death (Matthew 28:19; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26), including who may participate.

8. **Church Discipline**  
   Outline the biblical process of formative and corrective discipline for the restoration of sinners and the purity of the church (Matthew 18:15–20; 1 Corinthians 5; Galatians 6:1), including steps, confidentiality, and possible outcomes.

9. **Finances and Property**  
   Address stewardship, budgeting, handling of gifts, and ownership of property, ensuring transparency and that assets serve the church’s gospel mission.

10. **Amendments and Dissolution**  
    Provide a clear process for amending the constitution (usually requiring prior notice and a strong congregational majority) and a dissolution clause directing remaining assets to like-minded gospel ministries if the church closes.

### Pastoral Notes
- Keep the document clear, concise, and subordinate to Scripture. It should protect the church from confusion or abuse, not create unnecessary bureaucracy.
- Because church polity is a secondary doctrine, faithful Christians differ on details (for example, the precise balance of elder authority and congregational vote, or whether to include a lengthy confession versus a shorter statement). Present your church’s convictions charitably while remaining open to refine them by the Word.
- Involve the elders and the congregation in drafting or revising it, and seek counsel from trusted confessional resources or sister churches.

If your church is writing or revising its constitution, begin by praying through relevant passages (Acts 2:42–47; 1 Timothy 3; Titus 1; Hebrews 13:17) and discussing them with your elders. A well-ordered constitution serves the gospel by helping the church remain centered on Christ, clear in doctrine, and careful in love.

question: What is topical preaching? Should a pastor preach topically?
answer:
Topical preaching is a sermon approach in which the pastor selects a theme, doctrine, or practical issue (such as prayer, anxiety, marriage, or the attributes of God) and then draws together multiple passages of Scripture that address it, rather than working consecutively through a single biblical text or book.

This question concerns a matter of homiletical method and pastoral wisdom, not a core doctrine of the faith. Faithful Christians and historic churches have differed on the balance of approaches without breaking fellowship, and Scripture itself does not prescribe only one sermon form. Christian liberty applies here (Romans 14:1–6), provided the content remains the faithful proclamation of God’s Word.

One common view holds that pastors should preach almost exclusively by consecutive exposition (working verse-by-verse or paragraph-by-paragraph through books of the Bible). The strength of this approach is that it lets the biblical authors set the agenda, guards against the preacher’s personal hobby-horses, and helps a congregation hear “the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:27). Another historic view sees legitimate room for topical or doctrinal sermons, especially when a congregation faces a pressing need, when a central doctrine must be taught systematically, or when the church calendar or pastoral circumstances call for focused application. Advocates note that the apostles themselves sometimes addressed themes across multiple texts (for example, the use of the Old Testament in Romans or Hebrews) and that Jesus taught both expositionally and thematically.

A wise and balanced practice, shaped by the priority of Scripture’s authority, is for a pastor to give the large majority of his pulpit ministry to consecutive exposition of books of the Bible while still employing topical sermons occasionally and carefully. Exposition keeps the church tethered to the full range of God’s revelation and trains hearers to read Scripture in context; topical messages, when they arise organically from the text and are handled with the same exegetical care, can drive home a doctrine or apply the gospel to a specific season of church life. In every case the aim remains the same: to preach the word, to be ready in season and out of season, to reprove, rebuke, and exhort with complete patience and teaching (2 Timothy 4:2).

If you are evaluating a local church’s preaching, look first for whether Christ is central, the gospel of grace is clear, and the text is handled honestly—whatever the sermon structure. A helpful next step is to pray through Acts 20:27 and 2 Timothy 4:1–5, asking the Lord to give your pastors courage and clarity as they feed the flock, and to give you a hungry heart for the whole counsel of God.

question: What are tribulation saints?
answer:
**Tribulation saints** are believers who come to saving faith in Jesus Christ during the future period of intense global distress and persecution commonly called the Great Tribulation, as described especially in the book of Revelation.

The phrase itself is not a direct biblical title but a theological description drawn from passages such as Revelation 7:9–14, where John sees “a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb,” and is told, “These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” Other related texts include Revelation 13:7–10; Revelation 14:12–13; and Revelation 20:4, which speak of faithful saints who endure, refuse the mark of the beast, and some of whom are martyred for their testimony to Jesus.

### Why Christians Differ on the Details
Eschatology (the study of last things) is a tertiary matter—important for hope and holiness, yet not an essential of the faith on which Christian identity or fellowship hangs. Faithful believers disagree because Scripture gives vivid prophetic imagery whose precise timing and sequence are interpreted differently, and because the New Testament emphasizes readiness and perseverance more than a detailed timetable (see Matthew 24:36; 1 Thessalonians 5:1–11).

- **Dispensational premillennial view** (common in many evangelical circles): The church is raptured before a distinct seven-year tribulation. Those who then repent and trust Christ—often under severe persecution—are called “tribulation saints.” They are distinguished from the church age saints and include both Jewish and Gentile believers; many face martyrdom yet are sealed and ultimately victorious.
- **Historic premillennial, amillennial, and postmillennial views**: The church itself experiences tribulation (whether a future intensified period, the entire inter-advent age, or recurring seasons of distress). “Saints in tribulation” are simply believers who remain faithful under trial; there is no separate post-rapture group, because the people of God are one throughout redemptive history. The great multitude in Revelation 7 is often seen as the full number of the redeemed from all ages or the church triumphant.

Christian liberty applies here (Romans 14). What unites all orthodox views is far greater: Christ will return bodily, judge the living and the dead, vindicate His people, and renew all things. The call in every age is the same—perseverance by grace through faith.

### Pastoral Encouragement
Whether the tribulation is still future, already present in principle, or both, Scripture repeatedly calls believers to endure with hope. Revelation 14:12 says, “Here is a call for the perseverance of the saints who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus.” The blood of the Lamb is what cleanses and the presence of the Lamb is what sustains.

A concrete next step: Read Revelation 7 slowly this week, then pray through it, thanking God that salvation belongs to Him and asking for steadfastness for yourself and for persecuted believers worldwide today. Stay rooted in a local church that preaches the whole counsel of God, where you can encourage one another as the Day approaches (Hebrews 10:24–25).

question: Who are the Black Hebrews / Black Israelites?
answer:
**Black Hebrews / Black Israelites** are adherents of various religious movements (mostly arising in the United States from the late 19th and 20th centuries) that teach African Americans, or Black people more broadly, are the true biological and covenantal descendants of the ancient Israelites of the Bible, and that they alone (or primarily) inherit the promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

These groups are not a single organization. They range from cultural or nationalist identity movements to highly sectarian religious bodies with their own leaders, scriptures, and practices. Some well-known streams include earlier figures influenced by British Israelism ideas adapted to a Black context, the Church of the Living God, the Commandment Keepers, the Nation of Yahweh, and contemporary street-preaching camps often called “One West” or “hotep”-adjacent Hebrew Israelite groups. Beliefs differ sharply: some keep a form of Mosaic law and festivals, some reject the New Testament or radically reinterpret it, some teach racial supremacy or that White people (or Jews) are impostors or cursed, and some blend in elements of Christianity, Islam, or freemasonry. A few are relatively peaceful cultural associations; others have been linked to antisemitism, violence, or cult-like control. They are distinct from the Beta Israel (Ethiopian Jews), a historic Jewish community with ancient roots in Ethiopia that mainstream Judaism has recognized.

### Biblical evaluation
Scripture presents ethnic Israel as a real historical people whom God chose for His redemptive purposes (Genesis 12:1–3; Deuteronomy 7:6–8; Romans 9:4–5). Yet the New Testament consistently teaches that membership in the true people of God is defined by faith in Jesus Christ, not by genealogy, skin color, or Torah-keeping as a covenant badge. Paul writes, “For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel. Nor because they are Abraham’s descendants are they all his children” (Romans 9:6–7), and “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:28–29). Jesus Himself is the true Israel and the offspring of Abraham in whom the promises are fulfilled (Matthew 2:15; Galatians 3:16). The church—Jew and Gentile together—is the multi-ethnic people of God under the new covenant (Ephesians 2:11–22; 1 Peter 2:9–10).

Claims that reverse the biblical story by making salvation or covenant status hinge on African ancestry, or that demonize other ethnic groups, contradict the gospel of grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. They also typically deny or distort core Christian doctrines such as the Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Christ, and justification by faith. The Bible’s vision is not Black supremacy, White supremacy, or any ethnic supremacy; it is sinners from every nation washed clean by the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 5:9–10; Revelation 7:9–10).

If you are exploring these teachings because of questions about identity, history, injustice, or belonging, those longings are real. The only secure identity Scripture offers is found in union with the crucified and risen Jesus Christ—who died for people of every ethnicity, rose bodily on the third day, and now calls all people everywhere to repent and believe. Turn from sin and trust in Him alone for forgiveness and new life; He receives all who come. A wise next step is to read the letter to the Galatians or Romans slowly in a faithful local church that preaches Christ crucified, and to talk with mature believers there about what the Bible actually says concerning Israel, the church, and the gospel.

question: What does the Bible say about church-hopping?
answer:
The Bible does not use the modern phrase “church-hopping,” but it clearly calls believers to devoted, ongoing commitment to a local church body rather than a pattern of frequent, rootless movement from one congregation to another.

Scripture presents the local church as a covenant community where Christians are joined together under Christ’s headship for mutual edification, accountability, worship, and mission. In Acts 2:42 the early believers “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.” Hebrews 10:24–25 urges, “And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.” The repeated New Testament picture is one of steadfast belonging, not perpetual shopping.

The church is described as the body of Christ, in which every member is needed and gifted for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 4:11–16). Regularly leaving one body for another without serious cause undermines that design: it hinders the use of spiritual gifts, weakens accountability under qualified elders (Hebrews 13:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12–13), and can foster a consumer mindset that evaluates churches primarily by personal preference rather than by faithfulness to the gospel and the Word. Paul confronts a related spirit of division and self-seeking in the Corinthian church (1 Corinthians 1:10–13; 3:1–9), calling believers instead to unity and maturity in one local expression of Christ’s body.

Faithful Christians may sometimes need to leave a church for weighty biblical reasons (persistent false teaching, unrepentant sin in leadership, or a move to a new location). In those cases the transition should be marked by prayer, counsel, honesty, and a prompt search for a new gospel-preaching congregation to which one can commit. Habitual hopping for lesser reasons—music style, programs, personality clashes, or unmet felt needs—runs counter to the New Testament pattern of perseverance, service, and mutual love.

A wise next step is to examine your own heart before the Lord: ask whether restlessness or unmet expectations have driven frequent moves, then seek a biblically sound local church, place yourself under its teaching and elder care, and begin serving with the gifts God has given you. Speak with mature believers or the elders of a prospective church about membership and how you can put down roots for the long haul.

question: Dance in worship - what does the Bible say?
answer:
The Bible portrays dancing as a spontaneous expression of joy, celebration, and praise to God in several Old Testament passages, yet it never commands dance as a required element of gathered New Testament church worship.

This belongs among the non-essentials of the faith (a tertiary matter of worship practice), where faithful Christians may differ because Scripture gives clear examples of dance in Israel's life but does not prescribe it among the ordinary means of grace for the church under the new covenant. The New Testament emphasizes singing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, the public reading of Scripture, prayer, preaching, and the ordinances (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16; 1 Timothy 4:13; Acts 2:42), while calling for all things to be done decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40).

Two major historic Christian approaches appear:
- Many believers, especially in charismatic, Pentecostal, and various global church traditions, welcome dance in corporate worship as a biblical overflow of gladness before the Lord, pointing to texts such as Miriam's dance after the Red Sea (Exodus 15:20), David's dancing with all his might before the ark (2 Samuel 6:14), and the calls to "praise His name with dancing" and "praise Him with tambourine and dancing" (Psalm 149:3; Psalm 150:4).
- Other believers, including many in the Reformed and confessional Baptist stream, view those Old Testament instances as culturally situated celebrations rather than a standing ordinance for new-covenant assemblies; they therefore limit corporate worship to what Christ and the apostles explicitly instituted, while still rejoicing that individual believers may express gladness with their bodies in appropriate settings outside the gathered service.

In keeping with the regulative principle shaped by passages like Deuteronomy 12:32 and the simplicity of apostolic worship, I hold the second view as a faithful option: dance is not forbidden as personal or familial rejoicing, yet it is not an element Christ has required for the church's public worship. Christian liberty applies here (Romans 14:5-6); each should be fully convinced in his own mind, refuse to despise or judge a brother who differs, and above all guard the heart from showiness or sensuality so that everything truly edifies the body and glorifies Christ.

A concrete next step is to open the Psalms and 2 Samuel 6 this week, ask the Lord to search your motives for any desire to dance (or any resistance to it), and then humbly follow the teaching and practice of the elders in your own local church so that unity in the gospel remains greater than preference in form.

question: What is secular humanism?
answer:
**Secular humanism** is a non-religious worldview and philosophy that places human reason, science, ethics, and individual dignity at the center of meaning and morality, while rejecting belief in God, the supernatural, or divine revelation as necessary or authoritative.

It typically holds that people can (and should) determine right and wrong, pursue justice, and find purpose through critical thinking, empirical evidence, and human compassion alone, without reference to Scripture or a transcendent Creator. Influential statements of this view appear in documents such as the *Humanist Manifesto* (1933, revised later), which affirm atheism or agnosticism, naturalism, and the idea that this life is the only one we have.

Christians recognize that secular humanists often sincerely value education, human rights, scientific progress, and ethical living. Those concerns reflect real goods. Yet the Bible teaches that human beings are not autonomous; we are created in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27) and live in a world He made and governs. When reason and morality are detached from the living God, they become untethered from their true source and standard. Scripture describes this as exchanging “the truth of God for a lie” and worshiping the creature rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25). Human dignity, conscience, and the longing for justice are real because God has written His law on human hearts (Romans 2:14–15) and because Christ Himself is the true measure of what it means to be human.

In short, secular humanism seeks to elevate humanity by removing God; the Christian faith holds that humanity is only rightly understood, valued, and restored in relationship to the God who made us, judged our sin, and redeemed us through the incarnate Son.

question: Does the Bible predict the destruction of Damascus?
answer:
Yes, the Bible predicts the destruction of Damascus, most directly in the oracle of Isaiah 17:1: “This is an oracle concerning Damascus: ‘Behold, Damascus is no longer a city; it has become a heap of ruins.’”

Similar words of judgment appear in Jeremiah 49:23–27 and Amos 1:3–5. These passages announce that the city, once a proud center of Aramean power, would face devastating overthrow as part of the Lord’s righteous dealings with the nations.

Isaiah delivered this word in the eighth century BC, during the rise of the Assyrian empire and the Syro-Ephraimite crisis. In 732 BC Assyria under Tiglath-Pileser III captured Damascus, deported its people, and reduced it to a provincial backwater (see 2 Kings 16:9). Many faithful readers therefore see the prophecy as substantially fulfilled in that historical judgment. At the same time, because Damascus has remained continuously inhabited and some details (complete desolation, the fading of its glory “like the glory of the Israelites,” Isaiah 17:3–4) appear larger than the eighth-century event, other Christians regard the oracle as carrying a yet-future dimension, perhaps tied to end-time conflicts. Both approaches treat the text as genuine predictive prophecy and affirm that God’s word does not fail; the difference lies in how much remains outstanding.

This is a tertiary matter of prophetic interpretation on which believers may differ without dividing over the gospel. What is non-negotiable is that the Lord who spoke through Isaiah is sovereign over the nations, keeps His word, and will bring every purpose to pass in His perfect timing. The same God who judges cities also offers mercy to all who turn to Him through the crucified and risen Christ.

question: What does it mean to watch and pray?
answer:
To watch and pray means to stay spiritually alert and vigilant while continually depending on God through prayer, so that you do not fall into temptation or grow careless in the faith.

Jesus gave this command most clearly in the Garden of Gethsemane: “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak” (Matthew 26:41; see also Mark 14:38). The disciples were physically tired and emotionally overwhelmed, yet the real danger was spiritual dullness. “Watch” (from the Greek *gregoreō*) means to stay awake, keep guard, and remain sober-minded. Prayer is the means by which we draw strength from God rather than relying on our own resolve. Together they form a single posture of humble dependence: eyes open to danger, heart turned toward the Father.

Scripture widens this call beyond one night in the garden. Believers are told to “devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful” (Colossians 4:2), to “pray in the Spirit at all times... stay alert with all perseverance” (Ephesians 6:18), and to “be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray” because “the end of all things is near” (1 Peter 4:7). Watching guards against the schemes of the devil, the deceitfulness of sin, and the suddenness of Christ’s return (Luke 21:36; 1 Thessalonians 5:6). Praying keeps us from self-reliance and anchors us in God’s power and promises.

In practice this looks like regular self-examination before the Word, quick confession when conviction comes, and specific petitions for strength in known areas of weakness. It is not anxious hyper-vigilance but steady, grace-dependent readiness. The same Lord who commanded the disciples also supplies the Spirit who helps us in our weakness (Romans 8:26).

A simple next step: set aside ten unhurried minutes today. Read Matthew 26:36–46 slowly, ask the Lord to show you where your spirit is willing but your flesh is weak, and then pray honestly about those places, asking for His keeping power.

question: How is eternity in Hell a fair punishment for sin?
answer:
**Eternity in hell is a fair punishment because sin is committed against an infinitely holy God, and the just penalty matches the infinite worth of the One offended, not merely the length of time the sin took to commit.**

Many people wrestle with this, wondering how a finite lifetime of wrongs could deserve unending judgment, or how a loving God could allow such a destiny. Those questions are understandable. Scripture does not treat them lightly, yet it answers them with clarity about God's character and our condition.

### The Gravity of Sin
God is not a finite creature whose honor can be repaired by a temporary penalty. He is eternal, perfectly holy, and the rightful King over all He has made. Every sin is personal rebellion against Him. David confessed, “Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight” (Psalm 51:4). Because God’s worth is infinite, the offense of spurning Him carries infinite weight. The Bible calls the consequence “death” (Romans 6:23)—not merely physical death, but eternal separation from the life and favor of God.

Hell is the place where that separation is finalized and experienced forever. Jesus Himself spoke of “eternal punishment” in contrast to “eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). Paul described it as “eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might” (2 Thessalonians 1:9). The punishment is not arbitrary cruelty; it is the just outworking of God’s unchanging holiness and justice. He cannot simply overlook sin without denying His own nature (Habakkuk 1:13; Romans 3:25–26).

### Continuing Rebellion and the Nature of Justice
Those who enter eternity still rejecting God do not suddenly become lovers of His glory. Scripture portrays the unrepentant as remaining in their hostility (Revelation 22:11). Hell is therefore not merely a sentence imposed from outside; it is the confirmed trajectory of a heart that prefers self-rule over God’s rule. God does not force anyone into His presence against their will. The doors of hell are locked from the inside, in the sense that the damned continue to love darkness rather than light (John 3:19–20).

God’s justice is also seen in the cross. There the infinite Son of God bore the full weight of divine wrath in the place of sinners. Because of the infinite worth of His person, He could exhaust an eternal penalty in a finite span of suffering. That is penal substitution: Christ, the righteous One, took the punishment we deserved so that God could be both “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). The same justice that requires hell also provided the only escape from it.

### The Gospel Way of Escape
All of us have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). Left to ourselves we stand rightly condemned. Yet God, in love, sent His Son: Jesus lived the perfect life we could not live, died the death we deserved, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, conquering sin and death. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone—not by our works or moral improvement. “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever rejects the Son will not see life. Instead, the wrath of God remains on him” (John 3:36).

If you sense the weight of your own sin or the fear of judgment, that is not meant to crush you without hope. Turn (repent) from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. He receives all who come to Him.

A simple next step is to open the Gospel of John and read it slowly, asking God to show you who Jesus is and what He has done. Talk with a pastor or mature believer in a local church who can walk with you through the Scriptures. God delights to save, and His justice and mercy meet perfectly at the cross.

question: How is Satan god of this world (2 Corinthians 4:4)?
answer:
**Satan is called “the god of this age” (or world) in 2 Corinthians 4:4 because he exercises real but limited, temporary, and permitted influence as the ruler of the present fallen world system, blinding the minds of unbelievers to the gospel.** He is not a true deity, not equal to the one true God, and not sovereign; the title describes his usurped role as the object of the world’s allegiance and the agent of spiritual deception in this age.

Paul writes: “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4). The Greek term *aiōn* (“age”) points to the present evil era characterized by rebellion against God, not to God’s good creation itself. Satan functions as a counterfeit “god” whom the world effectively serves through sin, idolatry, and unbelief.

Scripture consistently describes this limited dominion:
- Jesus calls him “the prince of this world” who is already judged and will be cast out (John 12:31; John 14:30; John 16:11).
- Paul names him “the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience” (Ephesians 2:2).
- John states that “the whole world lies in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5:19).
- In the temptation, Satan claims authority over the kingdoms of the world and offers them to Jesus (Luke 4:5–7); Jesus does not deny the claim of temporary influence, yet He refuses worship and later defeats him.

This authority entered through humanity’s fall in Genesis 3, when Adam’s sin opened the door for the serpent’s influence over the human race and its systems. God remains absolutely sovereign (Psalm 24:1; Daniel 4:35); He permits Satan’s activity for His own wise purposes, as seen in Job 1–2, and uses even opposition to advance the gospel. Satan’s power is that of a defeated foe who still prowls (1 Peter 5:8) and deceives, yet he operates only within boundaries God sets.

Christ has already disarmed the rulers and authorities, triumphing over them by the cross (Colossians 2:15), and through death He destroyed the one who holds the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14). Believers have been delivered from the domain of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God’s beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). The blinding is therefore not final for those who hear and believe; God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” shines in hearts to give the light of the knowledge of His glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

**Practical next step:** If you sense spiritual blindness or opposition in your own life or in those you love, pray specifically that God would open blind eyes and shine the light of the gospel, then keep speaking the clear message of Christ crucified and risen. Resist the devil by submitting to God (James 4:7), put on the full armor of God daily (Ephesians 6:10–18), and stay rooted in a local church where the Word is preached and believers encourage one another. The true God reigns; Satan’s title is temporary, and Christ’s victory is sure.

question: Is faith intellectual assent?
answer:
**No. Biblical saving faith is more than intellectual assent.** It includes knowledge of the gospel, assent that it is true, and personal trust (fiducia) in Jesus Christ alone for salvation.

Scripture distinguishes mere mental agreement from saving faith. James 2:19 says, “You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that—and shudder.” Demons possess accurate knowledge and assent to facts about God, yet they remain unsaved. Saving faith goes further: it rests upon and receives Christ. Romans 10:9–10 declares, “If you confess with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. For with your heart you believe and are justified, and with your mouth you confess and are saved.” Hebrews 11:1 describes faith as “the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see,” and John 3:16 calls us to believe *in* the Son (a personal entrusting, not mere agreement with propositions).

In historic Christian teaching this is often summarized as *notitia* (knowledge of the truth), *assensus* (assent that it is true), and *fiducia* (trustful reliance upon Christ). Justification is by grace alone through this whole-hearted faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 3:28). Intellectual assent is necessary—one must know and affirm the facts of Christ’s person and work—but it is not sufficient. The heart must cast itself upon the crucified and risen Savior.

If your faith has felt mainly like agreeing with Christian ideas, examine whether you are actually resting in Christ Himself. Read the Gospels and ask the Lord to grant you living trust in His finished work. Speak with a mature believer or elder in a local church who can help you see the difference between head knowledge and heart reliance. Turn from self-reliance and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

question: What does it mean to be saved by grace?
answer:
**To be saved by grace means God freely rescues undeserving sinners from the guilt, power, and penalty of sin as a pure gift, not because of anything we do or deserve, but solely through faith in Jesus Christ.**

Scripture states this plainly: “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (Ephesians 2:8-9). Grace is God’s unmerited favor. We contribute nothing to earn it.

### Why We Need Grace
God is holy and just. His standard is perfect righteousness (Isaiah 6:3; Matthew 5:48). Every person has sinned and falls short of His glory (Romans 3:23). Sin separates us from God and brings death—eternal judgment under His righteous wrath (Romans 6:23; John 3:36). No amount of good deeds, religious effort, or moral improvement can erase that debt or make us right with Him (Titus 3:5; Romans 3:20).

### What God Has Done in Christ
Out of love, the Father sent His eternal Son. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, then died on the cross as our substitute. He bore the penalty our sins deserved (penal substitutionary atonement), satisfying God’s justice (Isaiah 53:5-6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily from the dead, conquering sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He is now exalted as Lord.

This is the Gospel: salvation is secured by Christ’s historical death, burial, and resurrection. Justification (being declared righteous before God) comes by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

### How We Receive It
We receive this gift by repenting—turning from sin and self-reliance—and trusting wholly in Jesus Christ and His finished work. Faith is not a work we perform; it is the empty hand that receives what Christ has already accomplished (Romans 3:24-25; Romans 5:1). Once justified, we are adopted as God’s children, indwelt by the Holy Spirit, and kept by His power (John 1:12; Ephesians 1:13-14). Good works follow as the fruit of new life, never the root of our acceptance (Ephesians 2:10; James 2:17).

This truth humbles the proud and comforts the broken. You cannot save yourself, and you do not have to. Christ has done it all.

If you have never turned from sin and trusted in Jesus alone, do so today. Repent and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ who died and rose for you, and you will be saved—forgiven, made new, and brought into everlasting life with God (Acts 16:31; John 3:16; Romans 10:9-10).

Talk to God honestly about your need. Open the Gospel of John or the book of Romans and read of Christ’s work. If you are able, connect with a local Bible-believing church where you can grow with other believers. What questions does this raise for you?

question: What is the kalam cosmological argument for the existence of God?
answer:
The kalam cosmological argument is a philosophical case for the existence of God that reasons from the beginning of the universe to a transcendent, personal First Cause. In its basic form it runs as follows:

1. Whatever begins to exist has a cause.  
2. The universe began to exist.  
3. Therefore, the universe has a cause.

That cause, the argument continues, must be uncaused, timeless, spaceless, immaterial, enormously powerful, and personal (able to choose to create), which Christians identify with the God revealed in Scripture.

The name “kalam” comes from medieval Islamic philosophy (*kalām*), though the core reasoning draws on earlier Christian and Jewish thinkers and has been refined in modern times, especially by William Lane Craig. Premise 1 rests on the metaphysical intuition that something cannot come from nothing without a cause. Premise 2 is supported both by philosophical arguments against an actual infinite past and by scientific evidence (such as the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem and the standard Big Bang model) that the universe had a finite beginning. From the conclusion, further analysis shows the cause cannot itself be physical or temporal, pointing beyond the universe to a Creator.

Christians see this line of reasoning as consistent with the Bible’s plain declaration that “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1) and that “by faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible” (Hebrews 11:3). The argument does not by itself prove every attribute of the triune God, yet it powerfully supports the existence of a personal Creator and removes a common intellectual obstacle to faith.

If you would like a deeper look at any premise, common objections, or how this argument relates to the gospel of Jesus Christ, just ask.

question: Why is the virgin birth so important?
answer:
The virgin birth is essential because it is the miraculous means by which the eternal Son of God took on true human nature, remaining fully God and fully man in the hypostatic union, while remaining sinless and able to save us.

Scripture presents this as historical fact, not legend. The angel told Mary, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. So the Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Matthew records that this fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy: “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”) (Matthew 1:23; Isaiah 7:14). Joseph was told the child was conceived by the Holy Spirit, so he could be named Jesus, “because He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:20-21).

This matters for several interlocking reasons. First, it secures the Incarnation itself: the second Person of the Trinity did not merely appear human or adopt a body later; He was conceived and born as a real man while remaining the eternal Son. Second, it protects Christ’s sinlessness. As the second Adam, He did not inherit the guilt and corruption of original sin that passes through ordinary human generation (Romans 5:12-19); He was holy from the womb, the Lamb without blemish. Third, only a Savior who is both truly God and truly man can offer a substitutionary atonement of infinite worth on behalf of human sinners. A merely human Jesus could not bear the full weight of divine wrath; a non-human Jesus could not represent us. The virgin birth is God’s appointed way of uniting those two natures in one Person forever.

Without it, the gospel unravels. If Jesus were the natural son of Joseph, He would be a sinner like us and could not be the spotless sacrifice. The early church rightly confessed this truth against every attempt to deny either His full deity or His full humanity.

You can rest in this: the same God who brought His Son into the world by the Spirit’s power is able to bring new life into any heart that turns from sin and trusts in Christ alone. Read slowly through Luke 1:26-38 and Matthew 1:18-25 this week, asking the Lord to deepen your wonder at Immanuel, God with us.

question: How can I overcome disappointment with life?
answer:
Disappointment with life can feel heavy, lingering, and deeply personal, as if the weight of unmet hopes or repeated setbacks has settled over everything. Scripture does not dismiss that ache; it meets it with honesty and hope.

The Bible teaches that we live in a fallen world where thorns, toil, and broken expectations are real (Genesis 3:17–19). Jesus Himself said, “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Disappointment often rises when we look for lasting satisfaction, security, or meaning in things that cannot finally hold them: careers, relationships, health, or plans. God is not the author of evil, yet He remains sovereign, good, and faithful, working even painful circumstances for the good of those who love Him and are called according to His purpose (Romans 8:28). His character does not change with our circumstances.

The deepest answer to disappointment is not simply better circumstances, but a better center: Christ Himself. He entered our suffering, lived the perfect life we could not, died as a substitutionary sacrifice for our sin, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, securing forgiveness and new life for all who turn from sin and trust in Him alone. Because He lives, our present afflictions are “light and momentary” compared with “an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 4:17). Justification by grace through faith unites us to Him, so that even when life disappoints, our identity and future are secure in the One who will never leave or forsake us.

Practically, begin by bringing your specific disappointments to God in honest prayer. Name them without polish, then ask Him to realign your heart with His promises. Meditate slowly on a passage like Psalm 42:5 (“Why are you downcast, O my soul? … Put your hope in God”) or Philippians 4:6–7, letting the truth reshape your perspective. Share the load with a mature believer or your local church elders; isolation deepens disappointment, while fellowship and the ordinary means of grace (Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper) strengthen weary saints. Progressive sanctification happens as the Holy Spirit uses these means to wean us from lesser hopes and root us more deeply in Christ.

One concrete next step: set aside fifteen quiet minutes today. Write down two or three specific disappointments, then read Romans 8:18–39 aloud and pray through it, asking God to help you trust His goodness and fix your eyes on Jesus. If the heaviness persists or deepens into despair, reach out to a pastor or a certified biblical counselor for ongoing care.

Hope is not denial of pain; it is confidence that the risen Christ is enough, both now and forever.

question: What is the Gemara?
answer:
The Gemara is the rabbinical analysis, commentary, and debate on the Mishnah (the earlier written collection of Jewish oral law). Together, the Mishnah and Gemara form the Talmud.

Compiled mainly between the 3rd and 5th centuries AD in Aramaic by Jewish sages called the Amoraim, the Gemara expands on the Mishnah’s legal rulings through discussion, stories, and interpretation. There are two main versions: the longer and more widely studied Babylonian Talmud, and the earlier Jerusalem (or Palestinian) Talmud.

From a Christian perspective, the Gemara belongs to post-biblical Jewish tradition rather than the inspired Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, which alone hold final authority for faith and practice (2 Timothy 3:16–17). It can offer historical insight into later Jewish thought, yet it is not treated as divine revelation.

question: How can I stop being a people-pleaser?
answer:
**People-pleasing is often the fear of man dressed up as kindness**, and Scripture names it clearly as a snare that keeps us from walking freely with God.

Proverbs 29:25 says, “The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high.” When we live for others’ approval, we quietly make their opinion an idol and forget that we already have the only verdict that matters in Christ. Galatians 1:10 presses the point: “Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

### The deeper issue
People-pleasing usually springs from a heart that feels insecure, afraid of rejection, or responsible for everyone else’s emotions. The Gospel meets that head-on. In Christ you are already fully known, fully loved, and fully accepted (Ephesians 1:3–14; Romans 8:1). His perfect life, substitutionary death, and bodily resurrection secure your standing so you no longer have to earn it from people. Progressive sanctification then works that freedom into daily life by the Holy Spirit through the ordinary means of grace.

### Practical steps toward freedom
1. **Name the fear before God**  
   When you catch yourself saying yes out of anxiety or reshaping your words to keep peace at any cost, pause and confess it specifically: “Lord, I am fearing their opinion more than Yours right now.” 

2. **Renew your mind with truth**  
   Memorize and pray through key texts: Proverbs 29:25; Galatians 1:10; Colossians 3:23–24 (“Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men”); 1 Thessalonians 2:4. Let these reshape what “success” looks like.

3. **Practice small, honest “no’s”**  
   Start in low-stakes situations. A simple, kind refusal—“I can’t take that on right now”—is not unloving; it is truthful stewardship. Love of neighbor never requires you to disobey God or neglect the responsibilities He has already given you.

4. **Root identity in union with Christ, not performance**  
   Each morning remind yourself: “I am accepted in the Beloved.” Serve others from that security rather than for it. True Christian love seeks their good under God’s authority, not endless approval.

5. **Invite accountability**  
   Share the struggle with a mature believer or elder in your local church. Ask them to pray with you and gently point out when they see the old pattern returning. Isolation feeds people-pleasing; fellowship starves it.

### One concrete next step
This week, choose one relationship or commitment where you normally over-accommodate. Before responding, pray briefly, open Galatians 1:10, and decide what faithfulness to Christ actually requires. Then act on that, even if it feels uncomfortable. Afterward, thank God for the freedom He is working in you.

You do not have to white-knuckle your way out of this. The same grace that justified you is sanctifying you. Bring the weariness of constant performance straight to Jesus, who already pleased the Father perfectly on your behalf. Ask Him to grow a holy fear of God that crowds out the fear of man, and trust that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion (Philippians 1:6).

question: What is the golden chain of salvation?
answer:
The golden chain of salvation is the unbreakable sequence of God's sovereign saving acts set out in Romans 8:29-30, often summarized as foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification, and glorification.  

Scripture says: "For those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers. And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified" (Romans 8:29-30). These five links form what theologians have long called a "golden chain" because each step is forged by God Himself and none can be broken; the same people who are foreknown are finally glorified. This passage stands at the heart of the biblical *ordo salutis* (order of salvation) and magnifies God's grace from eternity past to eternity future, showing that salvation rests entirely on His initiative rather than human effort.  

For the believer, this chain brings deep assurance: if God has begun the work, He will finish it (Philippians 1:6). Rest in that certainty today by thanking Him for every link He has already forged in your life and by walking in the good works He prepared beforehand.

question: Should Mark 16:9-20 be in the Bible?
answer:
**Mark 16:9-20 (the “longer ending”) appears in most Bibles today, yet the earliest and most reliable Greek manuscripts do not contain it, so it is widely regarded as a later addition rather than part of Mark’s original text.**

The Gospel of Mark ends abruptly at 16:8 in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (fourth century), the two oldest complete New Testament manuscripts we possess. Several early church fathers (Eusebius, Jerome) note that the majority of manuscripts available to them lacked verses 9–20. A shorter alternative ending also circulates in some copies. By contrast, the longer ending is present in the majority of later Byzantine manuscripts and thus entered the Textus Receptus, the King James Version, and most traditional printed Bibles. Modern critical editions (and many translations) therefore print 16:9-20 with a clear note or brackets indicating the textual uncertainty.

### Two main historic Christian approaches
- **Inclusion as received Scripture.** Many believers, especially those who prioritize the traditional ecclesiastical text (Byzantine/majority text or Textus Receptus), retain the passage because the church has read and preached it for centuries, and its content is theologically orthodox. They see God’s providence in its widespread acceptance.
- **Recognition as non-original.** Most evangelical textual scholars and the majority of modern translations treat it as a second-century addition that was never written by Mark. They still print it for historical and devotional reasons but do not build doctrine solely upon it. This view rests on the principle that we seek the original autographs (the inerrant text God inspired), not later scribal expansions.

Both approaches affirm the full authority, inspiration, and inerrancy of the original text of Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16-17; 2 Peter 1:20-21). The difference is a tertiary matter of textual criticism, not a denial of the Bible’s truthfulness. Faithful Christians may disagree here without dividing over the gospel.

### Why the question does not threaten the faith
Even without 16:9-20, Mark’s Gospel clearly proclaims Jesus’ death, empty tomb, and resurrection appearances promised by the angel (Mark 16:1-8). The same events are abundantly attested in Matthew 28, Luke 24, John 20–21, and 1 Corinthians 15:3-8. Nothing essential to the Christian faith—Christ’s deity, atoning death, bodily resurrection, or the call to repent and believe—hangs on these twelve verses. The longer ending itself contains nothing heretical; it summarizes resurrection appearances, the Great Commission, and signs that accompanied the apostles. (Passages about snake-handling or drinking poison have been dangerously misapplied by a few fringe groups; they describe what God sovereignly did in the apostolic era, not a standing command for every believer.)

God has preserved His Word with astonishing accuracy. The existence of known variants like this one actually demonstrates the transparency of the manuscript tradition: we can identify later additions precisely because so many early copies survive. The core message remains clear and unchanged.

**Practical next step:** When you read Mark, note the textual footnote in your Bible, then keep reading the rest of Scripture with confidence. Compare the resurrection accounts across the four Gospels and 1 Corinthians 15 this week; let the multiplied witnesses strengthen your assurance that Jesus is risen. If the question unsettles you, talk it over with a pastor or elder who handles the biblical languages or textual issues carefully, and pray through Psalm 119:89: “Your word, O LORD, is everlasting; it is firmly fixed in the heavens.”

The Lord Jesus who rose from the dead has not left His people without a sure word. Trust that word, rest in His finished work, and walk forward in faith.

question: What is the difference between a sect and a cult?
answer:
**A sect is typically a subgroup or offshoot within a broader religious tradition that shares its core beliefs while differing on secondary matters of practice, emphasis, or organization; a cult, by contrast, is a group that claims connection to a faith (often Christianity) yet rejects or radically redefines its essential doctrines, frequently centering on a charismatic leader, new revelation, or high-control structure that isolates members from outside accountability.**

In everyday and sociological use the words sometimes overlap or shift in tone, and “sect” can simply describe any distinct religious party (as when Paul speaks of having lived as a Pharisee, “the strictest sect of our religion,” Acts 26:5). In historic Christian theological usage, however, the distinction matters for guarding the gospel. A sect may still stand inside the boundaries of orthodox Christianity; a cult places itself outside those boundaries by denying one or more core truths—the Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Christ, His atoning death and bodily resurrection, justification by grace alone through faith alone, or the authority of Scripture.

Scripture repeatedly warns believers to test every teaching against the apostolic gospel. Paul writes, “But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse” (Galatians 1:8). Peter likewise cautions that “there will be false teachers among you” who “will secretly introduce destructive heresies” (2 Peter 2:1). The early church therefore drew clear lines around the essentials (summarized later in the ecumenical creeds) while allowing liberty on non-essentials.

Practically, evaluate any group by asking: Does it uphold the biblical Christ—truly God and truly man, whose once-for-all sacrifice reconciles sinners to a holy God? Does it submit to Scripture as the final authority rather than elevating a founder’s writings or private revelations? Does it produce the fruit of the Spirit and encourage believers toward a local church under qualified elders, or does it demand unquestioning loyalty and cut people off from family and other Christians? If core doctrines are denied, the group is not merely another “sect” of Christianity; it is a departure from the faith once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 1:3).

If you are sorting through a specific group or teaching, open the Bible itself (start with the Gospel of John and the letter to the Galatians), pray for wisdom, and talk with mature believers in a gospel-preaching church. The Lord is faithful to lead those who seek Him in spirit and truth.

question: Is "name it claim it" teaching biblical?
answer:
**No, "name it and claim it" teaching is not biblical.**

This teaching (often tied to Word of Faith or prosperity theology) claims that spoken words of positive confession, combined with enough faith, obligate God to grant health, wealth, success, or other desires. It treats faith like a spiritual force or formula that forces outcomes, and it often implies that suffering, poverty, or unanswered requests signal weak faith or negative speech.

Scripture presents a very different picture of God, faith, and prayer.

### God Is Sovereign, Not a Cosmic Vending Machine
The Bible teaches that the Lord rules over all things according to His wise and good will. We do not command Him. James writes, “Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit.’ You do not even know what will happen tomorrow! ... Instead, you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that’” (James 4:13-15). Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane, “Yet not as I will, but as You will” (Matthew 26:39). Biblical prayer submits to the Father’s will rather than demanding it bend to ours.

### Faith Trusts God; It Does Not Manipulate Outcomes
True faith is confident trust in the character and promises of God, not a technique to guarantee earthly results. Hebrews 11 recounts people of great faith—some who saw deliverance and many who suffered, were mocked, imprisoned, or killed without receiving the earthly outcome they might have desired—yet they were commended for trusting God (Hebrews 11:35-40). The apostle Paul pleaded three times for his “thorn in the flesh” to be removed; God’s answer was, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). Paul did not “claim” its removal and then fault his faith when it remained. He learned contentment in Christ amid need and plenty (Philippians 4:11-13).

### Common Proof Texts Are Misused
Passages such as Mark 11:23-24 (“whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it”) or John 14:13-14 are sometimes lifted out of context. These promises are given to disciples abiding in Christ and aligned with His purposes, not blank checks for personal desire. The same New Testament clarifies the condition: “This is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us” (1 John 5:14). James also warns, “When you ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures” (James 4:3). Words have no inherent creative power equal to God’s; only God speaks and it is so (Genesis 1; Psalm 33:9). We are creatures who speak truthfully and pray dependently.

### The Gospel Centers on Christ, Not Earthly Prosperity
“Name it and claim it” often shifts the focus from the finished work of Christ—His sinless life, substitutionary death on the cross for our sins, burial, and bodily resurrection—to material or physical blessing as the main evidence of God’s favor. The New Testament consistently ties the greatest blessings to reconciliation with God, forgiveness, the gift of the Spirit, and the hope of resurrection and new creation (Ephesians 1:3-14; 1 Peter 1:3-9). Jesus warned against storing up treasures on earth and called His followers to take up their cross (Matthew 6:19-21; Matthew 16:24-26). The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, and godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Timothy 6:6-10).

Faithful Christians through the centuries have suffered illness, persecution, and poverty while walking closely with the Lord. Their faith was not defective; it was refined. God does heal, provide, and answer prayer according to His perfect will and timing—sometimes dramatically, often through ordinary means, and always for His glory and our ultimate good in Christ (Romans 8:28-30). We are free to ask boldly for daily bread, healing, and help, yet we rest in the Father who knows what we need before we ask (Matthew 6:8, 11).

If this teaching has left you disappointed, condemned for “not having enough faith,” or confused about God’s character, bring those burdens honestly to the Lord in prayer. Read through the Gospels and the epistles slowly, noticing how Jesus and the apostles actually prayed and endured. Talk with a trusted pastor or mature believers in a local church that holds Scripture as final authority. The true riches are found in knowing Christ Himself—His grace is sufficient, and His power is made perfect in weakness.

question: What does the Bible say about cryonics or cryogenics?
answer:
The Bible does not mention cryonics or cryogenics at all, since these are modern scientific practices involving extremely low temperatures to preserve a body after clinical death in the hope of future revival by technology. Scripture does, however, speak clearly about death, the body, judgment, and the only true hope of resurrection.

Death is a fixed appointment for every person because of sin. Hebrews 9:27 states, “And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment.” Genesis 3:19 reminds us that the body returns to the dust from which it was taken, and Ecclesiastes 12:7 adds that “the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.” There is no biblical category for suspending death indefinitely or reversing it by human means; death is the doorway to standing before God.

The Christian’s confident hope is not technological preservation but the bodily resurrection secured by Jesus Christ. He declared, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies” (John 11:25). The apostle Paul explains that Christ is “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,” and that “in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:20, 22). At His return the dead in Christ will be raised imperishable, and living believers will be transformed (1 Corinthians 15:51–54; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). God alone has the power to raise the dead (Acts 26:8; Romans 8:11), and He will do so by His Spirit, not by cryogenic storage.

Attempts to escape death through cryonics can reflect a natural human fear of mortality and a desire for more time. Yet Scripture redirects that longing to the finished work of Christ, who conquered death by His own death and bodily resurrection. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone; no scientific procedure can remove sin or secure eternal life. If the uncertainty of death weighs on you, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and the sure promise of resurrection life.

A helpful next step is to read 1 Corinthians 15 slowly this week, asking God to deepen your confidence in Christ’s victory over the grave, and to talk with a pastor or mature believer in your local church about any fears surrounding death.

question: How can I obtain favor from the Lord (Proverbs 8:35)?
answer:
**You obtain the favor of the Lord by finding Wisdom, and true Wisdom is found in Jesus Christ.**

Proverbs 8:35 states, “For whoever finds me finds life and obtains the favor of the LORD.” In this chapter, Wisdom herself calls out, inviting all who will listen. The favor (Hebrew *ratson*, God’s gracious delight and acceptance) is not earned by human effort or moral performance; it is received by those who seek, hear, and embrace the Wisdom God freely offers.

### Wisdom Points to Christ
Scripture reveals that this personified Wisdom finds its fullest expression in Jesus. The apostle Paul writes that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24) and that God made Him “our wisdom from God—our righteousness, holiness, and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). In Christ “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). Finding Him is finding life and the favor of the Lord.

### How This Favor Is Received
God’s favor is His unmerited grace. We are sinners who fall short of His holiness (Romans 3:23) and deserve His just wrath. Yet the Father sent His Son, truly God and truly man, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. Jesus lived the perfect life of wisdom and obedience we could not live, then died on the cross as our substitute, bearing the penalty our sins deserved (penal substitutionary atonement). He was buried and rose bodily on the third day, conquering sin and death. He now reigns as Lord.

Salvation—and the favor of the Lord—is secured by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:1). When you turn from sin (repent) and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you, you are justified—declared righteous—and receive God’s favor forever. Those who are truly His are kept by His power and will persevere.

Proverbs itself shows the path of seeking: Wisdom says, “I love those who love me, and those who seek me early find me” (Proverbs 8:17), and “Blessed is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my doors” (Proverbs 8:34). This seeking is fulfilled when we come to Christ in humble faith.

### A Concrete Next Step
Open your Bible today to Proverbs 8 and John 1. Read slowly, asking the Lord to show you Christ as the Wisdom who gives life. Then speak to God directly in your own words: confess your need, thank Him for the cross and resurrection, and ask for grace to trust and follow Jesus. Connect with a faithful local church where the Bible is taught, and share this desire with a mature believer who can walk with you.

The Lord delights to give His favor to all who come to Him through His Son. Whoever finds Christ finds life.

question: Why is solo Christo important?
answer:
