A concrete next step is to examine your own approach to gathered and private worship this week: ask whether it is Spirit-dependent and Scripture-shaped, then pray through Psalm 51:10–12 and John 4:23–24, asking the Father to form you into the kind of worshiper He seeks.

question: Book of Obadiah - Bible Survey
answer:
The Book of Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament (one chapter, 21 verses), a prophetic oracle delivered by the prophet Obadiah (“servant of Yahweh”) announcing God’s judgment on Edom for its pride and violence against Judah, while promising deliverance for Israel and the triumph of the Lord’s kingdom.

### Historical Setting
Edom descended from Esau, Jacob’s brother (Genesis 36:1), and long nursed hostility toward Israel. The prophecy most naturally fits the aftermath of Jerusalem’s fall to Babylon in 586 BC, when Edom rejoiced, blocked fugitives, and looted the city (Obadiah 1:10–14; cf. Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21–22). Some place it earlier (ninth century), but the language of total devastation favors the later date. Obadiah stands among the Minor Prophets and shares material with Jeremiah 49:7–22.

### Structure and Content
- **Verses 1–9**: The vision and indictment. God summons the nations against Edom; its mountain strongholds and famed wisdom cannot save it from coming ruin.
- **Verses 10–14**: The specific sins—violence against brother Jacob, gloating over Judah’s calamity, cutting off escapees, and handing survivors to the enemy.
- **Verses 15–21**: The Day of the Lord. As Edom has done, so it will be done to them; Mount Zion will be holy, the house of Jacob will possess its inheritance, and “the kingdom will be the Lord’s” (Obadiah 1:21).

### Key Themes
God’s sovereign justice opposes human pride (Obadiah 1:3–4). National sins against God’s covenant people do not escape His notice. The “Day of the Lord” brings both judgment on the nations and restoration for the remnant. The closing promise that the kingdom belongs to Yahweh points forward to the Messiah’s reign, when Christ, the greater Son of Jacob, subdues every enemy and gathers His people (cf. Revelation 11:15).

### Doctrinal and Pastoral Significance
Obadiah displays penal justice—God repays evil in kind—while upholding His covenant faithfulness to Israel. Pride is the root sin exposed; the Edomites trusted geography, alliances, and intellect rather than the Lord. For believers today the book warns against gloating over another’s hardship and calls us to humble solidarity with God’s people. A concrete next step is to read Obadiah slowly alongside Romans 12:14–21, then ask the Lord to search your heart for any lingering bitterness or superiority toward others, confessing it and choosing active mercy instead.

The book ends not with despair but with hope: the kingdom will be the Lord’s. That certainty steadies God’s people in every age.

question: What does it mean to gain the whole world but lose your soul?
answer:
**To gain the whole world but lose your soul means that no amount of earthly success, wealth, power, pleasure, or acclaim can compensate for the eternal loss of your soul through unbelief and separation from God.**

Jesus asks this searching question in Mark 8:36: “For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul?” (see also Matthew 16:26 and Luke 9:25). He speaks right after calling His disciples to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him. In the immediate context, “gaining the whole world” pictures securing every possible temporal advantage—riches, status, comfort, influence—while “losing” or “forfeiting” the soul means missing eternal life and facing God’s judgment.

The soul here refers to the true self, the person who will stand before God forever. Scripture treats human beings as eternal: either enjoying the presence of God or enduring everlasting separation from Him (Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). Worldly gains are temporary and cannot buy forgiveness, righteousness, or resurrection life. The exchange is catastrophic because the soul’s value is infinite, while the world and its desires are passing away (1 John 2:17).

This teaching rests on core truths: God is holy and just, humanity is sinful and under wrath, and only Christ’s atoning death and bodily resurrection secure salvation. People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by accumulating the world’s goods or performing religious works. Penal substitution means Jesus bore the penalty our sins deserved so that all who repent and trust Him receive eternal life instead of forfeiture.

A concrete next step is to examine what you are currently chasing. Ask the Lord in prayer to show you any ambition, possession, or approval that has begun to outweigh obedience to Christ. Open Mark 8 and read verses 34–38 slowly, then talk with a mature believer in your local church about where your treasure truly lies (Matthew 6:19–21).

If you have never turned from sin and trusted Jesus, the invitation is open: repent and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, who died on the cross and rose again for you, and you will be saved—your soul kept secure forever. What stands out to you most as you consider this question?

question: Why did God send the flood when He knew sin would continue after the flood?
answer:
God sent the flood as a just judgment on the extreme, worldwide wickedness of that generation, while mercifully preserving Noah and his family as a remnant through whom His promise of redemption would continue, even though He fully knew the human heart would remain sinful afterward.

In Genesis 6:5–7, Scripture tells us that “the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time. And the LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart. So the LORD said, ‘I will blot out man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth.’” The violence and corruption had reached a point where God’s holy character required decisive action. Yet Noah “found favor in the eyes of the LORD” (Genesis 6:8), and through the ark God both judged sin and saved a people by grace.

After the flood, God Himself acknowledges that sin would continue: “I will never again curse the ground because of man, even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth” (Genesis 8:21). The flood was never meant to eradicate the root of sin in the human heart; only the finished work of Christ can do that. Instead, it served several clear purposes: it displayed God’s justice against unrepentant evil, it preserved the line through which the Messiah would come, it established the Noahic covenant with its rainbow sign of common grace (Genesis 9:8–17), and it stands as a historical warning and type of the final judgment to come (2 Peter 2:5; 2 Peter 3:5–7).

God’s foreknowledge does not make His judgments pointless. He acts in real history at specific times to uphold His holiness, restrain evil, and advance His saving plan. The flood cleaned the earth of that generation’s violence, but it also pointed forward to the greater salvation we need. Just as Noah and his family were brought safely through water, so baptism now corresponds to this as an appeal to God for a good conscience through the resurrection of Jesus Christ (1 Peter 3:20–21). The same God who judged in the days of Noah later sent His Son to bear the full judgment for sin on the cross and rise again, so that all who repent and trust in Him receive forgiveness and new life.

If this question stirs uncertainty about God’s fairness or your own standing before Him, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you. A simple next step is to read Genesis 6–9 slowly this week, asking the Lord to show you both His justice and His mercy, and to talk it over with a pastor or mature believer in a local church.

question: Should a church tithe 10% of the offerings it receives?
answer:
There is no biblical command requiring a local church to give away exactly 10% of the offerings it receives. Faithful Christians and churches may disagree on this as a matter of wisdom and liberty rather than a binding rule.

Some churches intentionally set aside 10% (or more) of their income for missions, church planting, or outside gospel work. They see this as a practical way to model the generosity they teach, prioritize the Great Commission, and guard against using every dollar only on internal needs.

Other churches reject a fixed percentage. Their elders prayerfully allocate funds according to clear biblical priorities (supporting faithful pastors, caring for the needy among them, and advancing the gospel) without treating 10% as a required “tithe of the tithe.” They emphasize Spirit-led stewardship over a formula carried over from Israel’s agricultural tithe system.

Scripture calls every church to generous, wise, and cheerful stewardship of what God provides, but it never legislates a 10% rule for the congregation’s corporate giving. Believers are to give as they have purposed in their hearts, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). The early churches collected funds for the saints in need and for those who labor in preaching and teaching (1 Corinthians 16:1–2; 1 Timothy 5:17–18; Philippians 4:15–18), always under the oversight of qualified leaders who must give an account (Hebrews 13:17). The Old Testament tithe supported the Levites and temple system under the Mosaic covenant; the new covenant people of God are not bound to that exact structure, though the principle of honoring the Lord with our first and best remains.

In short, a church is free to adopt a 10% missions commitment if its elders judge it wise and the congregation supports it with joy. It is equally free to budget differently so long as the gospel, the flock, and the needy are faithfully served. This falls under Christian liberty (Romans 14:1–6). The greater issue is not the percentage but whether the church’s spending visibly reflects Christ’s mission and the members’ cheerful obedience.

If you serve as an elder or ministry leader, gather with the other elders, open the Scriptures together, examine the church’s actual needs and opportunities, and seek the Lord’s wisdom in prayer before setting any policy. If you are a member, give generously and cheerfully to your local church and trust the leaders God has placed over you as they steward those gifts.

question: Easter Bible reading plan
answer:
**A simple 7-day Easter Bible reading plan** focused on Christ’s final week, atoning death, burial, and bodily resurrection. These passages center on the Gospel: Jesus’ sacrificial death for sinners and His victory over sin and death.

Read one section each day (about 10–15 minutes). Pause to note what it reveals about God’s holiness, human need, and Christ’s finished work. Then pray in your own words, thanking Him and asking for a heart that trusts and follows the risen Lord.

**Day 1 – The Triumphal Entry and Authority**  
Matthew 21:1–11; Matthew 21:12–17  
Jesus enters Jerusalem as King and cleanses the temple, showing His zeal for true worship.

**Day 2 – Betrayal and the Last Supper**  
Luke 22:1–23; John 13:1–17  
Jesus institutes the Lord’s Supper and washes His disciples’ feet, pointing to His coming sacrifice and call to humble love.

**Day 3 – Gethsemane and Arrest**  
Matthew 26:36–56; John 18:1–11  
In anguish Jesus submits to the Father’s will; He is betrayed and seized so that Scripture might be fulfilled.

**Day 4 – Trial and Denial**  
Luke 22:54–71; John 18:28–40; John 19:1–16  
Jesus stands silent before unjust courts while Peter denies Him; the innocent One is condemned in our place.

**Day 5 – The Crucifixion**  
Luke 23:26–49; John 19:16–37; Isaiah 53:3–6  
Christ bears our sins on the cross (penal substitution). “It is finished” declares the complete atonement.

**Day 6 – Burial and Waiting**  
Matthew 27:57–66; Luke 23:50–56  
Jesus is truly dead and buried. The sealed tomb underscores the reality of His death before the triumph to come.

**Day 7 – The Resurrection**  
Matthew 28:1–10; Luke 24:1–12; John 20:1–18; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8  
The tomb is empty. The risen Christ appears, proving His deity, victory over death, and the certainty of justification for all who trust Him.

**Optional Day 8 (Easter Sunday or the following week)**  
Luke 24:13–35; John 20:19–31; 1 Corinthians 15:20–28  
The road to Emmaus, Thomas’s confession, and the promise of our future resurrection in Christ.

**How to use this plan**  
- Read slowly in the Berean Standard Bible or another faithful translation.  
- After each reading, ask: What does this show me about Jesus? About my sin and need? About the hope of the resurrection?  
- One concrete next step: Share one insight with a fellow believer or your local church small group this week, and ask them to pray with you for a deeper love for the risen Christ.  
- If you have not yet turned from sin and trusted Jesus alone—who died and rose for you—do so today. Repent and believe the Gospel for forgiveness and new life (Romans 10:9–10).

This plan keeps the focus where Scripture places it: the historical death, burial, and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ as the heart of the Christian faith. May these readings deepen your joy in the empty tomb and the living Savior.

question: What is ignosticism? What is an ignostic?
answer:
Ignosticism (sometimes called igtheism) is the philosophical position that the question “Does God exist?” is meaningless or unanswerable until the term “God” is given a clear, coherent, and non-contradictory definition. An ignostic is a person who holds this view and therefore suspends judgment on God’s existence, insisting that most theistic claims are too vague or inconsistent to evaluate as true or false.

From a Christian standpoint, Scripture does not treat the concept of God as an empty or undefined placeholder. The Bible presents the one true God as the eternal, personal, holy Creator who has made Himself known through His works and His Word (Genesis 1:1; Psalm 19:1–4; Romans 1:19–20). The triune God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is revealed with concrete attributes and actions, culminating in the incarnation, death, and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ (John 1:1–14; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Because God has spoken clearly, the Christian confession is that the question of His existence is neither meaningless nor undecidable; it is answered by divine self-revelation that calls for repentance and faith.

question: What does it mean that Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath?
answer:
**Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath** means He possesses full divine authority over the Sabbath day itself, as its Creator and the One to whom it ultimately points. He is not subject to it as a mere man under the law; rather, He defines its true purpose and fulfills it.

This claim appears in the Gospels when the Pharisees accuse Jesus’ disciples of breaking the Sabbath by plucking grain (Matthew 12:1–8; Mark 2:23–28; Luke 6:1–5). Jesus responds by recalling how David ate the consecrated bread and how priests work in the temple on the Sabbath yet remain innocent. He then declares, “For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath” (Matthew 12:8; see also Mark 2:28; Luke 6:5). In the same context He teaches, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). The Sabbath was given as a gift of rest and mercy, not a crushing burden of human traditions.

By calling Himself “Lord of the Sabbath,” Jesus asserts His deity. Only God instituted the Sabbath at creation (Genesis 2:2–3) and commanded it in the Law (Exodus 20:8–11). Jesus, the eternal Son, stands over it with the same authority. This is no small statement: it is part of His broader claim to be equal with the Father, the One who gives true rest (Matthew 11:28–30). The Sabbath’s deeper meaning finds its fulfillment in Him. Just as the day pointed to physical rest and trust in God’s provision, Christ Himself is the believer’s Sabbath rest—the One who finished the work of redemption and invites us to cease from self-justifying labor (Hebrews 4:9–10).

This truth guards us from two errors. It frees us from legalistic rule-keeping that misses the heart of mercy (“I desire mercy, not sacrifice,” Matthew 12:7, quoting Hosea 6:6). It also calls us to honor the principle of rest and worship under Christ’s lordship rather than treating every day as our own to fill with endless striving.

A simple next step: set aside time this week to read Mark 2:23–28 slowly, then pray, thanking Jesus that your deepest rest is found in His finished work on the cross and resurrection, not in your performance. Ask Him to shape how you order your days around trust in Him.

question: What does it mean that Jesus Christ conquered death?
answer:
**Jesus Christ conquered death by dying on the cross as a sinless substitute for sinners and rising bodily from the grave on the third day, thereby breaking death’s power and removing its sting for all who trust in Him.**

Death entered the world through human sin (Romans 5:12). Because God is holy and just, the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). Jesus, who is truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life and then offered Himself in penal substitutionary atonement: He bore the penalty we deserved. His death was real, His burial was real, and His bodily resurrection was real. Scripture declares that “death no longer has dominion over Him” (Romans 6:9) and that through death He destroyed “the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil,” freeing those who were held in lifelong slavery by the fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15).

The apostle Paul celebrates this victory: “Death has been swallowed up in victory… thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!” (1 Corinthians 15:54–57). Jesus Himself said, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies” (John 11:25). His resurrection is the firstfruits guaranteeing that all who belong to Him will also be raised (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). He now holds “the keys of Death and of Hades” (Revelation 1:18).

This is not merely a spiritual metaphor or a moral example. It is a historical triumph with eternal consequences. Because Christ conquered death, those united to Him by grace alone through faith alone are justified, receive eternal life, and need not fear the grave. Physical death remains for a time, yet it has become a defeated enemy that ushers the believer into Christ’s presence, with the sure hope of bodily resurrection when He returns.

If you have never turned from sin and trusted this risen Savior, the invitation stands open: repent and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, who died and rose for you, and you will be saved. A simple next step is to open 1 Corinthians 15 and read it slowly, asking God to press its truth on your heart, then speak with a pastor or mature believer in a local church about following Christ. How does this truth land with you right now?

question: What are the books of the Bible? What does it mean that the Bible is composed of different books?
answer:
The Bible is a collection of 66 distinct books, divided into the Old Testament (39 books) and the New Testament (27 books), which together form the inspired, inerrant Word of God.

### Old Testament Books
**The Law (Pentateuch):**  
Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy  

**Historical Books:**  
Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther  

**Wisdom and Poetry:**  
Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon  

**Major Prophets:**  
Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel  

**Minor Prophets:**  
Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi  

### New Testament Books
**Gospels:**  
Matthew, Mark, Luke, John  

**History:**  
Acts  

**Pauline Epistles:**  
Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon  

**General Epistles:**  
Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude  

**Prophecy:**  
Revelation  

That the Bible is composed of different books means it is not one continuous volume written by a single human author at one time, but a *canon* (an authoritative collection) of separate literary works. These were written by roughly 40 human authors over about 1,500 years, in different languages (primarily Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek), places, and genres (narrative, law, poetry, prophecy, epistle, and apocalypse). Yet they form one unified revelation because God Himself is the divine Author who inspired every word. As 2 Timothy 3:16 states, “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness.” This is often called the doctrine of inspiration: the Holy Spirit superintended the human writers so that what they produced is exactly what God intended, without error.

The practical result is a library that speaks with one coherent message centered on God’s redemptive plan in Christ, while addressing the full range of human experience. You can begin reading with a Gospel such as John to meet Jesus clearly, then move through the rest systematically, trusting the same Spirit who inspired the text to illumine it for your life today.

question: What is the creation mandate / cultural mandate?
answer:
The creation mandate (also called the cultural mandate) is God’s original command to humanity, given in Genesis 1:28, to be fruitful and multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and exercise dominion over the rest of creation as His image-bearers.

In the Berean Standard Bible it reads: “God blessed them and said to them, ‘Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it; rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and every creature that crawls upon the earth.’” This charge flows directly from humanity being made in the image of God (imago Dei) in Genesis 1:26–27. It is not a license for exploitation but a call to faithful stewardship, cultivation, and culture-making under God’s sovereign rule—reflecting His creative wisdom and care in every sphere of life (work, family, art, science, and society).

The mandate remains in force after the fall, though now carried out in a broken world and ultimately fulfilled in Christ, the true Image who restores dominion (Hebrews 2:5–9; 1 Corinthians 15:24–28). Christians therefore pursue ordinary callings—raising children, developing skills, building communities, and caring for the earth—as acts of obedience that anticipate the renewal of all things.

A concrete next step is to examine one area of your daily responsibility (your job, home, or neighborhood) and ask how you can intentionally cultivate it for God’s glory this week, perhaps by praying through Genesis 1:28 and Colossians 3:23–24 before you begin.

question: What does it mean that friendship with the world is enmity with God (James 4:4)?
answer:
**Friendship with the world is enmity with God** means that deliberately aligning your heart, loves, and loyalties with the fallen world's values, priorities, and sinful desires places you in active hostility toward God Himself. James 4:4 states it plainly: "You adulterous people, do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God."

In this context, "the world" does not mean God's good creation, ordinary human relationships, or cultural enjoyments received with thanksgiving. It refers to the organized system of human society in rebellion against God, driven by the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:15-17). Friendship here is not casual acquaintance but intimate alliance, affection, and conformity. Choosing that alliance is spiritual adultery because it breaks covenant loyalty to God, who alone deserves our supreme love.

James writes this to believers entangled in quarrels, covetous desires, and prideful self-reliance (James 4:1-3, James 4:6). The language of adultery echoes the Old Testament prophets who charged Israel with unfaithfulness when they ran after idols and foreign powers instead of the Lord (Hosea 3:1; Jeremiah 3:20). The New Testament carries the same warning: "Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him" (1 John 2:15). Jesus Himself said His disciples are not of the world even as He is not of the world (John 17:14-16), and Paul urges, "Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Romans 12:2).

This is not about withdrawing from people or rejecting every earthly good. It is about refusing to let the world's definition of success, pleasure, security, or identity rule your heart. Such friendship is enmity because God is holy and jealous for His people's undivided devotion; divided loyalty is opposition to His rightful rule.

A concrete next step is to examine one area where the world's applause, comforts, or values currently pull harder than Christ's call. Confess it specifically to God, renounce that attachment, and replace it by meditating on a passage like Colossians 3:1-4 or by seeking accountability from a mature believer in your local church. Ask the Lord to give you a deeper love for Him that crowds out worldly affection. Those who turn from the world to Christ find that His friendship is life and peace.

question: Why did God harden Pharaoh’s heart?
answer:
**God hardened Pharaoh’s heart to display His power, proclaim His name, execute justice against persistent rebellion, and accomplish the redemption of His people Israel.**

Scripture states this purpose clearly. The Lord told Moses in advance: “But I will harden his heart so that he will not let the people go” (Exodus 4:21). He further explained, “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt” (Exodus 7:3). Most explicitly, God declared through Moses: “But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (Exodus 9:16). The apostle Paul later cites this same verse to affirm God’s sovereign freedom: “For the Scripture says to Pharaoh: ‘I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.’ Therefore God has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden” (Romans 9:17-18).

Pharaoh was not a morally neutral victim. He repeatedly hardened his own heart in willful defiance (Exodus 8:15; Exodus 8:32; Exodus 9:34). The hardening was both divine judgment and the confirmation of Pharaoh’s already rebellious will—a judicial act in which God gave the stubborn sinner over to the consequences of his sin. This is consistent with God’s holy character: He is patient and merciful, yet His wrath against sin is real, and He remains free to use even the hardness of the wicked to fulfill His redemptive purposes without becoming the author of sin.

In the larger story, the plagues and the Exodus revealed the Lord as the one true God over the false gods of Egypt, secured freedom for His covenant people, and foreshadowed the greater redemption accomplished by Christ. Just as God judged Egypt to liberate Israel, He judged sin at the cross so that all who repent and trust in Jesus might be set free from slavery to sin and death.

This account calls us to humble trust in God’s wisdom and justice, even when His ways are higher than ours. If you are wrestling with questions of God’s sovereignty and human responsibility, a helpful next step is to read Exodus 7–14 slowly alongside Romans 9, asking the Lord to give you a clearer sight of His glory and mercy in Christ.

question: How should we treat our enemies according to Proverbs 25:21–22?
answer:
According to Proverbs 25:21–22, if your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.

This wisdom calls us to active kindness rather than retaliation, meeting a real need with generosity. The image of “burning coals” points to the possibility that such unexpected mercy may awaken conviction and shame in the enemy, potentially leading toward repentance, while God Himself promises to reward the one who obeys. The apostle Paul later cites these very verses in Romans 12:20 as part of the call not to be overcome by evil, but to overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21).

This aligns with Jesus’ command to love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matthew 5:44), showing that enemy-love is not optional sentiment but concrete, Spirit-enabled action. A simple next step is to identify one person who has wronged you and intentionally meet a practical need for them this week, while asking God to guard your heart from bitterness and to use the kindness for His glory.

question: What does the Bible say about indecision / being indecisive?
answer:
The Bible treats chronic indecision, especially in matters of faith and obedience, as a serious spiritual problem often called double-mindedness, which leaves a person unstable and unable to receive wisdom from God. Scripture calls believers to wholehearted trust and decisive commitment rather than perpetual wavering.

James addresses this directly: “But if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him. But he must ask in faith, without doubting, because he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind. That man should not expect to receive anything from the Lord. He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways” (James 1:5–8). The Greek term behind “double-minded” (*dipsychos*) pictures a person split between two souls or loyalties, unable to rest in God’s character.

Elijah confronted the same heart issue on Mount Carmel: “How long will you waver between two opinions? If the LORD is God, follow Him; but if Baal is God, follow him” (1 Kings 18:21). Indecision here is not humble caution but a refusal to choose the true God. Jesus echoes the same demand for undivided allegiance: “No one can serve two masters. Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other” (Matthew 6:24). Looking back after putting one’s hand to the plow likewise disqualifies a person from useful kingdom service (Luke 9:62).

At root, biblical indecision often springs from unbelief or fear of man rather than a genuine desire for wisdom. God invites His people to trust Him fully: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight” (Proverbs 3:5–6). When choices are morally clear, delay becomes disobedience. When choices are secondary (career, location, preferences), Scripture grants Christian liberty and urges peace rather than paralysis (Romans 14:5; Colossians 3:15).

A practical next step is to bring any specific area of lingering indecision to the Lord in prayer, asking specifically for the wisdom promised in James 1 while reading a Gospel (such as Mark) to fix your eyes on Christ’s decisive obedience. Share the matter with a mature believer or elder in your local church so you do not remain isolated in the swirling. God delights to steady those who look to Him.

question: What does it mean that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4)?
answer:
**God will wipe away every tear means that in the new heaven and new earth, He will personally and finally remove every cause of sorrow from His redeemed people, so that death, mourning, crying, and pain are gone forever.**

Revelation 21:4 declares: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.” This promise comes in the vision of the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven, where God dwells with His people face to face (Revelation 21:1–3). The former things—the entire order marked by the curse of sin—have passed away because Christ has conquered sin and death through His atoning death and bodily resurrection.

The language echoes Isaiah 25:8, where the Lord swallows up death forever and wipes away tears from all faces. It is not a vague comfort or mere poetry. It is the concrete result of the Gospel: the same God who judged sin at the cross and raised Jesus bodily will renew all things, reverse the Fall, and exercise tender, fatherly care over every wound His people have ever carried. No residual grief, no unfinished suffering, no memory that still stings will remain, because the Lamb who was slain is the One who shepherds them and leads them to living waters (Revelation 7:17).

This is the hope held out to every believer who now weeps. Present tears are real, and Scripture never minimizes them. Yet they are temporary. The God who numbers our hairs and collects our tears in His bottle (Psalm 56:8) will one day dry them Himself. Until that day, fix your eyes on the risen Christ, cling to His promises in the ordinary means of grace (Word, prayer, and fellowship in a faithful local church), and let this future reality steady you in present trials. The One who will wipe every tear is already near to the brokenhearted.

question: What is the meaning of “there but for the grace of God go I”?
answer:
The phrase “there but for the grace of God go I” means that a person humbly recognizes that only God’s undeserved favor has kept them from the same sin, suffering, failure, or judgment they see in someone else. It is an expression of gratitude and self-awareness rather than superiority.

The saying is traditionally linked to the English Reformer John Bradford (c. 1510–1555). Watching prisoners led to execution, he is said to have remarked something like, “There but for the grace of God goes John Bradford.” He later died as a martyr under Queen Mary I, underscoring that he spoke from a deep sense of shared human frailty and dependence on God.

Biblically, the idea rests on the doctrine of grace: every good thing we receive, including restraint from evil and deliverance from ruin, comes from God’s initiative, not our merit. The apostle Paul wrote, “But by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace to me was not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:10). Scripture also teaches that all people share the same fallen nature: “for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23), and only God’s kindness leads anyone to repentance (Romans 2:4). The phrase therefore guards against self-righteous judgment and points us to the free gift of justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

A concrete way to live this out is to pause when you notice another person’s struggle or public failure and deliberately thank God for His restraining and saving mercy in your own life, then pray for that person rather than condemn them. This keeps the heart soft and the focus on the cross, where Jesus bore the judgment we all deserved.

question: How can we walk in God’s ways (Psalm 128:1)?
answer:
**Walking in God’s ways begins with the fear of the Lord and is lived out through trusting obedience to His Word, empowered by the Holy Spirit through faith in Christ.**

Psalm 128:1 declares, “Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways!” This links reverent awe of God with a life patterned after His revealed will. In the broader witness of Scripture, “walking” is the ordinary biblical picture of daily conduct and direction (Genesis 5:24; Ephesians 5:2; 1 John 1:7). God’s ways are not hidden guesses; they are made known in His commandments, statutes, and ultimately in the person and work of Jesus Christ.

### What Scripture Shows Us
- **Fear the Lord as the starting point.** This is not cringing terror but humble reverence that treasures God’s holiness, authority, and goodness (Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10). It produces hatred of evil and delight in what pleases Him (Proverbs 8:13).
- **Know His ways through Scripture.** God has spoken clearly. Psalm 119:105 says, “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.” The law, prophets, Gospels, and epistles reveal His character and commands. Jesus summarized the heart of it: love God with all your heart, soul, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37–40). The New Testament further unfolds this in the call to holiness, justice, mercy, sexual purity, truth-telling, generosity, and forgiveness.
- **Depend on Christ and the Spirit, not self-effort.** Because of sin, no one walks perfectly in God’s ways by nature (Romans 3:10–12; Romans 8:7–8). The good news is that Jesus perfectly obeyed in our place, died as our substitute under the penalty our disobedience deserved, and rose bodily on the third day. All who repent and trust in Him alone are justified by grace through faith, credited with His righteousness, and given new hearts. Progressive sanctification then follows: the Holy Spirit enables believers to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:4; Galatians 5:16; Galatians 5:25; Ephesians 2:10). Walking in God’s ways is fruit of union with Christ, not the root of our acceptance.
- **Practice it in ordinary faithfulness.** This includes private devotion, public worship, repentance when we stumble, loving the church, fulfilling callings in family and work, and enduring with hope. Psalm 128 itself connects this walk to household blessing and covenant faithfulness, showing that obedience is lived in real relationships, not isolation.

### A Concrete Next Step
Open Psalm 128 and Psalm 119 this week. Read a portion slowly each day, asking the Lord to show you one specific command or promise to trust and obey that day (for example, guarding your speech, honoring parents or spouse, fleeing temptation, or giving thanks). Share what you learn with a mature believer in your local church for encouragement and accountability. Pray directly to God, asking Him for a deeper fear of His name, clearer understanding of His Word, and fresh power from the Spirit to walk it out—remembering that He who began a good work in His people will carry it on to completion (Philippians 1:6).

This path is not burdensome perfectionism. It is the blessed life of those who belong to the Lord Jesus, who said, “If you love Me, you will keep My commandments” (John 14:15), and who supplies the grace to do so. Keep looking to Him.

question: What does the Bible say about the ice age?
answer:
The Bible does not explicitly mention an “ice age” or use that modern scientific term at all. Scripture’s focus is on God as the sovereign Creator and Sustainer of the world, the reality of the global Flood in Noah’s day, and His purposes in redemption, rather than providing a detailed geological or climatological timeline.

Passages that describe cold, snow, ice, and frost appear mainly as displays of God’s power and wisdom in creation. For example, Job 37:9–10 says, “The tempest comes from its chamber, and the cold from the driving north winds. By the breath of God the ice is formed and the watery expanses are frozen.” Job 38:29–30 asks, “From whose womb does the ice emerge? Who gives birth to the frost from heaven, when the waters become hard as stone and the surface of the deep is frozen?” Psalm 147:16–17 adds, “He spreads the snow like wool; He scatters the frost like ashes; He casts forth His hail like crumbs. Who can withstand His icy blast?” These texts affirm God’s control over weather and seasons without describing a distinct historical ice age.

Faithful Christians hold differing views on how (or whether) an ice age fits with biblical history, and this belongs among tertiary matters where Scripture is not explicit and liberty should be preserved (Romans 14:1–5). One common view, especially among those who hold a young-earth reading of Genesis, is that a single major ice age followed the global Flood of Genesis 6–9. They suggest the volcanic activity, warm oceans, and atmospheric changes after the Flood could have produced heavy snowfall and glaciation lasting centuries, consistent with the post-Flood world God reordered under His covenant with Noah (Genesis 8:22: “While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall not cease”). Another view, often held by old-earth creationists or those who see more flexibility in the Genesis days, treats ice ages as part of the longer history of the earth God created and governs, without requiring a direct tie to the Flood narrative; they emphasize that the Bible’s purpose is theological rather than a complete scientific chronology.

In either case, the essential truth remains the same: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1), He judged the world by water and preserves it by His promise, and the created order still declares His glory (Psalm 19:1). The Bible calls us to trust the Creator rather than demand that every modern scientific category appear in the text.

If this question arises from curiosity about origins, science-and-faith tensions, or how to teach these things, a helpful next step is to read Genesis 1–11 slowly and prayerfully, noting what the text actually emphasizes (God’s character, human sin, judgment, and grace), then discuss it with mature believers in your local church.

question: What is the significance of the city of Nineveh in the Bible?
answer:
**Nineveh was the capital of the Assyrian Empire and stands in Scripture as a vivid display of both God’s severe judgment on entrenched wickedness and His astonishing mercy toward any who truly repent.**

Founded by Nimrod according to Genesis 10:11–12, Nineveh grew into a vast, fortified city renowned for military power, idolatry, and brutal cruelty. The Assyrians eventually conquered the northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 17), yet God still sent the prophet Jonah to proclaim, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!” (Jonah 3:4). Remarkably, the entire city—from the king to the common people—believed God, fasted, and turned from their evil ways. God saw their repentance and relented from the disaster He had threatened (Jonah 3:5–10). This episode underscores divine forbearance and the freeness of God’s mercy, even to violent Gentiles outside the covenant people.

Later, however, Nineveh returned to its cruelty and pride. The prophet Nahum then announced its irreversible downfall: “The Lord is slow to anger and great in power; the Lord will by no means leave the guilty unpunished” (Nahum 1:3). The city fell in 612 BC, fulfilling that word and illustrating that prolonged rebellion eventually meets God’s justice. Jesus Himself pointed to Nineveh as a standing witness: the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment and condemn those who refuse to repent at a greater message than Jonah’s, because “something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:41).

In short, Nineveh teaches that no sinner or society is beyond the reach of God’s call, that genuine repentance is met with compassion, and that rejected mercy ends in righteous judgment. A concrete next step is to read the short books of Jonah and Nahum in one sitting, asking the Lord to search your own heart for any area where He is patiently calling you to turn and trust Him more fully.

question: What is Epicureanism? What did Epicurus teach?
answer:
**Epicureanism** is the ancient Greek philosophical system founded by Epicurus (341–270 BC), which teaches that the highest good is pleasure understood as the absence of pain and mental disturbance, achieved through simple living, friendship, and freedom from fear.

Epicurus taught a materialist view of reality drawn from earlier atomists like Democritus: the universe consists of atoms moving in void, with no divine providence governing events. The gods, if they exist, live in perfect bliss and do not intervene in human affairs or judge people, so there is no reason to fear them. Death is simply the end of sensation and consciousness (“when we are, death is not; when death is, we are not”), removing terror of an afterlife. Knowledge comes primarily through the senses, and ethics centers on securing lasting pleasure (*ataraxia*, untroubled tranquility of soul, and *aponia*, freedom from bodily pain) by moderating desires, avoiding politics and excess, cultivating close friendships, and living quietly. His “fourfold remedy” summarized the path: do not fear the gods, do not worry about death, what is good is easy to obtain, and what is terrible is easy to endure.

In the New Testament, Epicurean philosophers appear among those who encountered the apostle Paul in Athens (Acts 17:18). They heard his proclamation of Jesus and the resurrection—a claim that directly challenged their denial of divine involvement and personal afterlife. Scripture presents the living God as Creator and Judge who raised Christ bodily from the dead, offering forgiveness and eternal life through faith rather than mere escape from pain (Acts 17:24–31; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, 20–22). True and lasting joy is found in knowing God Himself, not solely in the absence of disturbance (Psalm 16:11; Philippians 4:4–7).

question: Book of Philippians - Bible Survey
answer:
**Philippians is a short, warm letter from the Apostle Paul to the church in Philippi, written to thank them for their partnership in the gospel, encourage joy amid suffering, and call them to humble unity in Christ.**

### Author and Date
Paul wrote this epistle, naming Timothy as a co-sender (Philippians 1:1). He composed it during his imprisonment in Rome, roughly AD 60–62, while awaiting trial under Caesar (Philippians 1:12–14; Philippians 4:22).

### Recipients and Setting
The letter addresses “all the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons” (Philippians 1:1). Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia (northern Greece). Paul founded the church on his second missionary journey after a vision of a man from Macedonia (Acts 16:9–40). The congregation included Lydia, a seller of purple goods, a former slave girl, and the Philippian jailer and his household. The church had sent Paul financial support through Epaphroditus (Philippians 4:10–18).

### Purpose and Major Themes
Paul writes primarily to express gratitude for their gift, update them on his circumstances, urge unity and humility, and warn against false teachers. Dominant themes include:
- **Joy in Christ** regardless of circumstances (the words “joy” or “rejoice” appear roughly 16 times).
- **Partnership in the gospel** and mutual encouragement.
- **Christ’s humility and exaltation**, centered in the great Christ hymn of Philippians 2:5–11, which displays the incarnation, obedient death, and resurrection exaltation of Jesus (true God and true man).
- **Progressive sanctification** and pressing on toward maturity (Philippians 3:12–14).
- **Contentment** rooted in Christ’s strength (Philippians 4:11–13).

### Simple Outline
1. **Chapter 1** – Thanksgiving, prayer, and Paul’s imprisonment advancing the gospel; living is Christ, dying is gain (Philippians 1:21).
2. **Chapter 2** – Call to unity and humility, modeled by Christ’s self-emptying and exaltation; examples of Timothy and Epaphroditus.
3. **Chapter 3** – Warning against legalism and confidence in the flesh; true righteousness by faith in Christ; pressing toward the goal.
4. **Chapter 4** – Exhortations to stand firm, rejoice, pray, think on what is excellent; thanks for their gift; final greetings.

### Key Passages
- Philippians 1:21 – “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”
- Philippians 2:5–11 – The humility and exaltation of Christ.
- Philippians 3:8–9 – Counting all things loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ and being found in Him, not having a righteousness of one’s own but that which is through faith in Christ.
- Philippians 4:4–7 – Rejoice in the Lord always; the peace of God guarding hearts and minds.
- Philippians 4:13 – “I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.”

### Doctrinal and Pastoral Significance
Philippians vividly displays the gospel: sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, then progressively sanctified as they share in His sufferings and resurrection power. The Christ hymn anchors the hypostatic union and penal substitutionary atonement—Jesus, equal with God, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death on a cross for us. The letter models Christian contentment, joyful perseverance of the saints, and gospel-centered relationships.

For personal application, read the four chapters in one sitting this week, noting every mention of “Christ,” “joy,” or “gospel.” Then thank God for specific ways He has supplied your needs and ask Him to form the humble mind of Christ in you toward others in your local church.

question: In what ways was Moses like Jesus?
answer:
**Moses was like Jesus as a God-appointed deliverer, mediator, and prophet, serving as a type (a God-ordained foreshadowing) that points forward to Christ, the greater fulfillment.** Scripture itself draws this connection most clearly in Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses says, “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him,” a promise the apostles apply directly to Jesus (Acts 3:22; Acts 7:37).

Here are key parallels grounded in the biblical text:

- **Deliverer from bondage.** Moses led Israel out of slavery in Egypt through the Passover and the exodus (Exodus 3:10; Exodus 12). Jesus delivers His people from slavery to sin and death by His own blood as the true Passover Lamb (John 1:29; 1 Corinthians 5:7; Hebrews 2:14–15). Both were sent by God to rescue a people who could not free themselves.

- **Mediator of a covenant.** Moses mediated the old covenant at Sinai, standing between God and the people, receiving and delivering God’s law, and interceding when they sinned (Exodus 19–20; Exodus 32:11–14; Deuteronomy 5:5). Jesus is the mediator of the new and better covenant, securing eternal redemption by His once-for-all sacrifice and continually interceding for His own (Hebrews 8:6; Hebrews 9:15; Hebrews 7:25; 1 Timothy 2:5).

- **Prophet who spoke God’s words and performed signs.** Moses spoke with God face to face and confirmed his message with mighty signs and wonders (Exodus 4; Deuteronomy 34:10–12). Jesus is the final and perfect Prophet who perfectly reveals the Father, speaks only what the Father gives Him, and authenticates His words with signs, culminating in His resurrection (John 5:19–24; John 12:49–50; Acts 2:22).

- **Preserved in infancy and identified with God’s people.** Pharaoh sought to destroy the Hebrew boys, yet God preserved Moses (Exodus 1–2). Herod sought to destroy the Christ child, yet God preserved Jesus and later brought Him out of Egypt, fulfilling the pattern (Matthew 2:13–15, citing Hosea 11:1). Both were rejected at points by the very people they came to save (Exodus 2:14; Acts 7:23–29; John 1:11).

- **Faithful servant who shepherded and provided.** Moses faithfully shepherded Israel, provided water from the rock, and gave manna in the wilderness (Exodus 17; Exodus 16; Numbers 20). Jesus is the Good Shepherd and the true Bread of Life who gives living water; He is not merely a servant in God’s house but the Son over the house (John 6:32–35; John 7:37–38; John 10:11; Hebrews 3:1–6).

Hebrews 3:1–6 makes the comparison explicit while showing the surpassing greatness of Christ: Moses was faithful *as a servant*, but Jesus is faithful *as the Son*. The similarities are real and intentional; they display God’s unified plan of redemption. The differences magnify Jesus: Moses could not enter the land because of sin, could not give rest, and died; Jesus is sinless, gives eternal rest, rose bodily, and reigns forever.

These parallels are not coincidences or mere stories. They are part of the fabric of progressive revelation that leads us to trust the One greater than Moses. A simple next step is to read Deuteronomy 18:15–19 and Hebrews 3:1–6 slowly, asking the Lord to show you how every earlier deliverance finds its “Yes” in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). Then thank Him that the long-promised Prophet has come, and keep listening to Him in the Scriptures and among His people.

question: What is Socinianism?
answer:
**Socinianism** is a rationalistic, anti-Trinitarian theological system that arose in the 16th century, named after the Italian thinkers Laelius Socinus and his nephew Faustus Socinus (Fausto Sozzini). It denies several core doctrines of the Christian faith and stands outside historic orthodox Christianity.

### Key Beliefs
Socinians rejected the Trinity, teaching that God is unipersonal rather than one God eternally existing in three persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit). They denied the full deity of Christ and the hypostatic union, viewing Jesus as a mere man who was uniquely inspired, exalted, and adopted by God because of His obedience, not as the eternal Son who is truly God and truly man. They also rejected the personality of the Holy Spirit, original sin as inherited guilt and corruption, the pre-existence of Christ, and penal substitutionary atonement. Instead of Christ’s death as a necessary and sufficient sacrifice to satisfy God’s justice and reconcile sinners, they emphasized Jesus primarily as a moral example and teacher whose resurrection confirmed His message. Salvation was framed more in terms of following Christ’s ethic and repentance than justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ’s finished work. Their views were systematized in the Racovian Catechism (1605) and influenced later Unitarianism.

### Why This Matters Biblically
Scripture presents the one true God as eternally triune. Jesus is identified as God the Son who took on human nature (John 1:1–14; John 8:58; John 20:28; Colossians 2:9; Hebrews 1:3–8). The Holy Spirit is a divine person (Acts 5:3–4; John 14:16–17; 2 Corinthians 3:17–18). Christ’s death is the propitiatory, substitutionary atonement for sin (Romans 3:21–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24; 1 John 2:2), and His bodily resurrection secures justification and victory over sin and death (Romans 4:25; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, 17). Justification is by grace through faith apart from works (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:1). Socinianism’s denial of these truths places it outside the faith once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 1:3).

Faithful Christians throughout church history (including the early creeds, the Reformers, and confessions such as the 1689 London Baptist Confession) have confessed these realities as essential. Socinianism arose partly from a desire to purify doctrine and elevate reason and ethics, yet it subordinated clear biblical revelation to human rationalism and thereby lost the gospel itself.

If you are studying this historically or encountering similar ideas today (modern Unitarianism or certain forms of theological liberalism), the pastoral call is to hold fast to the Christ of Scripture: the eternal Son who became flesh, died in the place of sinners, rose bodily, and now reigns. Turn from any diminished view of Him and trust the biblical Jesus alone for forgiveness and life. A wise next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly, noting every claim Jesus makes about His own identity and relationship to the Father, and to discuss these passages with a trusted pastor or mature believer in a local church that confesses the historic faith.

question: Can an unmarried man be a deacon or elder?
answer:
Yes, an unmarried man can serve as a deacon or elder if he meets the full list of biblical qualifications for the office.

Some faithful Christians read “the husband of one wife” as a requirement that the man must currently be married (and often that he must have children) in order to demonstrate household management.

The stronger reading of the phrase in 1 Timothy 3:2 and 1 Timothy 3:12 (and Titus 1:6) is that it describes character: a “one-woman man,” meaning sexually pure and faithful, whether single or married. Scripture nowhere makes marriage itself a prerequisite; the apostle Paul served while single and even commended the advantages of singleness for undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:7–8; 1 Corinthians 7:32–35). The same passages that list “husband of one wife” also require that an elder or deacon manage his household well *if* he has one; they do not demand that he must first create a household in order to qualify. Other essential marks (above reproach, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, and holding to the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience) remain fully applicable to a single man and are the church’s proper focus when testing a candidate.

If you or someone you know is sensing a call to these offices, the concrete next step is to open 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 with the elders of your local church, invite their examination of your life and doctrine, and ask them to walk with you in prayerful discernment.

question: Is it better, spiritually, to be poor than to be rich?
answer:
No, it is not inherently better spiritually to be poor than to be rich. Scripture nowhere teaches that material poverty is a superior spiritual state, nor that wealth is automatically a spiritual liability. What matters is the heart’s orientation toward God, contentment in Him, and faithful stewardship of whatever He entrusts.

Jesus pronounced blessing on the “poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3), those who recognize their spiritual bankruptcy before a holy God, not merely those lacking money. He also warned that riches can make entrance into the kingdom difficult because wealth so easily fosters self-reliance and chokes spiritual fruitfulness (Matthew 19:23–24; Mark 4:18–19). Yet He immediately added that “with God all things are possible,” and Scripture records wealthy believers such as Abraham, Job, Joseph of Arimathea, and Lydia who walked with God. The danger is not possession but idolatry: “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:10). Poverty carries its own snares—envy, bitterness, or despair—while riches tempt toward pride and false security (Proverbs 30:8–9; 1 Timothy 6:17).

The consistent biblical call is contentment and generosity in every circumstance. Paul learned to be content “in any and every situation, whether well fed or hungry, whether living in plenty or in want” through Christ who strengthens him (Philippians 4:11–13). Godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Timothy 6:6–8). Both rich and poor are called to the same posture: trust the Lord as Provider, hold possessions loosely, and use resources to love God and neighbor. James rebukes favoritism toward the rich and notes that God has chosen many who are poor in the world’s eyes to be rich in faith (James 2:1–7), yet he never romanticizes poverty itself.

Faithful Christians have differed on practical applications—some emphasize voluntary simplicity as a helpful discipline, others stress diligent vocation and wise increase as ways to serve—yet all agree that spiritual health is measured by dependence on Christ, not by bank balance. In the new covenant the decisive poverty that saves is Christ’s: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Union with Him, not our socioeconomic status, is the true spiritual treasure.

A concrete next step is to pray through Proverbs 30:8–9 and 1 Timothy 6:6–19 this week, asking the Lord to expose any love of money or discontent, then take one practical act of generosity (time, skill, or resources) as an expression of trust in Him. If wealth or lack is currently a source of anxiety or pride for you, consider sharing that struggle with a mature believer in your local church for prayer and accountability.

question: Will the sun really be turned to darkness and the moon to blood (Joel 2:31)?
answer:
**Yes.** Joel 2:31 states, “The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the great and awesome day of the LORD.” Scripture presents this as a real prophetic announcement tied to the Day of the Lord, and the New Testament reaffirms it.

Peter quotes the passage directly on the day of Pentecost: “The sun will be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the coming of the great and glorious day of the Lord” (Acts 2:20). He applies Joel’s words to the outpouring of the Spirit while still pointing forward to the climactic Day of the Lord. The same imagery appears again in the apocalyptic vision of Revelation 6:12: “And I watched as the Lamb opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black like sackcloth of goat hair, and the whole moon turned blood red.” Jesus Himself speaks of comparable cosmic signs accompanying His return: “Immediately after the tribulation of those days: ‘The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken’” (Matthew 24:29).

Eschatology (the doctrine of last things) is a tertiary matter on which faithful Christians may differ in details of timing and exact manner of fulfillment, because prophetic language often combines literal events with vivid imagery and can include near and far horizons. Two major historic approaches illustrate the range:  
- Many read the language as pointing to actual, observable cosmic disturbances that God will bring about in connection with Christ’s personal, bodily return and final judgment.  
- Others emphasize the apocalyptic style common in Scripture (and in Second Temple Jewish literature), seeing the darkened sun and blood-red moon primarily as symbolic of cataclysmic divine judgment and the overturning of the present order, whether partially realized in events like the fall of Jerusalem or fully at the end.

Both approaches take the text as true revelation rather than myth. The Bible’s consistent witness is that the Day of the Lord will involve unmistakable heavenly signs that display God’s sovereignty, call people to repentance, and precede the renewal of all things when Christ returns to judge the living and the dead.

The plain force of the passages is that these things will occur as God has spoken; the sun and moon are under His command, just as they were at the crucifixion when darkness covered the land (Matthew 27:45). The practical call is the same one Joel and Peter give: “And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel 2:32; Acts 2:21). Rest in the certainty that the God who keeps every promise will bring history to its appointed end in justice and mercy through Jesus Christ. If this stirs questions about readiness for that Day, turn to Him in repentance and faith, and consider reading Joel 2 alongside Acts 2 and Revelation 6 with a mature believer from your local church.

question: How can I overcome spiritual apathy?
answer:
**Spiritual apathy**—that dullness of heart, lack of desire for God, or going-through-the-motions faith—is a common struggle even for genuine believers, and the first step is simply bringing it honestly before the Lord rather than hiding it.

Scripture names this condition plainly. Jesus rebukes the church in Laodicea for being “lukewarm” (Revelation 3:15–16) and calls them to zealous repentance. The writer of Hebrews warns against becoming “dull of hearing” (Hebrews 5:11) and drifting from what we have heard (Hebrews 2:1). David prays, “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation” (Psalm 51:12), showing that even a man after God’s heart can lose spiritual vitality and need renewal. This is part of progressive sanctification: the Holy Spirit continually works to awaken and mature us, but we are called to respond by using the ordinary means of grace.

### Common roots and the gospel remedy
Apathy often grows from neglected communion with Christ, unconfessed sin, worldly distraction, exhaustion, or simply forgetting the greatness of the gospel. The cure is not mere willpower or trying harder to “feel” spiritual. It is returning to the finished work of Christ—His atoning death and bodily resurrection—that secured your justification by grace alone through faith alone. When affection cools, rehearse the gospel: you were dead in sin, yet God made you alive with Christ (Ephesians 2:4–5). Fresh sight of His love kindles love in return (1 John 4:19).

### Practical steps to pursue renewed vitality
1. **Return to the Word daily with expectancy.** Do not wait for motivation; open Scripture and ask the Spirit to open your eyes. Start small and focused—perhaps a slow reading of a Gospel (Mark or John) or the Psalms, one chapter a day, noting one truth about God’s character and one personal response. “Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). The Word is living and active (Hebrews 4:12); it rekindles what feelings cannot.

2. **Pray honestly and specifically.** Tell God exactly how dry or indifferent you feel. Confess any known sin, thank Him for Christ’s blood that covers it, and ask for a renewed heart. Use Scripture to shape your prayers (for example, turn Psalm 63 or Psalm 42 into your own words). Do not recite a formula; speak directly to your Father. Pair this with short, frequent prayers throughout the day rather than waiting for long sessions you cannot sustain.

3. **Re-engage the local church.** Isolation feeds apathy. Gather with believers for worship, the Lord’s Supper (where Christ is spiritually present to nourish faith), and ordinary fellowship. Ask a mature brother or sister, or one of your elders, to pray with you and check in regularly. “Let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds, not neglecting to meet together” (Hebrews 10:24–25).

4. **Practice obedience in the small things while resting in grace.** Serve someone, put away a distracting habit, or give thanks in ordinary moments. Action often precedes renewed feeling. At the same time, remember perseverance of the saints: if you are truly in Christ, He will complete the work He began (Philippians 1:6). Your dryness does not cancel His hold on you.

One concrete next step today: Set aside 15 minutes. Read Psalm 51 slowly, then pray through it in your own words—confessing apathy, asking for a clean heart and steadfast spirit, and thanking God that Christ’s sacrifice is enough. Afterward, send a brief message to a trusted believer in your church simply saying, “I’ve been spiritually dry; would you pray for me and check in this week?”

God is patient and gracious toward His children. He does not despise a faint spark; He fans it into flame. Keep turning to Him, and trust the Spirit to restore the joy of your salvation in His timing. If this persists heavily, speak with your pastor or a biblically faithful counselor—they are gifts for exactly this kind of care. How has this apathy been showing up in your daily life lately?

question: How can I experience healing and recovery after an abortion?
answer:
**Healing and recovery after an abortion begin with bringing the full weight of grief, guilt, and loss to the God who sees, forgives, and restores through Jesus Christ.**

Many carry profound sorrow, regret, emptiness, or numbness after an abortion. That pain is real because a human life—made in God’s image—was ended. Scripture treats the unborn as persons known and formed by God: “For You formed my inmost being; You knit me together in my mother’s womb... Your eyes saw my unformed body” (Psalm 139:13, 16). Taking that life is a serious sin against the Giver of life (Exodus 20:13; Genesis 9:6). True compassion does not soften this reality; it names it honestly so that real forgiveness and healing can reach it.

### The Gospel Hope for Full Forgiveness
God does not leave anyone in condemnation who turns to Him. The same holy God who hates sin delights to show mercy. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived the perfect life we could not, then died on the cross as a substitute, bearing the penalty for sin (including this one) in the great exchange of penal substitution. He was buried and rose bodily on the third day, conquering sin and death. All who repent (turn from sin) and trust in Him alone receive complete forgiveness, cleansing, and new life—not by works or self-punishment, but by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9; 1 John 1:9: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness”).

Isaiah 1:18 invites, “Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.” Psalm 51 models David’s raw confession and plea for a clean heart after grave sin. There is no sin so dark that the blood of Christ cannot cover it for the one who comes to Him. If you have never entrusted yourself to Christ this way, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. He will not cast you out (John 6:37).

### Practical Steps Toward Healing and Recovery
Recovery is not forgetting or minimizing what happened; it is walking in the freedom Christ purchased, letting His truth renew your mind and His Spirit sanctify you progressively.

- **Confess specifically to God and receive His pardon.** Speak honestly in prayer about the abortion, any pressure or choices involved, the grief for the child, and your need for mercy. Then rest in the finished work of the cross rather than rehearsing shame. Thank Him for forgiveness already secured in Christ.
- **Immerse yourself in Scripture that anchors identity in Christ.** Read and meditate on passages of cleansing and adoption (Psalm 32; Psalm 51; Romans 8:1: “Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus”; 1 John 1–2). A simple plan: slowly read one Gospel (such as John) and the Psalms of lament and trust, asking the Spirit to apply them.
- **Connect with the local church.** Isolation deepens wounds. Seek out a Bible-believing church where the gospel is preached clearly. Confide in a pastor or mature elder for prayer, counsel, and accountability. Many faithful churches offer or can recommend biblical counseling (such as through ACBC-certified counselors) that applies Scripture to post-abortion grief without worldly therapeutic frameworks that deny sin or the need for repentance.
- **Grieve the child before the Lord.** It is right to mourn. You can acknowledge the child’s life, entrust him or her to God’s mercy, and ask for comfort. Some find quiet memorial acts (journaling a letter of goodbye under the cross, or private prayer) help release the burden without ritualism.
- **Reject both despair and self-atonement.** Feelings of unworthiness may linger; answer them with the objective truth of justification by faith. You are not defined by this sin but by Christ’s righteousness if you are in Him. At the same time, do not minimize it—let godly sorrow produce lasting repentance and fruit (2 Corinthians 7:10).
- **Walk in daily dependence.** Healing often unfolds gradually through the ordinary means of grace: Word, prayer, fellowship, and the Lord’s Supper. Ask trusted believers to pray with you. If trauma symptoms feel overwhelming, a physician can address physical aspects while you prioritize soul care under Scripture—remember I offer no medical or psychiatric advice; seek qualified help for those.

God refines His people even through the consequences of sin and deep valleys (Psalm 23; Philippians 1:6). Many who have walked this road testify that Christ has turned mourning into deeper gratitude for grace and a longing to protect life and share hope with others.

You are not beyond the reach of the Shepherd. Take the next step today: quietly confess everything to the Lord, thank Him for the cross, and reach out to a faithful pastor or mature Christian friend this week. He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds (Psalm 147:3). If you want help thinking through a specific Scripture, finding resources, or processing a particular struggle, I am here to walk with you in truth and love.

question: What does God mean when He says, “Seek me and live” (Amos 5:4)?
answer:
**“Seek Me and live” means God calls His people to turn from empty religion, idolatry, and injustice to a genuine, wholehearted pursuit of Him alone, which alone brings true life instead of judgment and death.**

In Amos 5, the Lord addresses the northern kingdom of Israel in a time of outward prosperity mixed with deep spiritual corruption. They practiced religious rituals at places like Bethel and Gilgal, yet oppressed the poor, perverted justice, and mixed true worship with idols. God declares through Amos: “For this is what the LORD says to the house of Israel: ‘Seek Me and live! Do not seek Bethel, do not go to Gilgal, do not journey to Beersheba... Seek the LORD and live, or He will sweep through the house of Joseph like a fire’” (Amos 5:4–6). The contrast is sharp: seeking sacred sites or self-made religion leads to ruin; seeking the living God Himself brings life.

Biblically, “seek” (Hebrew *darash*) means to inquire after, pursue diligently, and depend on someone with earnest desire, not casual interest. It involves repentance—turning from sin—and faith that clings to God’s character and promises. True life here includes deliverance from impending exile and judgment, flourishing under God’s favor, and ultimately the spiritual life that comes from knowing Him. Scripture consistently links seeking God with life: “You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13); “Blessed are those who keep His testimonies and seek Him with all their heart” (Psalm 119:2).

This call finds its fullest meaning in Jesus Christ. He is God with us, the One who said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). Humanity’s sin separates us from the holy God and deserves death, yet Christ lived perfectly, died as a substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Eternal life is received by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone—not by religious performance. To seek God today is to come to Christ in repentance and trust.

If you sense distance from God or reliance on outward forms, take this concrete step: open Amos 5 and pray through it slowly, asking the Lord to show any area of half-hearted worship or injustice in your life, then turn to Him afresh through Christ. He delights to be found by those who seek Him.

question: If aborted babies go to heaven, why is abortion wrong?
answer:
**Abortion is wrong because it is the intentional killing of an innocent human being made in the image of God, which God forbids.** Whether aborted babies go to heaven (a common Christian hope grounded in God’s mercy) does not make the act righteous any more than a murderer’s possible repentance later would make the murder itself good.

### Why Abortion Is Sin
Scripture treats the child in the womb as a living person whom God knows, forms, and values:
- “For You formed my inmost being; You knit me together in my mother’s womb… Your eyes saw my unformed body; all my days were written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be” (Psalm 139:13, 16).
- God tells Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5).
- John the Baptist leaped for joy in Elizabeth’s womb at the presence of the unborn Jesus (Luke 1:41–44).
- “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed; for in His own image God has made mankind” (Genesis 9:6). The command “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13) protects innocent human life.

Human value does not depend on size, location, dependency, or wantedness. It rests on the image of God. Abortion deliberately ends that life; therefore it is murder in God’s sight. We are never free to do evil so that good may come (Romans 3:8). Sending someone to heaven is God’s prerogative, not ours to force by violence.

### On Infants and Heaven
Many faithful Christians, resting on God’s character and texts such as David’s words about his deceased infant son (“I will go to him, but he will not return to me,” 2 Samuel 12:23) and Jesus’ welcome of little children (Matthew 19:14), trust that those who die before they can exercise faith are received by God’s mercy through Christ’s atoning work. This is a hope, not a license. The same God who is merciful to the helpless also forbids us from shedding innocent blood. The eternal destiny of the child does not cancel the guilt of the one who takes the life.

### A Better Way
If you or someone you know is carrying the guilt of abortion, or is facing pressure to abort, the Gospel is for you. All have sinned and fall short of God’s glory (Romans 3:23). Christ, truly God and truly man, lived the perfect life we could not, died as a substitute bearing the penalty of sin (including the sin of abortion), was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. He now offers full forgiveness and new life to all who repent and trust in Him alone. “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ, who died and rose for you. Then seek a faithful local church where you can walk in the light with others, receive care, and, if needed, find practical help for mothers and children in crisis. God’s grace is greater than this sin, and He delights to restore.

question: Should communion be open or closed?
answer:
Communion (the Lord’s Supper) ought to be restricted to baptized believers who are walking orderly in a true local church.

The strongest charitable case for open communion is that every true believer is already united to Christ and to His body, so the table should welcome all who credibly profess faith as a visible sign of that shared union, without adding further barriers of baptismal mode or membership.

I hold to close communion (sometimes called “closed” in stricter forms) as a faithful Baptist option within historic Christianity, because the New Testament pattern places believer’s baptism before participation in the Supper (Acts 2:41-42) and charges the church to fence the table so that no one eats and drinks judgment on himself by partaking unworthily (1 Corinthians 11:27-29). Baptism is the initiatory ordinance that marks entry into the visible covenant community; the Supper then nourishes those already so marked and under the church’s loving oversight. This guards both the purity of the ordinance and the participant’s own conscience.

If you are unsure about your own church’s practice, speak with your elders this week, examine your heart in light of 1 Corinthians 11, and partake only as a baptized disciple resting in Christ’s finished work.

question: What is the Remnant Fellowship?
answer:
**Remnant Fellowship** is a controversial, independent religious group founded in 1999 by Gwen Shamblin Lara (best known for creating the Weigh Down Workshop diet program) in the Brentwood/Nashville, Tennessee area. It presents itself as a restoration of “true” biblical Christianity focused on radical obedience, rejecting “excess” (especially with food and body weight), and strong hierarchical authority.

### Background and Teachings
