**Zeal in the Bible is passionate, earnest devotion or fervent intensity, which God commends when it is directed toward His glory, truth, and good works, but warns against when it lacks knowledge or serves wrong ends.**

Scripture presents zeal as a godly virtue when rightly ordered. Jesus Himself displayed it when He cleansed the temple: “His disciples remembered that it is written: ‘Zeal for Your house will consume Me’” (John 2:17, quoting Psalm 69:9). Paul urges believers, “Do not let your zeal subside; keep your spiritual fervor, serving the Lord” (Romans 12:11). Christ “gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds” (Titus 2:14). Revelation records the risen Lord’s call: “Those I love, I rebuke and discipline. Therefore be zealous and repent” (Revelation 3:19). Galatians 4:18 affirms, “It is fine to be zealous, provided the purpose is good.”

The Bible also shows the danger of misdirected zeal. Paul describes his pre-conversion life: “as to zeal, persecuting the church” (Philippians 3:6), and later laments of Israel, “For I testify about them that they are zealous for God, but not on the basis of knowledge” (Romans 10:2). Zeal without the knowledge of God’s righteousness in Christ becomes destructive rather than life-giving.

In short, biblical zeal is Spirit-empowered earnestness that flows from knowing God truly, loves what He loves, hates what He hates, and pursues holiness and the advance of the gospel. It is not mere emotion or activism; it is the heat of a heart set on fire by the truth of who God is and what Christ has done.

A concrete next step is to open Romans 12 and Titus 2 this week, ask the Lord to search whether your energy is spent on His priorities or lesser ones, and deliberately channel one area of passion (time, speech, service) toward loving God and neighbor in concrete obedience.

question: What is the grace of God?
answer:
The grace of God is His free, unmerited favor and kindness poured out on undeserving sinners, most fully displayed in the gift of salvation through Jesus Christ.

Scripture presents grace not as something we earn or deserve, but as God’s initiative toward those who have rebelled against Him. Ephesians 2:8-9 declares, “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast.” In the same way, Romans 3:24 says we “are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,” and Titus 2:11 tells us that “the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone.”

This saving grace is rooted in God’s own character—He is “merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). It reaches its climax at the cross, where Christ bore the penalty our sins deserved (penal substitution), so that God could remain just while freely justifying those who trust in His Son. Grace does not merely overlook sin; it conquers it through Christ’s death, burial, and bodily resurrection, then applies that victory to us by the Holy Spirit.

A concrete way this truth shapes daily life is that believers no longer strive to earn God’s smile through performance. Instead, we rest in what Christ has already finished, growing in progressive sanctification as we continually receive fresh supplies of grace through the ordinary means He has given: Scripture, prayer, and the fellowship of the local church. If you have never turned from sin and trusted Christ alone, His grace stands ready—repent and believe the gospel today, and you will find forgiveness and new life in Him.

question: How young can you be to ask Jesus to be your Savior? Can a 3 or 4 year old truly believe?
answer:
There is no minimum age given in Scripture for trusting Jesus as Savior. A 3- or 4-year-old can truly believe, because saving faith is simple trust in Christ, not advanced theological knowledge, and God is able to open even a very young heart to the Gospel.

Jesus Himself welcomed little children and said, “Let the little children come to Me and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matthew 19:14). He also taught that we must become like children in humble dependence: “Truly I tell you, unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3). Childlike faith is not inferior faith; it is the very posture Jesus praises. Timothy is described as having known “the sacred Scriptures from infancy,” which were able to make him “wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15). The Bible never sets a cognitive threshold or age of accountability as a barrier to genuine belief.

True belief, even in a young child, involves the same essentials the Gospel always requires: a God-given awareness that they have sinned and need a Savior, a simple grasp that Jesus is the Son of God who died on the cross for sinners and rose again, and a sincere turning to Him in trust. A preschooler will not articulate penal substitution or justification by faith alone with precision, yet they can know “Jesus loves me, He died for my sins, and I want to follow Him.” The Holy Spirit is the One who grants new birth (John 3:5–8); He is not limited by age or vocabulary.

Of course, young children often repeat what they hear. Discernment comes over time as parents and the local church look for growing fruit: love for Jesus, sorrow over sin (however simple), desire to obey, and perseverance in that trust. Many faithful believers can point back to a clear conversion at age three, four, or five that proved genuine across decades. Others come to fuller assurance later. Either way, we never discourage a child who wants to come to Christ; we gently clarify the Gospel and entrust them to the Lord who knows His own.

If you are a parent or caregiver, keep sharing the good news in plain words they can grasp: God made us, we have all sinned, Jesus died and rose to save us, and anyone who turns from sin and trusts Him is forgiven and made new. Read Bible stories that center on Christ, pray with them (encouraging them to speak to God in their own words), and involve them in the life of a gospel-preaching church. Ask the Lord to give them genuine faith, and rest in His promise that He will finish the good work He begins (Philippians 1:6).

The same Savior who said “Let the little children come” still receives all who come to Him in faith, whatever their age. If you yourself have never trusted Christ, or if you are unsure, turn from sin today and rest in Jesus alone—He died on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day so that whoever believes in Him will not perish but have eternal life (John 3:16).

question: Is it wrong for a Christian husband and wife to attend separate churches?
answer:
**No, it is not inherently sinful or forbidden in Scripture for a Christian husband and wife to attend separate churches**, though it is generally unwise and falls short of the unity God designed for marriage and the local church. Faithful Christians may disagree on the practical wisdom here as a matter of Christian liberty in a non-essential area of application (Romans 14:1-12), provided both are in sound gospel-preaching churches and neither is using it to avoid accountability or biblical headship.

Scripture presents husband and wife as “one flesh” (Genesis 2:24; Ephesians 5:31), called to profound spiritual oneness that mirrors Christ and the church. The husband is to lead sacrificially as head (Ephesians 5:23-28), which ordinarily includes guiding the family in shared worship, teaching, and church life. The New Testament also stresses the local church as the ordinary context for mutual edification, elders’ oversight, the ordinances, and not forsaking assembling together (Hebrews 10:24-25; Acts 2:42; 1 Corinthians 12). Attending separately can weaken family discipleship, shared fellowship, consistent teaching for children, and the husband’s ability to shepherd well, and it may signal or create drift in doctrine or priorities.

At the same time, the Bible never issues a direct command that spouses must hold membership or weekly attendance in the identical congregation. Legitimate (if imperfect) situations arise: differing convictions on secondary matters such as baptism or church governance, geographic or work constraints, a season of caring for an ailing parent in another fellowship, or one spouse already deeply rooted while the other is newly converted. In such cases the priority remains that both sit under faithful preaching of the gospel, practice the ordinary means of grace, and pursue holiness together at home.

The wiser path, pursued with patience and charity, is usually to labor toward the same local church. This strengthens oneness, models unity to children and outsiders, and allows the couple to serve, give, and submit to the same elders side by side. If doctrinal differences are the barrier, the husband should lovingly lead a careful study of Scripture (beginning with the gospel essentials you already share) rather than indefinitely divide. Prefer a church that clearly holds the core doctrines—the Trinity, the deity and humanity of Christ, justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, His atoning death and bodily resurrection, and the authority of Scripture—over secondary or stylistic preferences.

**A concrete next step:** Set aside time this week to pray together (ask the Lord for unity of mind and a shared local body), then openly discuss what each of you values in a church and what Scripture requires. If needed, invite counsel from mature elders or a pastor who knows you both. Seek a congregation where you can both thrive under the Word, and let the husband’s gentle leadership aim at that shared commitment for the good of your marriage and the glory of Christ.

question: What is the Druze religion?
answer:
The Druze religion is a monotheistic, esoteric ethnoreligious faith that emerged in the 11th century from Ismaili Shia Islam, primarily among communities in the Levant (especially modern-day Lebanon, Syria, and Israel). It centers on the absolute oneness of God (tawhid) and regards itself as a distinct path rather than a branch of Islam.

Its origins trace to the Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt around 1017 under the influence of the caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah and the teachings of Hamza ibn Ali. The Druze closed their community to converts shortly thereafter, so membership is by birth and the faith is practiced endogamously. Their sacred texts are the *Epistles of Wisdom* (*Rasa'il al-Hikma*), accessible mainly to an initiated religious elite known as the *uqqal* (“knowers”), while the majority *juhhal* (“uninitiated”) live by ethical principles without full doctrinal access. Core beliefs include strict monotheism, the transmigration of souls (reincarnation within the Druze community), a cyclical view of history, and reverence for a line of prophets and sages that includes figures such as Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, Muhammad, and also Greek philosophers like Plato and Pythagoras. Jethro (Shuʿayb) holds special honor. They reject polygamy, emphasize honesty, loyalty to the state in which they live, and mutual aid within the community, while maintaining secrecy about deeper doctrines.

From a Christian perspective, the Druze faith differs fundamentally from biblical teaching on several essential points. Scripture reveals one God eternally existing in three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14)—and presents Jesus Christ as truly God and truly man, whose once-for-all atoning death and bodily resurrection secure salvation by grace alone through faith alone (John 1:1–14; John 14:6; Romans 5:1; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The Bible does not teach reincarnation but rather that “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). Christians therefore hold that eternal life is found only in the finished work of Christ, not in an esoteric or cyclical system.

Faithful Christians can and should treat Druze neighbors with genuine respect, kindness, and neighbor-love (Matthew 22:39), while gently bearing witness to the unique person and work of Jesus when opportunity arises.

question: What is an invocation prayer?
answer:
An invocation prayer is a prayer that calls upon God at the beginning of a worship service, gathering, or event, asking for His presence, guidance, and blessing.

The word comes from the idea of “calling upon” the Lord, which Scripture presents as a normal and right response of God’s people. From the earliest days, people “began to call upon the name of the LORD” (Genesis 4:26). In corporate worship this often takes the form of an opening prayer that acknowledges God’s holiness, confesses dependence on Him, and invites the Holy Spirit’s work among those assembled.

Biblically, such prayers rest on God’s promise to draw near to those who draw near to Him (James 4:8) and on Jesus’ assurance that where two or three gather in His name, He is present (Matthew 18:20). They are not magic formulas that force God’s hand, but humble acts of faith that recognize His sovereignty and our need.

In practice, an invocation might briefly praise God for who He is, thank Him for the opportunity to meet, ask for open hearts to His Word, and seek the Spirit’s help so that everything done glorifies Christ. You can use this pattern yourself: before a Bible study, family meal, or church service, simply and sincerely call on the Father through the Son, trusting that He hears and delights to meet with His people.

question: What is the spiritual gift of prophecy?
answer:
The spiritual gift of prophecy is a Spirit-given ability to receive and proclaim a message from God that strengthens, encourages, and comforts the church, as described in 1 Corinthians 14:3: "But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort."

Continuationists argue that this gift continues today in forms of spontaneous, Spirit-prompted speech that may include fresh insight or mild predictive elements, always subject to testing by Scripture, because the New Testament nowhere explicitly states that prophecy would cease before Christ's return (1 Corinthians 13:8-12).

As a Reformed Baptist, I hold that the revelatory gift of prophecy ceased with the close of the apostolic age and the completion of the biblical canon, since the foundation of the church has already been laid by the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and Scripture is now sufficient for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16-17). What remains is the ordinary ministry of proclaiming and applying God's written Word with Spirit-empowered clarity and boldness.

In practice, this means we test every claimed "word from the Lord" strictly against Scripture, and we pursue the greater gifts of clear gospel preaching and mutual edification in the local church rather than seeking new revelations.

question: What does the Bible say about purification?
answer:
The Bible presents purification as God's gracious work of cleansing His people from ritual uncleanness and, far more deeply, from the defilement of sin, so they may draw near to Him in holiness. In the Old Testament this was pictured through ceremonial washings, sacrifices, and the blood of animals; in the New Testament it is fulfilled once for all through the blood of Jesus Christ and applied by the Holy Spirit.

Under the Mosaic covenant, purification laws guarded Israel's approach to a holy God. Contact with death, disease, childbirth, or certain bodily discharges rendered a person ceremonially unclean and required washing with water, waiting periods, and sometimes sacrifice (Leviticus 12–15; Numbers 19). On the Day of Atonement the high priest made atonement “to cleanse you, that you may be clean from all your sins before the Lord” (Leviticus 16:30). These rites were never merely external; they pointed to the deeper need for a pure heart. David prayed, “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow... Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:7, 10). The prophets promised a coming day when God Himself would sprinkle clean water, cleanse from idols, and give a new heart and Spirit (Ezekiel 36:25–27).

The New Testament declares that these shadows find their substance in Christ. His once-for-all sacrifice purifies the conscience in a way animal blood never could: “For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling those who are defiled sanctify for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!” (Hebrews 9:13–14). Believers are already clean through the word Jesus has spoken (John 15:3) and have their hearts purified by faith (Acts 15:9). Ongoing purification continues as we walk in the light: “the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin... If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:7, 9). This is the double grace of justification (declared righteous) and progressive sanctification (made actually holy).

Practically, then, purification is both a finished gift and a daily calling. Rest in the finished work of the cross; do not try to scrub your own guilt clean by religious effort. At the same time, draw near to God, resist the devil, cleanse your hands and purify your hearts (James 4:7–8), and let the Word and Spirit keep washing you (Ephesians 5:26). A simple next step is to open Psalm 51 or 1 John 1 in prayerful confession today, thanking Christ that His blood is enough, and asking the Spirit to expose and cleanse whatever still clings.

question: Does the Bible say that an increase in technology is a sign of the end times?
answer:
No, the Bible does not say that an increase in technology is a sign of the end times.

The passage most often cited for this idea is Daniel 12:4: "But you, Daniel, shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end. Many will roam to and fro, and knowledge will increase." Some interpreters take "knowledge will increase" and "roam to and fro" as predictions of modern technological advance and global travel. Others understand the verse more narrowly, as an increase in understanding of Daniel's own prophecies (or of Scripture generally) as the end draws near, rather than a reference to scientific or technical progress. The text itself does not mention tools, machines, or inventions.

Clear biblical descriptions of the last days focus on other realities: the worldwide proclamation of the gospel (Matthew 24:14), moral decay and self-love (2 Timothy 3:1-5), wars, famines, earthquakes, false christs, and persecution (Matthew 24:6-12), the rise of lawlessness, and the personal, bodily return of Christ to judge the living and the dead. Scripture never lists technological growth among the signs.

Faithful Christians have differed on how much weight to give modern developments when reading prophetic texts. Some see rapid technological change as consistent with a world racing toward the climax of history; others caution that equating every new invention with fulfilled prophecy goes beyond what the text warrants and can distract from the plain commands to watch, pray, and remain faithful. Because details of eschatological timing and secondary signs are not essential to the gospel, believers may hold these interpretive differences with charity and liberty (Romans 14:1-6).

What matters most is not charting technological trends but clinging to Christ, who died for our sins, was buried, and rose on the third day. Technology itself is a neutral tool that can spread the gospel or amplify evil; the call on every believer is the same in every age: repent, trust Jesus alone, and live ready for His return. A simple next step is to read Matthew 24–25 slowly this week and ask the Lord to shape your daily obedience around His clear words rather than speculative timelines.

question: What does the Bible say about caring for our old parents?
answer:
The Bible clearly commands God’s people to honor, respect, and practically care for their parents, including in old age, as a lasting duty of love that reflects God’s own faithful character.

This begins with the fifth commandment: “Honor your father and your mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you” (Exodus 20:12; see also Deuteronomy 5:16). The New Testament reaffirms this: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. ‘Honor your father and mother’ (which is the first commandment with a promise)” (Ephesians 6:1–2). Honoring parents is not limited to childhood obedience; it includes lifelong respect, provision, and care when they grow weak or dependent.

Jesus strongly rebuked religious leaders who used pious-sounding excuses to neglect this duty. He said, “For God said, ‘Honor your father and mother’ and ‘Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death.’ But you say that if anyone says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever you would have received from me is Corban’ (that is, a gift devoted to God), he is no longer permitted to do anything for his father or mother. Thus you nullify the word of God by your tradition” (Matthew 15:4–6; see also Mark 7:9–13). True devotion to God never cancels out concrete care for aging parents.

The apostle Paul makes the responsibility unmistakable for adult children and households: “But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and to repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God... If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:4, 8). Caring for elderly parents is presented as a basic expression of godliness and faith; neglecting them while claiming to follow Christ is a serious contradiction.

Jesus Himself modeled this care even while dying on the cross. Seeing His mother Mary, He entrusted her to the disciple John: “Woman, here is your son.” Then He said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” And from that hour the disciple took her into his home (John 19:26–27). In His agony He still arranged for her practical provision.

This duty flows from the broader biblical call to love, justice, and mercy. It images God’s fatherly care for His people and His command to defend the vulnerable. It is not mere sentiment but tangible support—financial help where needed, presence, protection from isolation, and advocacy—offered in humility and gratitude for the life and care they once gave us.

A simple next step is to examine your own situation prayerfully before the Lord: ask Him to show you one concrete way this week to honor your parents (a phone call, a visit, help with a need, or a conversation about their future care), and if the load feels heavy, involve mature believers in your local church for wisdom and shared support. God delights to give grace for this good work.

question: Does salvation affect more than just the afterlife?
answer:
Yes, salvation affects far more than the afterlife. It is God's complete rescue of sinners that begins the moment a person trusts in Christ and continues into eternity.

The Bible teaches that salvation includes **justification** (being declared righteous before God right now), **regeneration** (being born again with a new heart), **adoption** (becoming God's child), and **sanctification** (being progressively transformed into Christ's likeness in this life). Eternal life is not merely a future destination; Jesus defined it as knowing God now: "Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent" (John 17:3).

When someone turns from sin and trusts in Jesus Christ alone, who died on the cross as a substitute for sinners and rose bodily from the dead, several present realities take hold:
- Peace with God replaces condemnation (Romans 5:1).
- The Holy Spirit indwells the believer as a guarantee and helper (Ephesians 1:13–14; Romans 8:9–11).
- Old patterns of sin lose their mastery as the believer walks in newness of life (Romans 6:4–14; 2 Corinthians 5:17).
- Daily access to God in prayer and the comfort of His promises become normal (Hebrews 4:16; Philippians 4:6–7).
- Belonging to Christ's body, the church, provides fellowship, accountability, and mutual encouragement (1 Corinthians 12:12–27).

These present benefits flow from the same finished work of Christ that secures the future: freedom from final judgment and the hope of bodily resurrection and life in the new creation (Romans 8:1; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Revelation 21:1–4). Salvation is therefore past (we have been saved), present (we are being saved), and future (we will be saved).

If you have already trusted Christ, a simple next step is to thank God specifically today for one present fruit of salvation you are experiencing (peace, a changed desire, assurance) and ask Him to deepen your walk through regular time in Scripture and prayer with other believers. If you have not yet trusted Him, turn from sin and rely on Jesus alone who died and rose for you; He gives new life now and forever.

question: What is the difference between Judaism and Islam?
answer:
**Judaism and Islam are both monotheistic Abrahamic faiths that affirm one eternal Creator God and trace spiritual ancestry to Abraham, yet they differ sharply in their scriptures, prophets, view of Jesus, covenant focus, and practices.**

### Core Points of Contrast
- **Scriptures and Revelation**: Judaism holds the Tanakh (Hebrew Bible, especially the Torah given through Moses) as its foundational and enduring revelation, later interpreted through the Talmud and rabbinic tradition. Islam holds the Quran as the final, perfect, and uncorrupted word of God revealed to Muhammad, viewing earlier scriptures (Torah and Gospel) as originally divine but subsequently altered.
- **Prophets**: Judaism centers on the prophets of Israel (Abraham, Moses, David, Isaiah, and others), with Moses as the supreme lawgiver; it does not accept Muhammad. Islam accepts many biblical prophets (including Abraham, Moses, and Jesus) but teaches that Muhammad is the final “seal of the prophets,” bringing the complete and universal message.
- **Jesus**: Traditional Judaism does not accept Jesus as the promised Messiah or as divine; the Messiah is still awaited. Islam highly reveres Jesus (Isa) as a virgin-born prophet and messiah who performed miracles, yet insists he is not God, not the Son of God, and was not crucified (someone else was made to appear like him); he will return before the Day of Judgment.
- **Covenant, Law, and Community**: Judaism emphasizes God’s particular covenant with the people of Israel, expressed through the 613 mitzvot (commandments), circumcision, Sabbath, kosher laws, and festivals such as Passover and Yom Kippur. Islam presents a universal call to submission (the meaning of “Islam”) through the Five Pillars (confession of faith, ritual prayer, almsgiving, fasting in Ramadan, and pilgrimage to Mecca) and Sharia as guidance for all humanity.
- **Origins and History**: Judaism’s roots reach back to the patriarchal narratives and the Exodus (traditionally dated many centuries before Christ). Islam arose in 7th-century Arabia with Muhammad’s recitations and the rapid expansion of the early Muslim community.

Both faiths reject the Christian confession of the Trinity and of Jesus Christ as the eternal Son of God who became incarnate. They also differ from one another in calendar, worship language and direction, dietary details, and approaches to religious law versus ethnic-religious identity (Judaism historically tied to the Jewish people; Islam a multi-ethnic ummah).

### A Christian Perspective
Christians gratefully recognize the shared affirmation of one Creator and the moral seriousness found in both traditions, yet we hold that the full self-revelation of God is given in the person and work of Jesus Christ—truly God and truly man—who fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, died as an atoning sacrifice for sin, and rose bodily on the third day (see Isaiah 53; Luke 24:44–47; John 1:1–14; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The apostles proclaimed that “there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

If you are comparing these faiths out of personal spiritual searching, I encourage you to read the Gospel accounts (especially John or Luke) and ask God to show you who Jesus is. A simple next step is to open the New Testament, begin with the Gospel of John, and pray for light as you read. I am glad to discuss any specific point further or point you toward resources that compare the claims carefully and charitably.

question: What does it mean to trust in the person and work of Jesus Christ?
answer:
To trust in the person and work of Jesus Christ means to rely completely on who He is and what He has done for your salvation, rather than on your own goodness, efforts, or religious performance. This is the heart of justifying faith: receiving Christ alone as He is offered in the Gospel, by grace alone through faith alone.

### His Person
Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God, truly God and truly man (the hypostatic union). He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, lived a sinless life in perfect obedience to the Father, and is the one Mediator between God and humanity. Trusting His person means resting in His full deity, His real humanity, His sinless perfection, and His exclusive authority as Lord. Scripture declares, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:1, 14). And again, “There is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

### His Work
His work centers on His sacrificial death, burial, and bodily resurrection. On the cross He accomplished penal substitutionary atonement: He bore the wrath of God against sin in the place of sinners, satisfying divine justice and securing forgiveness and reconciliation. He died, was buried, and rose again on the third day in victory over sin and death, and He now reigns as the exalted Lord. Trusting His work means depending entirely on this finished accomplishment rather than adding your own merits. As Paul writes, “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). And, “He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness” (1 Peter 2:24).

### What Trust Looks Like
This trust is not mere intellectual agreement. It is a wholehearted turning from sin (repentance) and a resting of the soul upon Christ alone for acceptance with God. It is the empty hand that receives the free gift of righteousness. “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9). The result is justification: God declares the believing sinner righteous on the basis of Christ’s obedience and blood, and the believer is brought into peace with God (Romans 5:1).

You may wonder whether faith must be strong or perfect, or whether you need to clean yourself up first. The Bible’s answer is that even weak faith in a strong Savior saves, and Christ receives sinners who come as they are, then transforms them. Saving trust unites you to Christ so that His Spirit begins the lifelong work of sanctification, making you more like Him.

If you have never consciously placed your trust in Him, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. Speak to God directly in your own words, confessing your need and relying on Christ’s finished work. Then take the concrete next step of opening the Gospel of John and reading it slowly this week, asking God to show you more of who Jesus is, and connect with a local church that preaches this Gospel so you can grow among other believers.

question: Who was Plato? How did Platonism / Platonic thought influence society in Bible times?
answer:
**Plato** (c. 428–348 BC) was a Greek philosopher from Athens, a student of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle. He founded the Academy and wrote dialogues exploring metaphysics, ethics, politics, and knowledge. Central to his thought (Platonism) is the Theory of Forms: eternal, perfect, non-material ideals (such as Justice or Beauty) of which the physical world is only an imperfect shadow. He held a dualistic view of an immortal soul temporarily housed in a body, emphasized reason’s ascent to truth, and sketched an ideal state ruled by philosopher-kings in works like *The Republic*.

### Influence in Bible Times
Plato lived after most Old Testament events and writings, so direct influence on the Hebrew Scriptures is nonexistent. His ideas spread widely in the Hellenistic world after Alexander the Great (late 4th century BC), shaping education, rhetoric, and elite culture across the eastern Mediterranean—the setting of the later Old Testament period, intertestamental Judaism, and the New Testament.

In that environment:
- Greek philosophy, including Platonic elements, formed part of the intellectual air of cities like Alexandria, Athens, Ephesus, and Rome. Middle Platonism (a development of Plato’s ideas) was active in the first century AD.
- Some Hellenistic Jewish thinkers, most notably Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC–AD 50), blended Platonic concepts (immortality of the soul, allegorical reading, a transcendent God approached through intermediaries) with the Torah. This was a minority intellectual project, not mainstream synagogue Judaism.
- In the broader Greco-Roman society of New Testament times, Platonic dualism (spirit valued over matter), ideas of an afterlife for the soul, and the pursuit of virtue through reason influenced pagan ethics, mystery religions, and educated discourse. The apostles encountered this world directly (see Paul’s engagement with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers in Athens, Acts 17:16–34; the “wisdom” language addressed in 1 Corinthians 1–2).

Scripture itself is not derived from Platonism. The Bible’s teaching stands on its own revelatory authority: God created the material world good (Genesis 1); humans are embodied souls; sin is moral rebellion, not mere ignorance of Forms; salvation comes through the incarnate Son’s atoning death and bodily resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Luke 24:39–43), not escape from the body into pure intellect. Where early Christian writers later used familiar Greek vocabulary, they filled it with biblical content that often corrected Platonic assumptions (for example, the goodness of creation and the resurrection of the body versus soul-only immortality).

In short, Platonism helped shape the cultural and philosophical backdrop of the Hellenistic and Roman world in which the New Testament was written and first preached, but the gospel confronted and transformed that world rather than borrowing its core message. The apostles proclaimed Christ crucified and risen as God’s wisdom, distinct from the speculative systems of the age (1 Corinthians 1:20–25; Colossians 2:8).

question: Is a virtual/online communion service biblical?
answer:
**No, Scripture does not directly address virtual or online communion, since the Bible was written long before digital technology, so faithful Christians differ on whether it fits the biblical pattern of the Lord's Supper as a church ordinance.**

This is a non-essential matter of application and wisdom where believers may disagree in good conscience. The New Testament gives clear principles for the Supper but leaves room for judgment on modern circumstances (such as technology, isolation, or necessity), much like other questions of worship form that are not spelled out in exhaustive detail.

One common view holds that online communion can be legitimate. Proponents note that Christ is spiritually present to worthy receivers by faith (not confined to one physical room), that real-time video can let scattered believers share the same elements and words of institution together, and that pastoral care for shut-ins, the persecuted, or those in crisis may warrant it as an extension of the church's ministry.

Another historic and widely held view insists the normative biblical pattern is in-person observance when the local church gathers. The Apostle Paul repeatedly frames the Supper around the assembled body: "when you come together as a church," "when you come together to eat," and the call to "wait for one another" (1 Corinthians 11:18, 20, 33). The physical sharing of one bread and cup visibly portrays the unity of the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16-17) and occurs in the context of mutual accountability, discipline, and fellowship that a purely virtual setting can weaken.

Christian liberty applies here (Romans 14:1-6, 19). Neither side should despise or judge the other as unfaithful simply for reaching a different practical conclusion, provided the Supper is treated with reverence, self-examination, and clear gospel focus on Christ's body and blood given for sinners (1 Corinthians 11:23-29).

From a confessional Baptist perspective that treasures the spiritual presence of Christ in the Supper as a means of grace, the gathered local church remains the proper and ordinary setting. Online formats risk reducing a corporate ordinance to a private or loosely connected experience, so they are best avoided as a regular practice. In genuine hardship, the priority is still to pursue in-person fellowship as soon and as faithfully as possible.

If this question touches your own situation, talk with the elders of a local Bible-preaching church about how they fence and observe the Table. Examine your heart before participating in any form, remember that the Supper points us to Jesus' finished work on the cross and His bodily resurrection, and keep seeking the ordinary means of grace (Word, prayer, and gathered worship) where Christ meets His people.

question: Why do some churches thrive while others die?
answer:
**Churches thrive when they cling faithfully to Christ and His Word, and they wither when they drift from Him.** Numerical size is not the ultimate measure; spiritual vitality, Gospel fruit, and perseverance in the truth are. Jesus promised, “I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18), yet He also warned local congregations that He may remove their lampstand if they abandon Him (Revelation 2:5).

### Biblical Pattern
The early church in Acts thrived not through clever strategies but through devotion “to the apostles’ teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer” (Acts 2:42). The Lord added to their number as they proclaimed Christ crucified and risen, lived in holy community, and relied on the Spirit. By contrast, the letters to the seven churches in Revelation show decline when first love cools, doctrine is compromised, immorality is tolerated, or self-sufficiency replaces dependence on Christ (Revelation 2–3).

God is sovereign over the growth and pruning of His people, yet He ordinarily works through ordinary means: the faithful preaching of Scripture, prayer, the ordinances, disciplined membership, and Spirit-empowered witness.

### Common Reasons Churches Thrive
- **Christ-centered, Scripture-saturated ministry**: The whole counsel of God is taught with clarity and authority (2 Timothy 4:1–5; Acts 20:27). The Gospel of penal substitutionary atonement, justification by faith alone, and the call to repentance and faith remains central rather than secondary to felt needs, politics, or entertainment.
- **Prayerful dependence and holiness**: Leaders and members pursue progressive sanctification, practice church discipline lovingly when needed, and refuse to normalize what Scripture calls sin.
- **Biblical leadership and membership**: Qualified elders shepherd the flock (1 Timothy 3; Titus 1; 1 Peter 5:1–4), and members take their covenant responsibilities seriously—serving, giving, evangelizing, and bearing one another’s burdens.
- **Outward focus with inward depth**: Evangelism and missions flow from a healthy grasp of the Gospel, not from programs that replace it. Discipleship multiplies mature believers rather than consumers.
- **Unity in the essentials**: They guard the core doctrines (Trinity, deity of Christ, authority of Scripture, justification by faith, bodily resurrection, etc.) while extending charity in secondary and tertiary matters.

### Common Reasons Churches Die or Decline
- **Doctrinal drift or Gospel dilution**: When the authority of Scripture is softened, the uniqueness of Christ is blurred, or sin is redefined to fit culture, the church loses its saltiness (Matthew 5:13). Man-centered messages that avoid repentance produce temporary crowds but hollow discipleship.
- **Prayerlessness and self-reliance**: Activity replaces abiding in Christ (John 15:5).
- **Unaddressed sin, poor leadership, or consumerism**: Tolerated immorality, authoritarian or absentee elders, factionalism, or treating church as a product to consume rather than a body to serve slowly starves vitality (1 Corinthians 5; 3 John 9–10).
- **Loss of mission and love**: Inward focus, nostalgia for past glory, or bitterness replaces the Great Commission and the command to love one another (Matthew 28:18–20; John 13:34–35).
- **Neglect of the means of grace**: When the Word, prayer, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper are sidelined for novelty, spiritual life atrophies.

Faithful small churches can be deeply alive; large churches can be spiritually dying. God sometimes prunes or even removes lampstands in judgment or for the wider good of His kingdom. Yet He delights to revive those who return to Him.

### A Pastoral Word
If you are grieved over a struggling church, begin with humble self-examination and intercession rather than mere critique. Pray that Christ would be exalted, that elders would shepherd faithfully, that the Word would run and be glorified (2 Thessalonians 3:1), and that members would repent of apathy or sin. Consider how you yourself can strengthen what remains—by consistent presence, sacrificial service, gentle truth-speaking, and personal evangelism. Involve yourself under the shepherds God has placed there, or, if the church has abandoned the Gospel essentials, seek a biblically faithful congregation where you can be planted and fruitful.

The health of any local church ultimately rests on the risen Christ who walks among the lampstands. He is able to restore, purify, and cause His people to flourish for His glory. Turn to Him afresh, hold fast to the Gospel once for all delivered to the saints, and labor in hope. What specific aspect of church life are you seeing or carrying right now?

question: How much authority should a pastor have over a church?
answer:
A pastor (or elder) should exercise real spiritual authority to preach the Word, shepherd souls, and lead the church under Christ’s headship, yet that authority is always limited by Scripture, shared with a plurality of elders where possible, and exercised with the congregation’s involvement rather than as absolute personal control.

Many faithful Christians in episcopal or strongly hierarchical traditions argue that clear top-down authority (through bishops or a single senior pastor with broad unilateral power) best protects unity, doctrine, and effective oversight across churches, reflecting the apostolic pattern of ordered leadership.

In the Reformed Baptist understanding, Scripture points to elder-led congregational governance: pastors/elders hold genuine authority to rule and teach (1 Timothy 5:17; Hebrews 13:17; 1 Peter 5:1–3), yet the local congregation retains final responsibility under Christ for affirming leaders, maintaining membership, and guarding the gospel (Matthew 18:15–20; Acts 6:3–6; 2 Corinthians 2:6). This guards against both autocracy and pure democracy, keeps Christ as the sole Head of the church (Ephesians 1:22–23; Colossians 1:18), and treats pastoral authority as a stewardship of service rather than domination—an under-shepherd feeding the flock, not lording it over them. 

Practically, a healthy church will expect its pastors to lead decisively in doctrine and direction while remaining accountable to fellow elders, the congregation, and above all to the plain teaching of Scripture; if you are sensing tension over authority in your own church, the wise next step is to open the relevant passages with your elders and ask how your church’s practice seeks to honor both the call to obey leaders and the priesthood of all believers.

question: What is Luciferianism?
answer:
**Luciferianism** is a modern occult or philosophical system that venerates Lucifer (often identified with the “light-bearer” figure of Isaiah 14:12) as a symbol or deity of enlightenment, knowledge, individualism, rebellion against tyranny, and self-deification. It is distinct from, though sometimes overlapping with, Satanism: many Luciferians reject the idea of pure evil or devil-worship and instead portray Lucifer as a liberator who challenges divine authority and brings hidden wisdom to humanity. Forms range from theistic (literal veneration of a spiritual being) to atheistic/symbolic (Lucifer as an archetype of human potential).

### Biblical Assessment
Scripture presents a radically different picture. The figure popularly called Lucifer is the proud rebel who sought to exalt himself above God and was cast down:

> “How you have fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of the dawn! You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations. You said in your heart: ‘I will ascend to the heavens; I will raise my throne above the stars of God… I will make myself like the Most High.’ But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the Pit.” (Isaiah 14:12–15)

The New Testament identifies this adversary as Satan, the devil, “a murderer from the beginning” and “the father of lies” (John 8:44), “the god of this age” who blinds minds (2 Corinthians 4:4), and the serpent who deceives the whole world (Revelation 12:9). He does not liberate; he enslaves. He does not enlighten; he darkens. True light and knowledge come only from the triune God through Jesus Christ, “the true light who gives light to every man” (John 1:9) and in whom “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

Luciferianism therefore inverts the biblical order: it treats rebellion as virtue, self-exaltation as enlightenment, and the creature as equal or superior to the Creator. This is the original lie of Genesis 3:5 (“you will be like God”) and is spiritual idolatry. Scripture repeatedly warns against occult practices, consulting spirits, and any alliance with the powers of darkness (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Acts 19:18–19; 1 Corinthians 10:20–21; Ephesians 6:12).

### Pastoral Word
If you have encountered Luciferian ideas through books, online communities, music, or personal searching, know that curiosity about “hidden knowledge” is ancient and powerful, yet it leads away from the God who alone is light (1 John 1:5). The gospel offers something far better than self-deification: forgiveness of sin, reconciliation with the holy God, and genuine freedom through the crucified and risen Lord Jesus Christ. He died as a penal substitute for sinners, rose bodily on the third day, and now invites all people to turn from darkness and trust Him alone for salvation (Acts 26:18; Colossians 1:13–14).

Turn from every false light and trust in Jesus Christ, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. If this topic has stirred questions about spiritual reality, guilt, or meaning, consider reading the Gospel of John and speaking with a trusted pastor in a local Bible-believing church. The true Light still shines, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:5).

question: What is the satisfaction or commercial theory of the atonement?
answer:
The satisfaction theory of the atonement (sometimes called the commercial theory) teaches that Christ’s death pays the infinite debt human sin owes to God’s honor, thereby satisfying divine justice and restoring what sin has taken.

Anselm of Canterbury developed this view most clearly in his work *Cur Deus Homo* (“Why God Became Man”) around 1098. He reasoned that sin is not merely a moral failing but an infinite offense against the honor of the infinite God. Finite human beings cannot repay that debt, so the God-man Jesus Christ, living a perfect life and freely offering Himself, provides a satisfaction of infinite worth. In commercial language, the cross is the full payment that balances the scales of divine honor.

This theory differs from the earlier ransom theory (which focused on a payment to free captives from Satan) and from later moral-influence views (which treat the cross mainly as an inspiring example). It also stands distinct from penal substitutionary atonement, the view emphasized in the Reformation and historic Reformed confessions. Penal substitution holds that Christ bore the actual penal wrath and curse of the law in the place of sinners (Isaiah 53:5–6; Galatians 3:13; 2 Corinthians 5:21), not only satisfying honor but absorbing the judicial penalty our guilt deserved.

Scripture presents Christ’s death as a real propitiation that turns away God’s righteous wrath and as a substitutionary sacrifice that secures forgiveness (Romans 3:25–26; 1 John 2:2; Hebrews 9:26). The satisfaction theory rightly stresses the objective, Godward achievement of the cross and the necessity of a mediator who is both God and man. Yet the fuller biblical picture includes the penal dimension: Jesus was “pierced for our transgressions” and “crushed for our iniquities,” and “the LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:5–6).

In short, the satisfaction or commercial theory helpfully recovers the seriousness of sin against God’s honor and the sufficiency of Christ’s offering, while penal substitution more completely captures the biblical teaching that Christ endured the curse and judgment we deserved so that we might be justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him.

question: Who are the Shakers?
answer:
The Shakers, formally known as the United Society of Believers in Christ’s Second Appearing, were a small Protestant Christian sect that emerged in mid-18th-century England and flourished mainly in America. They began as an offshoot of the Quakers under the leadership of Ann Lee (often called “Mother Ann”), who emigrated to the American colonies in 1774 and taught that she embodied the second coming of Christ in female form.

They practiced communal living, pacifism, equality of the sexes in leadership, confession of sins, and complete celibacy, believing sexual relations to be the root of human sin. Because they did not marry or bear children, their communities grew only through converts and adopted orphans. Their worship included ecstatic shaking, dancing, and singing, which earned them the nickname “Shakers.” They became well known for simple, high-quality craftsmanship (especially furniture), architecture, and hymns. At their peak in the mid-1800s they numbered several thousand members across multiple villages; today only a tiny handful of adherents remain.

From the standpoint of historic orthodox Christianity, several core Shaker teachings stand outside the faith once for all delivered to the saints. Scripture reveals one God eternally existing in three co-equal persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14)—not a dual Father-Mother deity. Jesus Christ is the unique, eternal Son of God who took on human nature through the virgin birth, lived sinlessly, died as a substitutionary atonement, rose bodily, and will return personally and visibly (John 1:1–14; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Acts 1:11). No later figure, male or female, fulfills or replaces that unique incarnation and return. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not through communal perfection or celibacy (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Christians can appreciate the Shakers’ sincerity, industry, and rejection of worldliness while still holding firmly that their distinctive doctrines on God, Christ, and the second coming depart from the plain teaching of Scripture. If you are exploring their history, writings, or villages as a matter of interest, that can be done with clear biblical discernment.

question: What is the favor of God, and how can I get it?
answer:
**The favor of God is His gracious kindness, approval, and blessing extended to people—not because they earn it, but because of His merciful character.** Scripture often links this favor with the word *grace* (unmerited favor), as when Noah “found favor in the eyes of the Lord” (Genesis 6:8) or when Mary was greeted as one who had “found favor with God” (Luke 1:30).

God’s favor is not a vague feeling or a reward for moral performance. It flows from who He is: holy, loving, just, and full of mercy. In the fullest sense, His saving favor is shown in the Gospel. All people have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23), standing under His righteous wrath against sin. Yet God demonstrated His love by sending His Son: Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died on the cross as a substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, conquering sin and death. Through His finished work, sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone—not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:1–2).

You receive God’s favor by turning from sin (repentance) and trusting in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. This is not something you achieve by trying harder, performing religious duties, or cleaning yourself up first; it is a gift received by faith. Once you belong to Christ, you stand in God’s abiding favor as His adopted child, and He continues to show kindness through the means of grace—His Word, prayer, and the fellowship of a local church—while progressively sanctifying you by the Holy Spirit.

A simple next step is to open the Gospel of John and read it prayerfully this week, asking God to show you the truth about Jesus. Talk with a pastor or mature believer in a Bible-preaching church about what you are learning, and pray directly to God, confessing your need and asking Him for the faith to trust Christ. God’s favor is freely offered in His Son; receive it with an open hand.

question: What does it mean that Jesus is the Savior?
answer:
**Jesus is the Savior** means He is the only One who rescues sinners from the guilt, power, and eternal penalty of sin, reconciling them to God through His perfect life, substitutionary death, and bodily resurrection.

God is holy and just, and His wrath against sin is real (Habakkuk 1:13; Romans 1:18). Every person has sinned and stands separated from Him, unable to save themselves by good works or religious effort (Romans 3:23; Ephesians 2:1–3). Into this hopeless condition, God the Son took on full humanity through the virgin birth (the incarnation), lived a sinless life, and offered Himself as the atoning sacrifice. On the cross He bore the penalty our sins deserved in our place—this is called penal substitutionary atonement—so that God’s justice is satisfied and mercy is freely given (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily from the dead, proving His victory over sin and death and confirming that His sacrifice was accepted (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). He is now exalted as Lord and will return to judge the living and the dead.

Salvation is therefore by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. It is not earned; it is received as a gift when a person turns from sin and trusts Jesus as the sufficient Savior (Ephesians 2:8–9; John 14:6; Acts 4:12). Those who do are justified—declared righteous before God—and begin the lifelong work of sanctification by the Holy Spirit.

If you have never personally trusted Him, turn (repent) from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. A simple next step is to open the Gospel of John, read a chapter slowly each day, and ask God to show you the truth about His Son; then share what you are learning with a mature believer in a local church who can walk with you.

question: What is baby dedication? Is child / baby dedication biblical?
answer:
**Baby dedication** is a voluntary church ceremony in which parents publicly present their infant or young child to the Lord, commit themselves before God and the congregation to raise the child in the nurture and instruction of the Lord, and receive prayer from the church for the child’s salvation and the family’s faithfulness. It is not baptism, confers no saving grace, and does not make the child a church member.

### Is child/baby dedication biblical?
Scripture contains no command or prescribed New Testament ordinance called “baby dedication.” The practice is therefore a matter of Christian liberty rather than a required ordinance (Romans 14:5–6). Faithful Christians may participate or refrain without compromising orthodoxy.

Some draw illustrative parallels from passages such as Hannah presenting Samuel to the Lord (1 Samuel 1:27–28), Joseph and Mary presenting the infant Jesus at the temple according to the Law (Luke 2:22–24), or Jesus welcoming and blessing little children (Mark 10:13–16). These texts show parental devotion and Christ’s care for children, yet none institute a standing church ceremony identical to modern dedication. The clearer, abiding biblical call is that parents bring children up “in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4) and diligently teach God’s words in daily life (Deuteronomy 6:6–7).

In churches that practice believer’s baptism (credo-baptism) by immersion—the position of historic Baptists and the plain New Testament pattern of baptizing those who repent and believe (Acts 2:38–41; Acts 8:12; Matthew 28:19)—dedication serves as a public parental vow, not a substitute for the child’s own future baptism upon personal faith. It underscores that salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by parental act or ceremony (Ephesians 2:8–9). The child remains in need of the new birth and must one day personally repent and trust Christ’s atoning death and bodily resurrection.

**Pastoral counsel:** If you are a parent considering dedication, use it as a sober opportunity to examine your own walk with Christ, to pray specifically for your child’s salvation, and to ask your local church elders how the congregation will partner with you in gospel nurture. Whether or not you hold a formal service, the daily means of grace—Scripture, prayer, and faithful church involvement—remain the ordinary path God uses. If you have not yet trusted Christ yourself, turn from sin and believe in the Lord Jesus who died and rose for sinners; that is the foundation from which any godly parenting flows.

question: Will God continue to forgive you if you commit the same sin over and over again?
answer:
Yes, God will continue to forgive you when you genuinely repent and turn to Him, even for the same sin repeated many times. His forgiveness rests on the finished work of Christ, not on your ability to stop failing perfectly.

Scripture is clear and comforting on this. “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). The promise is not limited to first-time offenses. Jesus told Peter to forgive “not seven times, but seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18:22), showing the boundless mercy that reflects the Father’s heart. David sinned grievously and repeatedly, yet found cleansing when he cried out in true repentance (Psalm 51:1–2, Psalm 51:17). The blood of Jesus is sufficient for every confessed sin of those who trust Him.

At the same time, the Bible never treats grace as a license to keep sinning without a fight. “What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not! How can we who died to sin live in it any longer?” (Romans 6:1–2). Genuine faith produces progressive sanctification—the Holy Spirit steadily conforms us to Christ, even if the process is slow and marked by setbacks. Willful, unrepentant persistence in sin while claiming forgiveness is a dangerous presumption that Scripture warns against (Hebrews 10:26–27). True repentance includes both sorrow over sin and a Spirit-enabled desire to turn from it, even when we stumble again.

If you are weary from the same struggle, take heart: Christ intercedes for you, and those who are truly His will be kept by God’s power (Hebrews 7:25; 1 Peter 1:5). Your repeated failures do not exhaust His mercy when you keep coming back to the cross in faith.

A concrete next step: Confess the specific sin to God today without excuse, thank Him for Christ’s penal substitutionary atonement that fully covers it, and ask the Spirit for fresh strength. Then tell a trusted mature believer in your local church so you can receive prayer and accountability (James 5:16). Stay in the ordinary means of grace—Scripture, prayer, and gathered worship—where God normally grows His people.

question: Can monotheism be proven?
answer:
Yes, monotheism can be firmly established as true through the combined witness of reason, the created order, and especially the clear revelation of Scripture, though it is not a laboratory-style proof that forces belief against a hardened will.

The Bible presents monotheism as foundational reality, not a human theory. Deuteronomy 6:4 declares, “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One.” Isaiah 45:5 adds, “I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me.” This one God is not a bare unity but the triune God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—eternally existing as three persons who share the one divine essence (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14). That is historic Christian monotheism.

Philosophically, several classical arguments converge on a single necessary Being rather than many gods or none:
- The cosmological argument notes that everything that begins to exist has a cause. The universe began to exist; therefore it requires a cause outside itself that is eternal, immaterial, immensely powerful, and personal (able to choose to create). Multiple such ultimate beings would be unnecessary and would themselves require explanation, violating the principle of sufficient reason.
- The teleological argument observes the fine-tuned order and information in nature, which points to one intelligent Designer rather than competing deities with conflicting wills.
- The moral argument recognizes that objective moral duties and human conscience imply one ultimate moral Lawgiver; rival gods with clashing moral codes cannot ground universal right and wrong.

These lines of evidence do not “force” faith the way a math equation forces assent, because human beings suppress truth in unrighteousness (Romans 1:18–20). Yet they render atheism and polytheism far less coherent. Common objections—such as the claim that science has eliminated the need for God, or that many cultures have worshiped many gods—are understandable, yet they mistake methodological limits of science for metaphysical conclusions, and they overlook how Israel’s strict monotheism stood out sharply against the polytheistic Ancient Near East and was vindicated by fulfilled prophecy and the resurrection of Jesus.

Scripture itself treats the existence of the one true God as plain enough that all people are without excuse, while still calling for a response of trust. The fullest proof is not abstract argument alone but the historical self-revelation of this God in Jesus Christ—His incarnation, sinless life, substitutionary death on the cross for sinners, and bodily resurrection. Knowing that there is one God is meant to lead us to know Him personally through the Son.

If you are weighing these things, a concrete next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly this week, asking the living God to show you whether Jesus is the unique revelation of the one true God. Turn from self-reliance and sin, and trust in Christ alone who died and rose for you; He alone brings us to the Father. What particular aspect of monotheism or the evidence feels most pressing or doubtful to you right now?

question: What is impartation?
answer:
**Impartation**, in Christian usage, refers to the idea that a spiritual gift, anointing, blessing, or grace can be transferred or conferred from one believer to another, often through the laying on of hands, prayer, or close association.

The concept draws from several New Testament passages. Paul writes to Timothy, “Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given you through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders” (1 Timothy 4:14), and later urges him, “I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands” (2 Timothy 1:6). He also expresses a desire to visit the Roman believers “that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you” (Romans 1:11). In Acts, the apostles lay hands on new believers so they receive the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:17; Acts 19:6). These texts show God using human means, especially apostolic or elder ministry, in the distribution of gifts and empowerment in the early church.

Christians differ on how far this extends today. Continuationist traditions (especially Pentecostal and charismatic) often teach that impartation remains a normal means by which the Holy Spirit transfers gifts, anointing, or fresh empowerments through anointed leaders. Cessationist and many confessional Reformed believers hold that the extraordinary sign gifts and unique apostolic authority tied to those foundational moments have ceased, so modern claims of “imparting” miraculous gifts or special anointings go beyond the ordinary means of grace (the Word, sacraments/ordinances, and prayer). The laying on of hands continues in ordination and prayer for blessing, but it does not create a pipeline for transferring the Spirit’s power as a repeatable technique.

From a Reformed Baptist perspective shaped by the ordinary means of grace and the sufficiency of Scripture, true spiritual enablement comes from the Holy Spirit’s sovereign work through the gospel, not from a transferable substance or aura that one person can dispense to another. God may encourage and strengthen us through the prayers and fellowship of mature believers, yet every good gift remains His to give as He wills (1 Corinthians 12:11; James 1:17).

A concrete next step is to examine your own hunger for spiritual vitality in light of Scripture: read 1 Corinthians 12–14 and Ephesians 4:11–16 slowly this week, asking God to show you how He has already gifted you for the building up of Christ’s body in your local church, and then talk with a trusted elder or pastor about how those gifts can be recognized and used.

question: What is Atenism? Did either Judaism or Christianity borrow from Atenism?
answer:
**Atenism** was a short-lived religious reform in ancient Egypt under Pharaoh Akhenaten (Amenhotep IV, ruling roughly 1353–1336 BC). He elevated the Aten (the sun disk) as the sole deity to be officially worshiped, built a new capital at Akhetaten (Amarna), composed hymns to the Aten, and suppressed the traditional Egyptian pantheon and priesthoods, especially that of Amun. After his death the reforms were reversed, his monuments defaced, and polytheism restored. Atenism was essentially a royal, solar cult focused on the visible disk of the sun; it was monolatrous or henotheistic in practice rather than the absolute, ethical, personal monotheism of Scripture, and it left no lasting Egyptian tradition.

Neither Judaism nor Christianity borrowed from Atenism. The Bible presents the knowledge of the one true God as divine revelation from the beginning, not as an idea adapted from Egyptian royal religion. God is the eternal Creator who spoke to Adam, Noah, and Abraham centuries earlier (Genesis 1–12; Genesis 12:1–3), long before Akhenaten. He revealed Himself to Moses at the burning bush as “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14), the personal, covenant-keeping Lord who is spirit, holy, and transcendent—not a solar disk. The Exodus and the giving of the Law are presented as historical acts of this God, distinct in character, ethics, and worship from anything in the Amarna period.

Some modern theories note a rough chronological overlap (depending on one’s dating of the Exodus) and the shared rejection of many gods, then speculate about influence. Those theories remain speculative. Atenism collapsed immediately and was deliberately erased in Egypt; there is no textual, archaeological, or literary trail showing Hebrews adopting Atenist theology, liturgy, or hymns. The Great Hymn to the Aten has poetic parallels to parts of Psalm 104 in celebrating creation, yet the differences are decisive: the psalm addresses Yahweh as the personal, moral Sovereign who made all things by His word and who enters covenant with His people, not an impersonal sun-disk. Parallel language about nature is common across the ancient Near East and does not prove dependence.

Christianity stands on the same foundation. It confesses the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob fully revealed in Jesus Christ—truly God and truly man—whose death and bodily resurrection accomplish salvation by grace through faith (John 1:1–14; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Ephesians 2:8–9). That gospel did not emerge from Egyptian solar reform.

The living God has made Himself known in Scripture and climactically in His Son. If you are weighing claims about the origins of biblical faith, the consistent witness of the text is that He speaks, acts, and saves; He is not a borrowing from Pharaoh’s court. A simple next step is to read Genesis 1–12 and Exodus 3 slowly, asking what kind of God is actually described there, then compare that portrait with any ancient Near Eastern text.

question: What happens to babies and young children when they die? Where do I find the age of accountability in the Bible?
answer:
The Bible does not name a specific “age of accountability,” nor does it give a fixed number of years at which a child suddenly becomes morally responsible before God. That phrase is a later theological summary, not a verse you can turn to. What Scripture does teach is that every person inherits a sinful nature from Adam (Romans 5:12; Psalm 51:5) and that salvation is always by grace alone through the finished work of Christ alone. At the same time, God is perfectly just and abundantly merciful, and He alone knows the heart.

### Reasons for Hope Concerning Infants and Young Children
Several passages give strong biblical warrant for confidence that God receives little ones who die before they can consciously trust Christ:

- Jesus welcomed small children, declaring, “Let the little children come to Me and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these” (Mark 10:14). He did not treat them as outside His saving concern.
- After the death of his infant son, David said, “I will go to him, but he will not return to me” (2 Samuel 12:23). David expected conscious reunion with the child in the presence of God.
- Deuteronomy 1:39 distinguishes “your little ones… who do not yet know good from evil,” showing that God Himself recognizes a stage of life in which moral knowledge and accountable choice are not yet present.
- Romans 1:20 roots human culpability in the clear perception of God’s power and nature; infants and the severely impaired lack that capacity.

Because of these texts, historic Christian teaching has consistently held that God is able to apply the benefits of Christ’s atonement to those who never reach the point of outward, conscious faith. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (chapter 10) states it this way: elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where, and how He pleases. The same mercy extends to others incapable of being outwardly called by the Word.

### Two Main Historic Views
Faithful Christians have differed on the precise scope:

- Many hold that **all** who die in infancy are saved by Christ’s blood, pointing to God’s character, Jesus’ words about children, and the absence of any biblical example of an infant under condemnation.
- Others (including the Reformed Baptist tradition) affirm that **elect** infants are certainly saved, while leaving the identity of the elect in God’s secret counsel. This view guards the doctrines of original sin and particular redemption without limiting God’s freedom to save whom He will.

Both positions agree on the essentials: no one is saved by personal innocence or by a free pass; every saved person, infant or adult, is saved only through the penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ. No one is condemned for lacking a conscious opportunity they never possessed.

### Pastoral Next Step
If this question arises from the loss of a child, know that the God who numbers the hairs on every head (Matthew 10:30) is neither cruel nor indifferent. You may freely pour out your grief to Him, asking Him to comfort you with the same mercy you trust He has shown your little one. Stay close to a faithful local church where the Word is preached and where brothers and sisters can weep and hope with you. Read and pray through Psalm 23, 2 Samuel 12, and Mark 10, asking the Lord to settle your heart in His goodness and justice.

The Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25). We can rest there.

question: What is the Church of Spiritualism?
answer:
**The Church of Spiritualism** (often called Spiritualist churches or the Spiritualist movement) is a religious movement that teaches the living can communicate with the spirits of the dead, usually through mediums, séances, or psychic practices. It affirms an afterlife, personal spiritual progression, and that spirit messages can offer guidance, comfort, or proof of survival beyond death.

It emerged in the mid-19th century in the United States (commonly dated to the 1848 Fox sisters events in Hydesville, New York) and spread through organized bodies such as the National Spiritualist Association of Churches. Services often resemble Protestant gatherings with hymns, prayers, lectures, and “spirit messages” delivered by mediums. Core ideas typically include the fatherhood of God, the brotherhood of man, continuous existence of the soul, personal responsibility, and compensation/retribution in the afterlife for deeds done on earth. It is distinct from historic Christianity and from Spiritism (the Kardecist tradition more common in places like Brazil).

Many people are drawn to Spiritualism out of grief, a desire for contact with deceased loved ones, or dissatisfaction with what they see as rigid or silent traditional religion. The longing for comfort and certainty about the afterlife is understandable.

Scripture, however, clearly forbids attempting to contact the dead. God commanded Israel: “Let no one be found among you who... practices divination or conjury, interprets omens, practices sorcery, casts spells, consults a medium or familiar spirit, or inquires of the dead. For whoever does these things is detestable to the LORD” (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). Isaiah warns, “When they say to you, ‘Consult the spirits of the dead and the spiritists who whisper and mutter,’ should not a people consult their God? Should they consult the dead on behalf of the living?” (Isaiah 8:19). The Bible presents such practices as opening the door to deception; what appears as a departed human spirit can be a demonic counterfeit (see 2 Corinthians 11:14; 1 Timothy 4:1).

Historic Christianity teaches that the dead do not return to give messages (Luke 16:19–31; Hebrews 9:27). Our only reliable revelation about God, salvation, and eternity is the inspired Word of God, centered on Jesus Christ—truly God and truly man—who died as a substitutionary atonement for sin, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Forgiveness and eternal life come by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not through spirit contact or personal spiritual progression.

If you are wrestling with grief, questions about the afterlife, or curiosity about Spiritualism, the living Christ invites you to turn from every false refuge and trust Him alone for forgiveness and new life. A wise next step is to open the Gospel of John and read it prayerfully, asking God to show you the truth about His Son, and to speak with a pastor in a Bible-teaching local church who can walk with you.

question: What is Chrislam?
answer:
**Chrislam** is a modern syncretistic movement that attempts to blend Christianity and Islam into a single faith, treating the Bible and the Quran as complementary revelations and presenting Jesus and Muhammad as compatible messengers of the same God.

It emerged primarily in Nigeria in the 1970s (with groups such as the Chrislam Movement founded by Tela Tella and later expressions like the Oke Tude church), and similar ideas have appeared elsewhere under names promoting “Abrahamic” unity or dual religious identity. Adherents may attend both churches and mosques, mix Christian and Islamic prayers or festivals, and claim the two religions share the same essential truth.

Historic orthodox Christianity rejects Chrislam because it denies core doctrines essential to the faith. Scripture teaches that God is one Being eternally existing in three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14)—while Islam explicitly denies the Trinity and the deity of Christ. The Bible declares that Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, the eternal Word made flesh (John 1:1, 14; Colossians 2:9), conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, who died on the cross as a substitutionary atonement for sin and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Islam denies Christ’s deity, His crucifixion as saving atonement, and His resurrection in the Christian sense.

Jesus Himself said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). The apostles proclaimed, “There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by mixing revelations or prophets (Ephesians 2:8–9). Any system that places the Quran alongside Scripture as equal authority, or Muhammad alongside Christ as a necessary guide, departs from the gospel and the faith once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3).

Christians are called to love Muslim neighbors, live peaceably, and share the good news with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15; Matthew 5:44). Yet love does not require blurring the unique person and work of Jesus. True unity is found only in the biblical Christ who died and rose again.
